Brooks wrote this as a serious novel about institutional failure, geopolitical miscalculation, and human resilience dressed up as a zombie book, and the disguise is so effective that it keeps getting shelved in horror sections where half its audience will never find it. The 2013 Brad Pitt film shares a title and almost nothing else. Dads who picked this up expecting pulp entertainment found something considerably more interesting — a genuine argument about how societies collapse and what it takes to rebuild them. The most surprising novel on this list.

books.title: Master and Commander
books.author: Patrick O'Brian
books.blurb: In 1800, a young Royal Navy captain named Jack Aubrey meets a ship's surgeon and amateur naturalist named Stephen Maturin at a concert in Minorca, nearly comes to blows with him over the tempo of a Corelli piece, and then hires him as his ship's doctor. What follows across twenty novels is one of the great friendships in English literature and the most authentic portrait of life in Nelson's navy ever written. O'Brian spent thirty years getting the period detail so precisely right that naval historians treat the books as primary sources. W.W. Norton reissued the complete series in 1990 and the American dad cult built steadily through the decade. The 2003 Peter Weir film Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World starring Russell Crowe drove an enormous second wave of readership. Start here, then clear your calendar for the next nineteen.

books.title: The Broker
books.author: John Grisham
books.blurb: Joel Backman is a Washington super-lawyer and power broker who brokered the sale of a classified satellite surveillance system to parties unknown, got caught, and has spent six years in federal prison. On his last day in office the President pardons him — quietly, at the CIA's request — and the CIA immediately relocates him to Bologna, Italy under a new identity to see who tries to kill him first. Grisham spent most of his career in courtrooms and this is him stepping outside them — a straight international espionage thriller set almost entirely in northern Italy, with a middle-aged American learning the language, eating extraordinary food, and trying not to get assassinated. It's lighter and funnier than his early work and considerably more fun than his later courtroom procedurals. Grisham appears once more in this project via The Firm on the 90s Dad list.

books.title: Pillars of the Earth
books.author: Ken Follett
books.blurb: Twelfth century England. The old king is dead, two claimants are fighting for the throne, and a master builder named Tom wants more than anything to build a cathedral. Follett spent years researching medieval construction and it shows — the architectural detail is specific enough to feel like a manual and propulsive enough that you never notice you're learning anything. The novel is eight hundred pages and most dads who started it finished it in under two weeks, which is the real testament to what Follett pulled off. The 2010 Starz miniseries starring Ian McShane and Rufus Sewell drove an enormous wave of readership and is worth watching after. The sequel World Without End covers the same territory a century later during the Black Death and is nearly as good.

books.title: All the Light We Cannot See
books.author: Anthony Doerr
books.blurb: A blind French girl named Marie-Laure flees Paris with her father when the Germans invade, carrying a possibly legendary diamond. A German orphan named Werner builds radios and gets recruited into the Wehrmacht because of it. Their paths converge in the walled city of Saint-Malo during the Allied liberation in 1944. Doerr spent ten years writing this novel and it shows in every sentence — the prose is precise and luminous in ways that most popular fiction never attempts. It won the Pulitzer in 2015 and spent three years on the bestseller list, which means it cleared the bar of being both genuinely literary and genuinely readable. The 2023 Netflix adaptation is visually stunning. The literary outlier on this list, the same slot Catch-22 holds on the 60s list, operating in a completely different register.

books.title: Gone Girl
books.author: Gillian Flynn
books.blurb: Nick Dunne's wife Amy disappears on their fifth wedding anniversary. The media descends. Nick becomes the obvious suspect. Flynn tells the story in alternating voices — Nick in the present, Amy in diary entries — and the novel turns on itself so completely and so precisely that the less you know going in the better. Gone Girl launched an entire decade of unreliable narrator domestic thrillers and remains the best of them by a significant margin because Flynn is actually a serious novelist underneath the plot machinery. The 2014 David Fincher film starring Ben Affleck and Rosamund Pike is one of the finest adaptations on any of these lists — Fincher understood exactly what Flynn was doing and did it justice. The most purely surprising reading experience on this list.

books.title: The Martian
books.author: Andy Weir
books.blurb: Astronaut Mark Watney gets left behind on Mars when his crew evacuates during a storm and assumes he's dead. He's not dead. He's got a habitat, some equipment, a background in botany, and four years before the next Mars mission arrives. What follows is four hundred pages of one man solving consecutive impossible problems with math, duct tape, and a specific brand of profane optimism that makes Watney one of the most purely enjoyable protagonists on any of these lists. Weir self-published this in 2011 and it spread through engineering departments and dad circles by word of mouth before Crown picked it up in 2014. The 2015 Ridley Scott film starring Matt Damon is one of the rare adaptations that captures a book's tone perfectly. The most fun you will have with any novel on this list.

books.title: The Gray Man
books.author: Mark Greaney
books.blurb: Court Gentry is the CIA's most effective assassin. When the agency decides he's become a liability and puts a thirty-two million dollar contract on his head, every professional killer in the world comes after him simultaneously. Greaney launched one of the decade's best pure action series with this novel and built a devoted dad readership that worked through the backlist the way Reacher fans do — compulsively and in order. Where Reacher on the 2000s list is about a man with no past and no attachments, Gentry is a man trying to hold onto his conscience while doing unconscionable things. The 2022 Netflix film with Ryan Gosling and Chris Evans is entertaining if shallow. The books are considerably better and considerably more morally complicated than the film suggests.

books.title: Lone Survivor
books.author: Marcus Luttrell
books.blurb: In June 2005, a four-man SEAL reconnaissance team was inserted into the mountains of Afghanistan to locate a Taliban commander. Their position was compromised by goat herders. What followed — Operation Red Wings — became the largest loss of life in Navy SEAL history. Marcus Luttrell was the only man who made it out. Luttrell wrote this with Patrick Robinson and the result is both a straight combat memoir and a sustained argument about the rules of engagement that got his teammates killed — a politically honest perspective that the book doesn't soften and that you can agree or disagree with, but which deserves to be engaged seriously. The nonfiction outlier on this list. The 2013 Peter Berg film starring Mark Wahlberg drove enormous readership and is a faithful and brutal adaptation.

books.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
books.author: Stieg Larsson
books.blurb: A disgraced Swedish financial journalist is hired by an elderly industrialist to investigate the disappearance of his niece forty years earlier. The journalist's reluctant partner is Lisbeth Salander — a brilliant, damaged, socially catastrophic computer hacker who becomes one of the great characters in popular fiction of the decade. Larsson wrote three novels before dying of a heart attack in 2004 and never saw any of them published. The English translation arrived in America in 2008 and the David Fincher film in 2011 drove enormous dad readership throughout the decade. The Swedish original films with Noomi Rapace are also excellent and worth watching first. The novel is slow for the first hundred pages and then becomes completely impossible to put down. The two sequels maintain the quality, which almost never happens.

books.title: A Delicate Truth
books.author: John le Carré
books.blurb: A junior British diplomat named Toby Bell discovers that a covert operation he helped facilitate in Gibraltar three years earlier — a private military contractor hunting a terrorist arms dealer — went badly wrong and that everyone involved is pretending it didn't happen. Le Carré is on the 70s Dad list via Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, but this late-career novel is doing something different — the Cold War institutional betrayal he spent fifty years documenting has been privatized, and somehow that makes it worse. Written when le Carré was in his eighties, it's leaner and angrier than his earlier work. Nothing else on this list asks harder questions about what Western governments are actually doing in the war on terror or answers them with less comfort. The most politically uncomfortable novel on this list.

books.title: Where'd You Go, Bernadette
books.author: Maria Semple
books.blurb: Bernadette Fox is a brilliant, reclusive architect living in Seattle who hasn't worked in twenty years, feuds with her neighbors via passive-aggressive email, and outsources her entire life to a virtual assistant in India. When she disappears before a family trip to Antarctica, her fifteen-year-old daughter Bee assembles the story from emails, invoices, psychiatric evaluations, and FBI documents. Semple worked in television and it shows — the comic timing is immaculate, the satirical portrait of Seattle tech culture is sharp without being mean, and the Antarctica third act is genuine adventure. The humor entry on this list, the same slot True Grit holds on the 60s list. The 2019 Cate Blanchett film is decent but misses the book's structural cleverness almost entirely. Read it on a plane and try not to laugh out loud.

books.title: The Revenant
books.author: Michael Punke
books.blurb: In 1823, fur trapper Hugh Glass is mauled nearly to death by a grizzly bear in the Dakota Territory. His companions, unwilling to wait for him to die, take his rifle and knife and leave him. Glass spends the next months crawling, then walking, then running several hundred miles across the frontier to find them. Punke based this on a real historical incident and the novel reads like it — spare, cold, and completely unromanticized about what it actually took to survive in the American wilderness in the 1820s. Published in 2002 but almost nobody read it until Alejandro González Iñárritu's 2015 film starring Leonardo DiCaprio drove an enormous wave of dad readership. The film is visually staggering and faithful to the book's spirit. Under 300 pages. The pure adventure entry on this list.

books.title: The Goldfinch
books.author: Donna Tartt
books.blurb: Thirteen-year-old Theo Decker survives a bomb blast at a New York museum that kills his mother. Walking out of the rubble in shock, he takes a small Dutch masterpiece — a painting of a goldfinch, chained to its perch — and spends the next decade and a half being slowly destroyed by it. Tartt spent eleven years writing this novel and it shows — the prose is some of the most controlled and beautiful in American fiction of the decade, and the plot moves with the momentum of a thriller despite being eight hundred pages of genuinely literary fiction. It won the Pulitzer in 2014 and sold enormously, which means it passed the test of being both serious and readable. The 2019 film is a well-intentioned disaster. Read the book and skip the film entirely. The literary outlier on this list, the same slot Bonfire of the Vanities holds on the 90s list.

books.title: On the Road
books.author: Jack Kerouac
books.blurb: Sal Paradise and Dean Moriarty crisscross America in the late 1940s chasing something neither of them can name — freedom, experience, the secret to being alive. Kerouac wrote the novel in three weeks on a single continuous scroll of paper, and the prose reads like it: breathless, frenetic, occasionally exhausting. It's easy to dismiss this as a book that only means something when you're twenty-two and restless. Read it at thirty-five and it becomes something different — less a celebration of perpetual motion than a warning about it. Kerouac's characters are forever arriving somewhere new and never getting anywhere at all. The canonical road trip novel, the one every list has to start with, and the one that rewards rereading more than most people expect.

books.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
books.author: Robert Pirsig
books.blurb: A father and his son ride motorcycles from Minnesota to California. Pirsig uses the trip as a frame for one of the more ambitious philosophical arguments in American popular nonfiction — a sustained inquiry into the nature of Quality, what it means to do something well, and why that question matters more than most people realize. The philosophical tangents are genuinely demanding and occasionally bewildering. Push through them. Beneath the metaphysics is one of the most honest books ever written about craftsmanship, meaningful work, and what a man passes on to his son whether he intends to or not. Published in 1974 after being rejected by 121 publishers. It has sold five million copies since. The unexpected angle entry on this list — nobody comes to a road trip book expecting to think this hard.

books.title: Harry Truman's Excellent Adventure
books.author: Matthew Algeo
books.blurb: In the summer of 1953, a few months after leaving the White House, Harry Truman and his wife Bess climbed into their Chrysler and drove east with no Secret Service, no advance team, and no particular plan. Truman had always loved cars and America's roads, and he wanted, briefly, to be an ordinary citizen again. It didn't entirely work — they were recognized everywhere — but the Trumans pulled off something no former president has managed since. Algeo tells this forgotten story with warmth and real humor, weaving in the history of American highway culture alongside the trip itself. The shortest and most purely enjoyable book on this list. Under 250 pages. Clears in a weekend. The kind of book you press on someone the moment you finish it.

books.title: Travels With Charley
books.author: John Steinbeck
books.blurb: In 1960, Steinbeck was sixty years old, famous, and convinced he no longer knew the country he'd spent his life writing about. So he bought a truck, built a camper on the back, loaded his French poodle Charley into the passenger seat, and drove 10,000 miles around America to find out. The result is one of the great American travel narratives, even accounting for the fact that Steinbeck almost certainly embellished significant portions of it. What he captured honestly is the feeling of America on the cusp of enormous change — interstates reshaping the landscape, regional identities beginning to blur, the old ways quietly disappearing. His observations are funny, wistful, and occasionally melancholy in ways that feel more relevant now than when he wrote them. Read it before a long drive.

books.title: The Lincoln Highway
books.author: Amor Towles
books.blurb: It's 1954. Eighteen-year-old Emmett Watson is released from a juvenile work farm in Kansas and intends to drive west to California with his younger brother to start over. Two uninvited companions derail that plan entirely, sending the group east along the historic Lincoln Highway instead. Towles writes elegant, character-driven fiction — the prose is precise, the dialogue is sharp, and every detour the characters take becomes a moral choice as much as a navigational one. The road trip as a structure for examining what men tell themselves about who they are and where they're headed. Already flagged in our survey of 2020s dad reading as one of the defining novels of the decade. The most purely novelistic entry on this list and the most recent. Towles also wrote A Gentleman in Moscow, which operates on the same frequency in a completely different setting.

books.title: Blue Highways
books.author: William Least Heat-Moon
books.blurb: After his marriage ends and he loses his teaching job in the same week, Heat-Moon gets in his van and drives the back roads of America — the ones marked in blue on old maps, the routes the interstates bypassed and forgot. What he finds is a country invisible from the highway: small towns, diners, eccentric characters, landscapes that haven't changed in fifty years. Heat-Moon is a careful and patient observer, and Blue Highways is less a travel narrative than a sustained act of attention — what happens when you slow down enough to notice what's actually there. Published in 1982, beloved by a specific kind of serious reader ever since, and almost completely unknown outside that circle. The deep cut on this list. If you've never heard of it, that's exactly why it's here.

books.title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
books.author: Hunter S. Thompson
books.blurb: Raoul Duke and his attorney Dr. Gonzo drive from Los Angeles to Las Vegas in a rented Chevy loaded with an amount of controlled substances that Thompson lists, helpfully, in the first paragraph. The assignment is to cover a motorcycle race. The actual subject is the death of the American Dream, which Thompson pursues with a commitment to research that is either admirable or insane depending on your perspective. The funniest road trip book ever written and simultaneously one of the darkest — the comedy and the despair are inseparable, which is the point. The 1998 Terry Gilliam film with Johnny Depp captures the book's surface perfectly and about half of its depth. The gonzo entry on this list, the one that makes every other road trip narrative look slightly naïve by comparison. Not for everyone. Essential reading.

books.title: Bound for Glory
books.author: Woody Guthrie
books.blurb: Woody Guthrie's autobiography covers his years drifting across Depression-era America — Oklahoma to California and back, riding freight trains, hitchhiking, playing guitar in labor camps and migrant settlements, writing songs that are still being sung. Guthrie wrote the way he talked — direct, funny, unpretentious, and completely without self-pity about circumstances that would have broken most people. This is the primary source entry on this list, the account of the American road from someone who had no choice but to travel it, which makes it a fundamentally different kind of road book than anything else here. The 1976 Hal Ashby film starring David Carradine is worth watching after. If Kerouac's road trip is about seeking freedom and Thompson's is about losing it, Guthrie's is about surviving without it — and finding something worth singing about anyway.

books.title: Nomadland
books.author: Jessica Bruder
books.blurb: Linda May is in her sixties, has almost no retirement savings, and can't afford rent. So she buys a van, joins a loose community of older Americans living in vehicles, and follows the seasonal work circuit — Amazon warehouses in the fall, sugar beet harvests in the Midwest, national park campgrounds in the summer. Bruder spent years embedded with this community and the result is the most uncomfortable book on this list — a road trip narrative about people on the road not from choice but from economic necessity, in a country that has quietly stopped providing for its old. The 2020 Chloé Zhao film won the Academy Award for Best Picture and is excellent; the book is darker and more specific. The why it matters now entry on this list. Kerouac made the open road romantic. Bruder shows you what it actually costs.

books.title: Fun Home: A Family Tragicomic
books.author: Alison Bechdel
books.blurb: This groundbreaking and bestselling graphic memoir from Alison Bechdel is the story of her unpleasant and damaged relationship with her late father, Bruce. Bruce Bechdel worked as both an English teacher and funeral home in town, a place Alison and her family dubbed “the Fun Home.” Not long after Alison came out as a lesbian, she discovers her father is gay, and a few weeks after this revelation, Bruce passes away. The award-winning Fun Home took seven years to make, in part because of Bechdel’s fascinating artistic process. She photographs herself in poses for each human figure before drawing the panel.

books.title: Giovanni’s Room
books.author: James Baldwin
books.blurb: In this short, seminal novel by the great James Baldwin, David, an American expat living in Paris circa the 1950s, wrestles with his identity and his sexuality as his lover awaits the guillotine. In a heartbreaking study of character, Baldwin lays bare David’s denial and self-deception, illuminating how his inability to live authentically bears fatal consequences for the alluring and vulnerable Giovanni. Before the novel was published in 1956, Baldwin’s publisher encouraged him to burn the draft, fearing that he would alienate his readership with a story of gay love. Today, Giovanni’s Room is widely recognized as one of the best LGBTQ+ novels of all time—a one-sitting must-read for anyone seeking to understand the pain and power of love under threat.

books.title: Red, White & Royal Blue
books.author: Casey McQuiston
books.blurb: I hate to describe a novel as cute, but gosh darn it, Red, White & Royal Blue is capital-C “Cute.” And weirdly, I feel like that’s kind of a big deal for an LGBTQ+ novel, as so many of them end in tragedy. Here, you’ll find a sweet love story between the first son of the United States and his princely counterpart in the United Kingdom. If it sounds cheesy … OK, it kind of is, but it’s also a deeply moving read.

books.title: Under the Udala Trees
books.author: Chinelo Okparanta
books.blurb: Though Under the Udala Trees is certainly a devastating read (centering as it does on the Nigerian Civil War), it is also a beautiful one, especially as we watch protagonist Ijeoma fall in love with her best friend, Amina. Circumstances may rip the young lovers apart, but not before providing us with a series of strikingly intimate scenes between the pair.

books.title: Christopher and His Kind
books.author: Christopher Isherwood
books.blurb: Christopher and His Kind is a tender and funny memoir from writer Christopher Isherwood. The book focuses on the decade between 1929 and 1939 in which Isherwood ditched his staunch British upbringing for the decadent world of Weimar Berlin (first characterized in Goodbye to Berlin and, later, Cabaret). For those familiar with the writer’s other works, this memoir feels fresh and unapologetically queer in ways his earlier novels weren’t.

books.title: Dancer from the Dance
books.author: Andrew Holleran
books.blurb: Dancer from the Dance is a slightly pulpy, slightly dated novel about a group of queer folks in 1970s New York. It’s lush, evocative, and exuberant, perfectly encapsulating a very specific time and a very specific cast of city dwellers. If you like colorful characters, boozy party scenes, and finely detailed sex scenes, this is the book for you.

books.title: Gay New York
books.author: George Chauncey
books.blurb: A beast of a non-fiction tome, Gay New York tells the story of the burgeoning queer scene in 20th-century New York. Though it can read a bit dry in some places, the history is rich with details, names, major figures, stories, and scintillating gossip. It’s a must-read for folks looking to learn about the forebears of modern LGBTQ+ culture.

books.title: We Are Everywhere
books.author: Matthew Riemer
books.blurb: Adapted from the uber-popular @lgbt_history Instagram account (which you should follow immediately), We Are Everywhere offers a sweeping photographic history of the Queer Liberation Movement. In a word, it’s stunning and could make for a fantastic coffee table book. I especially like that it highlights and uplifts the trans and POC (people of color) voices that have been leading the movement since day one.

books.title: Stung with Love
books.author: Sappho
books.blurb: Ah, mesmerizing and prolific Sappho. The foremother of an entire literary tradition, this ancient poet wrote exquisite (and oftentimes explicit) verse about her many queer love affairs. Though her poems survive today mostly in fragments, Stung with Love does a fantastic job of bringing together the disparate pieces to form a cohesive portrait of the Greek writer.

books.title: Beyond Magenta
books.author: Susan Kuklin
books.blurb: In a collection of interviews with genderqueer and trans teens, author Susan Kuklin paints a compelling portrait of what it means to live outside the binary . The resultant Beyond Magenta is a fabulous read for folks looking to learn more about the T and + communities of the rainbow, as well as what it’s like to exist all over the gender spectrum. For more delicious book content, check out our guide to the coolest indie bookstores in the United States .

books.title: Little Women
books.author: Louisa May Alcott
books.blurb: The four March sisters — Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy — navigate the Civil War years with their father away at the front and their mother holding everything together. Jo is one of the great characters in American fiction: ambitious, funny, and perpetually at war with the conventions that try to contain her. Around 449 pages and the daughters entry on this list. The dad who reads this with his daughter is introducing her to a book that has shaped what American women think about ambition and independence for 150 years. Beth's illness and death in the second half should not be prepared for in advance.

books.title: Letters from Father Christmas
books.author: J.R.R. Tolkien
books.blurb: If you think about it, it should be obvious that J.R.R. Tolkien — master creator of fantasy worlds — was a big fan of Christmas and Santa Claus. And so every year from 1920 to 1942, an envelope arrived from Father Christmas for the Tolkien children, complete with a stamp from the North Pole. Inside would reveal not only a letter from the jolly old man himself, but also a series of drawings depicting that season’s rollicking mishaps and adventures. This was of course all conceived and executed by Tolkien himself. The letters tend to be short (sometimes Father Christmas is awfully busy), but every once in a while they would run multiple pages, describing Polar Bear’s hijinks, run-ins with Goblins trying to make a mess of the holiday, and more. This is a book to definitely get in print, and I recommend this edition particularly, as it not only includes the typed text of the letters, but also high-quality scans of the letters and drawings themselves so that you can see the real whimsy Tolkien put into them. This collection is fun for adults and kids alike and is sure to get you into that magical Christmas spirit. (Especially if you’ve just read Christmas: A Biography.) If the fantasy genre is your thing, Father Christmas also makes a pretty memorable appearance in C.S. Lewis’ The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe from the Narnia series.

books.title: The Snow Child
books.author: Eowyn Ivey
books.blurb: With some solid vacation time ahead of you, perhaps you’re just looking to get lost in an absorbing winter’s tale. We suggest The Snow Child, an imaginative debut novel rooted in a beloved Russian fairytale. In 1920s Alaska, where loneliness and despair cast a pall across the harsh frontier, a childless pioneer couple builds a child out of snow. The next morning, their snow child is gone, and in its place, an ethereal little girl has appeared. They come to love this surrogate child as their own daughter, but the mysteries of who she is and what she’s capable of loom large. Magical and mysterious, set in a spellbindingly beautiful and dangerous landscape, The Snow Child will seize your imagination and refuse to let go.

books.title: Christmas Days
books.author: Jeanette Winterson
books.blurb: From the visionary writer of Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit and Written On the Body come a dozen imaginative Christmas tales, each one suffused with Winterson’s infectious enthusiasm for the season. From mysteries to romances to ghost stories, there’s a welcome blend of nearly everything here, all of it elevated by Winterson’s distinctive prose. Recipes and recollections link each of the stories, making for a deeply personal keepsake. Feel free to dive in and out at will, rather than read cover to cover—you’ll discover something new every year.

books.title: Holidays on Ice
books.author: David Sedaris
books.blurb: Does it get any better than this seminal volume of side-splitting holiday essays? In the iconic “Santaland Diaries,” David Sedaris remembers his years as Crumpet the Elf, a Macy’s department store elf who finds nothing to celebrate in Santaland. In “Let It Snow,” he bottles the exuberance of childhood snow days, all while weaving a hilarious story about getting locked out of the house during a blizzard. Holidays On Ice is a contemporary classic—and the best medicine for anyone who gets a little misty during this time of year.

books.title: The Night Before Christmas
books.author: Nikolai Gogol
books.blurb: The godfather of Russian literature delivers a folktale unlike anything you’ve likely read before; to this day, it’s still read aloud on Christmas Eve to Russian and Ukrainian children. Gogol unspools the tale of the humble blacksmith Vakula, who goes toe to toe with the devil in a battle for the heart of Oksana, his village’s most beautiful woman. When the devil steals the moon and unleashes a snowstorm on Vakula’s village, Vakula fights back, making for a transporting Old World fairytale about good and evil. A Treasury of African American Christmas Stories, edited by Bettye Collier-Thomas Anthologized from Black newspapers and periodicals published between 1880 and 1953, these enchanting Christmas tales are drawn from the Black literary tradition that flowered after the Civil War. Ranging from tragedies to comedies, fables to romances, these stories tackle powerful themes of love, spirituality, racial identity, and so much more. If you’re lured in by writers you know and love, like Langston Hughes and W .E. B. Du Bois, go ahead and get comfortable, because you’re bound to discover so many more.

books.title: The Twelve Terrors of Christmas
books.author: John Updike
books.blurb: and Edward Gorey This gimlet-eyed little tome brings together two extraordinary minds: Updike, one of the twentieth century’s greatest writers, and Gorey, the legendary gothic illustrator. Together they take the piss out of “the happiest time of year,” revealing the hidden dark side of familiar holiday tropes, like the tick-ridden reindeer flying the friendly skies. And what’s the big deal about Santa, anyway? “If he’s such a big shot, why is he drawing unemployment for eleven months of the year?” Updike asks. When holiday stress has you at your breaking point, turn to The Twelve Terrors of Christmas for a restorative dose of levity.

books.title: Desert Solitaire
books.author: Edward Abbey
books.blurb: Abbey spent two seasons as a ranger at Arches National Monument in the late 1950s — before the paved roads and the visitor centers — and wrote this account of the Utah desert as both a place of extraordinary beauty and an argument about what industrial tourism was doing to the American wilderness. Published in 1968 and still the angriest book in the American nature writing tradition: Abbey had no patience for sentimentality about nature or for the national park machinery that was converting wilderness into a drive-through experience. Note the political argument throughout — this book is making a case about land use and the specific cost of comfort. Walden is the ancestor Abbey was consciously writing against; this is what Thoreau's philosophy looks like with the New England gentility removed. Around 269 pages. Cross-seeds with the American West History list.

books.title: The Snow Leopard
books.author: Peter Matthiessen
books.blurb: In 1973, Matthiessen accompanied the biologist George Schaller on a trek through the Himalayas of Nepal to the Tibetan plateau — ostensibly to observe the Himalayan blue sheep, actually to search for the nearly mythical snow leopard, and underneath both of those things to grieve the death of his wife from cancer the year before. Buddhism runs through the book as both intellectual framework and personal necessity. Around 338 pages and the international philosophical entry on this list: wilderness writing in which the landscape becomes a form of argument about impermanence, attention, and what a man does with grief when there is no adequate response to it. Cross-seeds with the Mountain & Rock Climbing list and the Books on Death & How to Face It list. The Snow Leopard is never seen until the final pages, and the ending is one of the great moments in American nature writing.

books.title: The Living
books.author: Annie Dillard
books.blurb: The only novel we recommend on this list because, well, because we can. If you think you know Annie Dillard from her Pulitzer-winning Pilgrim at Tinker Creek , buckle up. This novel, set during the founding days of Washington State, throws you headlong into a gripping portrayal of the rigors of frontier life. Following a family from the moment their boat runs aground on the desolate shore of Bellingham Bay, through the frequently life-threatening enterprise of settling in this monolithic landscape, to the frenzied overpopulation that came with the gold rush, this novel is sweeping in its scope and breathtaking in the stark beauty of its language. You’ll never look at a forest the same way again.

books.title: The World Without Us
books.author: Alan Weisman
books.blurb: This one’s a little weird but in a good way. Based on journalist Alan Weisman’s 2005 essay “Earth Without People,” this book predicts what would happen to the environment, natural and constructed, if all human life suddenly disappeared. How long would it take for cities to drown in forests and jungles? What would happen to landmarks like the Statue of Liberty or Mount Rushmore? What would really be the long-term effect of all the plastic we live with? Would new life forms ever come into being, and would they be anything like us? Weisman’s predictions aren’t just spitballing; he interviewed dozens of academics, scientists, and other experts to create his compelling portrait of what might very well happen if science fiction became the new reality.

books.title: Blood Orchid
books.author: Charles Bowden
books.blurb: Bowden reputedly walked out of defending his dissertation because he thought the review board was asking him stupid questions. That should give you an idea of where this guy is coming from, tone-wise. His writing style has been compared to the Old Testament in its prophetic fury, and nowhere is that better on display than in Blood Orchid , a book that carries the reader on a journey through both natural and urban wildernesses to uncover the brutal roots of American society.

books.title: The Living Great Lakes
books.author: Jerry Dennis
books.blurb: The Great Lakes contain a fifth of the entire world’s freshwater and their surface area is nearly as big as that of New England. Michigan native Jerry Dennis tells a natural, social, and personal history of these iconic American landmarks, offering observations from all seasons as well as perspectives from all the lifestyles defined by the lakes: fishermen, sailors, biologists, vacationers, and locals. This book offers a little of everything: evocative descriptions of the environment, entertaining portraits of local life, meditation on human responsibility, and celebration of everything beautiful about the Great Lakes.

books.title: The Hour of Land
books.author: Terry Tempest Williams
books.blurb: For those of us who can’t commit to an exhaustive tour of every piece of public land in the system, there is The Hour of Land , Terry Tempest Williams’ travelogue of visiting, well, not every park, but an appreciable and diverse range. From Grand Teton to Acadia, from Big Bend to the Gulf Islands, Williams paints a series of portraits that not only highlight the natural features that make these public lands precious but also relay the personal and political histories that make them significant in our national identity, past, and future.

books.title: The Pine Barrens
books.author: John McPhee
books.blurb: How do you pick just one John McPhee book to recommend? The guy cranked out natural writing faster than a Ford assembly line, and if you’ve read one, chances are you’ve read several. The scientific slant can get pretty dense, but get into the rhythm and you’ll find yourself falling in love with rock strata. The Pine Barrens is a deep dive into the history of New Jersey’s southern half, a 650,000-acre forest reserve known for quaking bogs, pyromaniacs, and a half-bat, half-kangaroo creature known as the Jersey Devil. In contrast with the highly urbanized northern half of the state, almost nobody lives in the Pine Barrens, and those who do are … well, a particular breed of folks. The setting will remind you of M. Night Shamalyan’s The Village. If it wasn’t for McPhee’s unimpeachable journalism, you’d think you were reading a Washington Irving fairy tale.

books.title: Deep Creek
books.author: Pam Houston
books.blurb: A personal account of how nature heals the deepest wounds, this memoir by Pam Houston are mainly set in the author’s mountain homestead in Colorado. Through wildfires and brutal winters, the never-ending work of running a ranch teaches the author about what ties us as humans to the earth, and how caring for the land comforts, teaches, and restores us. Love and loss, heartache and hope, reasons to give up and reasons never to give up — this book has it all. Bring Kleenex.

books.title: The One-Straw Revolution
books.author: Masanobu Fukuoka
books.blurb: Who says you need farmers to grow food? This book tells how scientist Masanobu Fukuoka tossed aside modern agriculture (and by modern, we mean the last several hundred years) to cultivate a garden in alignment with nature’s laws. For three decades, he developed a series of shockingly effective practices that were not only environmentally sustainable, but required practically no work from him. Fukuoka depicts farming as more than a means of producing food, but as a spiritual practice — the goal of cultivating the earth was really to cultivate ourselves as human beings. Foodies, tree-huggers, “green city” types, and spiritual seekers alike will love this one.

books.title: Make Prayers to the Raven
books.author: Richard K. Nelson
books.blurb: If you liked Into the Wild in your twenties, you’ll love Make Prayers to the Raven in your 30s. In it, anthropologist Richard K. Nelson documents the year he spent living among the Koyukon people of western Alaska. His account of their intimate relationship with the land shows the reality of how indigenous Americans nurture a mystical connection with the natural world. But rest assured, Nelson’s openly skeptical perspective keeps this from being a romanticized, “noble savage” type of story. It’s frank, detailed, and funny when you least expect it.

lists.title: 10 Best True Crime Books to Qui

books.title: In Cold Blood
books.author: Truman Capote
books.blurb: In November 1959, two men drove to a farmhouse in Holcomb, Kansas and killed the four members of the Clutter family for $40 and a radio. Capote spent six years reporting the story — the crime, the investigation, the killers' backgrounds, and the execution — and published it in 1966 as the book that invented literary true crime. The prose is as controlled as fiction, the portrait of Perry Smith is one of the most empathetic accounts of a killer ever written, and the moral argument about capital punishment runs underneath every page without ever surfacing as editorializing. Around 343 pages and the anchor entry on this list. Cross-seeds with the Halloween list. The reader who finishes this and wants more Capote goes to Music for Chameleons; the reader who wants more literary true crime starts with everything else on this list.

books.title: The Devil in the White City
books.author: Erik Larson
books.blurb: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago was the greatest engineering achievement of the nineteenth century — built in two years on a swamp, visited by 27 million people, and responsible for introducing Americans to the Ferris wheel, the dishwasher, and Cracker Jack. H.H. Holmes used it to lure victims to his hotel a mile from the fairgrounds, where he had installed a kiln, a gas chamber, and a dissection table. Larson tells both stories simultaneously and the effect is the most purely readable true crime book in print — the architecture and the murder feeding each other's momentum. Around 447 pages and the literary true crime entry on this list. Cross-seeds with the US History list, where it belongs equally. The reader who thinks history is dry will find Larson a reliable cure.

books.title: I'll Be Gone in the Dark
books.author: Michelle McNamara
books.blurb: McNamara spent years hunting the Golden State Killer from her laptop — a serial rapist and murderer who operated in California in the 1970s and 1980s and was never caught — and died in 2016 before she finished the book. Her husband Patton Oswalt and two researchers completed it from her notes, and the result is the most formally unusual entry on this list: as much a portrait of obsession as an investigation, as much about what cold cases do to the people who pursue them as about the killer himself. Around 360 pages. The unexpected angle entry on this list — McNamara's first-person voice makes the reader complicit in the hunt rather than merely a spectator. Published in 2018; the Golden State Killer was identified and arrested the same year, which gives the book an ending McNamara never wrote.

books.title: Helter Skelter
books.author: Vincent Bugliosi
books.blurb: Bugliosi prosecuted Charles Manson for the Tate-LaBianca murders and wrote the definitive account of the case: the killings, the investigation, the trial, and the specific mechanism by which Manson controlled the people around him without personally committing most of the murders. Around 528 pages and the iconic murder entry on this list — the Manson case is the most written-about crime of the twentieth century and this is the book that established everything subsequent writers have had to reckon with. Bugliosi is a prosecutor rather than a literary writer, which means the account is relentlessly evidentiary rather than atmospheric: he is building a case on every page, and the case is airtight. The reader who wants to understand how Manson actually worked — the psychology, the control mechanisms, the specific vulnerability of the people he recruited — comes here.

books.title: The Stranger Beside Me
books.author: Ann Rule
books.blurb: Rule was working the night shift at a Seattle crisis hotline in 1971 when she was paired with a charming, intelligent volunteer named Ted Bundy. She liked him. They became friends. She was already under contract to write a book about an unknown serial killer operating in the Pacific Northwest when Bundy was arrested, and the book she wrote is the definitive Bundy account precisely because she knew him before she knew what he was. Around 438 pages and the most unsettling entry on this list — not because of the murders, which are documented with appropriate restraint, but because Rule's portrait of Bundy-before-capture is so ordinary. The reader who finishes this will spend time afterward thinking about the specific difficulty of identifying dangerous people who are also genuinely pleasant, which is the question the book is actually asking.

books.title: My Dark Places
books.author: James Ellroy
books.blurb: James Ellroy is known the world over as a bestselling crime fiction author. The thing is, he has a reason for being obsessed with crime – in 1958, his mother was murdered and the crime was never solved. After over three decades of trying to get away from the crime that haunted him, Ellroy did an about-face and decided to try and solve it. My Dark Places is Ellroy’s account of what it was like to not only have one’s mother murdered but what it takes to try and solve a cold case that you are inextricably linked to.

books.title: Mindhunter
books.author: John Douglas
books.blurb: Douglas spent his career at the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit developing the methodology of criminal profiling — the systematic analysis of crime scenes, victimology, and offender behavior that made it possible to build a psychological portrait of an unknown killer before he was caught. This memoir covers the cases that built the methodology: the interviews with Manson, Bundy, and Ed Kemper in prison; the Atlanta child murders; the development of the organized-disorganized framework that became the foundation of modern forensic psychology. Around 370 pages and the serial killer forensics entry on this list. The television series Mindhunter is based on this book and is considerably less accurate than it suggests. The reader who wants to understand how the FBI actually catches serial killers — the specific intellectual work of it — comes here rather than to the screen adaptation.

books.title: The Road to Jonestown
books.author: Jeff Guinn
books.blurb: Jim Jones was a preacher from the middle of nowhere America who rose to prominence as the founder of Peoples Temple, a cult that would eventually end up at a compound, Jonestown, in the jungles of Guyana where over 900 followers would eventually be forced to swallow poison, killing themselves. The Road to Jonestown explores Jones’ life leading up to the mass murder, as well as the cultural context of the cult, and the aftermath, as told by survivors of the events.

books.title: Deviant: The Shocking True Story of Ed Gein, the Original Psycho
books.author: Harold Schechter
books.blurb: Like Ann Rule, Harold Schechter has made his career writing about some of the most prolific killers in history. In Deviant , Schechter does a deep dive into Ed Gein, the man who so many horror movie icons have been based on over the years (he was the inspiration for Psycho and The Texas Chainsaw Massacre , just to name a couple). Gein’s bizarre crimes are detailed in the book, and Schecter does a great job of recounting the events, providing not only details but the context for how and why they most likely occurred.

books.title: Homicide: The View From Inside the Yellow Tape
books.author: Cloyd Steiger
books.blurb: It shouldn’t be a surprise, but television and movies don’t always get crime “right.” Things are portrayed that don’t actually happen or time is squeezed together to make everything fit into a convenient 42-minute package. Homicide is former homicide detective Cloyd Steiger’s account of his time on the job in Seattle. The memoir provides a first-hand account of what it’s like to work a case. From the abhorrent to the darkly comical, Steiger does a great job of putting you in the cop car with him.

lists.title: 10 Best War Books to Add to You

books.title: The Kite Runner
books.author: Khaled Hosseini
books.blurb: Hosseini grew up in Kabul, left before the Soviet invasion, and wrote this novel about an Afghan boy who betrays his best friend and spends the rest of his life trying to redeem himself — against the backdrop of Afghanistan from the 1970s through the Taliban era and the post-2001 reconstruction. Already on the Redemption list, it belongs here too as the essential Afghan civilian perspective: the country before the wars that the GWOT is the latest chapter of, the Taliban's specific brutality documented by someone who knew the Afghanistan it destroyed, and the experience of a diaspora watching their homeland unmade from the outside. The reader who finishes Ghost Wars and Filkins with the strategic and military picture now has the book that gives it a human face and a human cost.

books.title: The Things They Carried
books.author: Tim O'Brien
books.blurb: O'Brien served as an infantryman in Vietnam and spent twenty years writing the book that processed what he experienced. The Things They Carried is not quite a novel, not quite a memoir, not quite a short story collection — it is something O'Brien invented because no existing form was adequate to what Vietnam required. The opening chapter, cataloguing the literal and metaphorical weight carried by the men of Alpha Company, is one of the great pieces of American prose of the 20th century. The book interrogates the relationship between truth and storytelling with a philosophical precision that never interrupts the narrative momentum, and the portrait of young American men discovering what their country has sent them to do is the definitive literary account of the war. Karl Marlantes's Matterhorn is the great Vietnam novel that this book overshadows only because O'Brien got there first — read both.

books.title: All Quiet on the Western Front
books.author: Erich Maria Remarque
books.blurb: The deliberate counterpoint to Storm of Steel and one of the best-selling novels of the 20th century. Paul Bäumer enlists at eighteen with his classmates, full of the rhetoric of glory and duty their teacher has fed them, and the Western Front systematically strips every illusion away. Remarque served on the front himself and the physical details — the mud, the rats, the gas, the specific sounds of an artillery barrage — carry the authority of a man who was there. The Nazis burned this book in 1933. Jünger declined to condemn the burning. Both facts are more instructive than any literary analysis. These two books should be read back to back, in either order, with the understanding that both men survived the same war and came back with irreconcilable accounts of what it meant.

books.title: War And Peace
books.author: Leo Tolstoy
books.blurb: Much of this epic tome is not set in conflict at all, but don’t worry, even the “peace” parts of War and Peace are plenty enjoyable. The scenes Tolstoy sets during Russia’s epic struggles against Napoleon’s forces in the early 19th century have some of the finest moments ever wrought on paper. You see in this novel heroism but also have myriad examples of the utter stupidity of warfare, and often Tolstoy manages to entwine these two aspects masterfully, such as when Prince Andrey Bolkonsky rises up after an injury and charges back into battle with a mighty “Hurrah!” At first, your heart surges and you charge alongside him, but in seconds you’re thinking: “Actually … what the hell are you doing?”

books.title: The Yellow Birds
books.author: Kevin Powers
books.blurb: Powers served as a machine gunner in Iraq in 2004-05, came home, got an MFA, and wrote this novel about a young soldier who makes a promise to a dead comrade's mother and then has to live with what keeping it costs him. The achievement is writing about the Iraq War with the same literary seriousness O'Brien brought to Vietnam — the specific moral weight of combat decisions, the specific damage that sustained violence does to a young man's interior life, and the specific difficulty of returning to a country that has already moved on. Won the Hemingway Foundation/PEN Award, finalist for the National Book Award. David Finkel's Thank You for Your Service documents the reintegration failure in non-fiction with equal honesty, and Phil Klay's short story collection Redeployment covers the full range of the Iraq experience from deployment through return — both belong on your reading list after this one.

books.title: The Red Badge of Courage
books.author: Stephen Crane
books.blurb: Crane was born half a decade after the Civil War ended and died without quite making it to age 40, but you’d never know either of those things from reading The Red Badge of Courage . Crane creates scenes of battle so realistic you would think them drawn from experience, and in his protagonist, Henry Fleming, Crane creates a character so real and nuanced you’d think the author had lived many more years to so fully experience the complexity that comes with being human. Fleming considers himself a coward for having fled a battlefield, but in him, we see a man who reflects much of ourselves.

books.title: The Time in Between
books.author: Maria Duenas
books.blurb: This novel is 600-plus pages long but manages to be a fast read nonetheless thanks to how quickly the story moves. That story centers on a girl named Sira whom we meet at 12 and follow as she briskly reaches adulthood just at the outset of the Spanish Civil War, which prompts her to leave her native Iberia and embark on a journey that winds through the rest of the 1930s and right into WWII, a conflict during which she takes on a potentiality deadly role as double agent for the Allies. As much period piece as war novel, the story does a fine job of painting the scenery of two of the 20th century’s worst conflicts.

books.title: Birdsong
books.author: Sebastian Faulks
books.blurb: If you don’t get enough WWI action from All Quiet on the Western Front , crack open Birdsong next. Much of the book is about love and its many complications, but WWI is at the heart of the novel and its many unflinching scenes of death and suffering will stay with you well after you’ve turned the last page. Much as with Stephen Crane’s Civil War writing, you will be impressed that Faulks was born after WWI and had no firsthand experience therein. (In fact, he was born after WWII.)

books.title: A Pale View of Hills
books.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
books.blurb: Kazuo Ishiguro won the Nobel Prize for Literature, and you can rest assured that his writing is superlative. This novel is actually set in London after World War II, but the main character’s many recollections of the war as it ravaged Japan plunge us back into that carnage again and again, and with a decidedly new point of view for most readers: The protagonist here is a Japanese woman, a far cry from the American fighting man through which we usually see

books.title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
books.author: Ernest Hemingway
books.blurb: Many mistakenly believe Hemingway to be a war veteran, but in reality, the closest he came to combat was being insignificantly wounded while volunteering as a Red Cross ambulance driver during the First World War. However lacking in firsthand experience, he would continue to revisit mortal conflict in both his fiction and his nonfiction. Like another book later in this list, Bell does have some basis in reality. It was researched by Hem himself while working as a war correspondent during the Spanish Civil War and going behind enemy lines to meet a man very much like his protagonist, Robert Jordan. The theme of one man against long odds not only betrays the writer's admiration for the trait but also for the cause itself, and he, like the late photographer Robert Capa and many others, deeply sympathized with the Second Spanish Republic's doomed fight against fascism. Its antagonists would prove a durable enemy, as the rise of the Nazi Germans during World War II would play a role in both Hemingway's own life and in that of his fiction.

books.title: Critique of Pure Reason
books.author: Immanuel Kant
books.blurb: Kant can be a real slog, but his attempt at understanding what aspects of human life are universal and how to create a systematic morality by extrapolating certain values endemic to the human experience were necessary for the trajectory of philosophy and ethics. His writing is dense and quite frankly very boring, but if you can make it through his tedious perseverations, everything that comes after will be much easier to digest.

books.title: Beyond Good And Evil
books.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
books.blurb: Things get really interesting with Nietzsche, who begins asking really big questions by turning the concepts he had inherited on their head: What if there’s actually no meaning to anything at all? What if the ideas around which Western civilization are constructed are illusory and ephemeral, based upon dogmatic ideas derived from obsolete Christian values? In the popular imaginary, Nietzche’s philosophy boils down to an angry rejection of all humanity, but in reality, his thoughts were far more complex.

books.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem
books.author: Hannah Arendt
books.blurb: Is there any meaning to this world following the brutality of the Holocaust? Hannah Arendt invents the concept of “the banality of evil” to explain how normal people wind up committing atrocities — and what it means for the political future of the world. Her close analysis of Nazi exterminator Adolf Eichmann’s trial explores the repugnant realities of mass genocide while asking important questions about the nature of justice.

books.title: Gender Trouble
books.author: Judith Butler
books.blurb: The contemporary LGBTQ movement owes a lot to Judith Butler, who asserted back in 1990 that gender is a social construction and has no real relation to biology. If gender is a series of performed acts rather than essential, biological facts, what does the history of gender reveal about the power relations between men, women, and people beyond the binary? Butler re-imagines the basic beliefs of feminist philosophy by questioning the extent to which the category of “woman” is even ideologically coherent.

books.title: Discipline and Punish
books.author: Michel Foucault
books.blurb: A noted BDSM enthusiast, Michel Foucault explores the history of criminal justice and realizes that most seemingly innocuous organizations — like hospitals and schools — actually resemble jails in formal structure. To what extent are our lives defined by competing, punitive, and ideological power relations, and to what extent have we all become prisoners to the hegemonic order? Foucault’s thinking would form the basis of what is called postmodern philosophy, a sub-field that questions enlightenment conclusions about universal human values.

books.title: Black Skin, White Masks
books.author: Frantz Fanon
books.blurb: Frantz Fanon is considered a key player in what would eventually become known as postcolonial philosophy, a sub-field that examines how human thought was shaped by the subjugation of racial minorities. In Fanon’s seminal text, he explores the impact of racism and slavery on the development of Western thinking and how it transformed the psyches of those who survived it.

books.title: Civilization and its Discontents
books.author: Sigmund Freud
books.blurb: Put all your preconceived notions about Freud aside for a moment — there are definitely some wacky ideas in this deeply influential extended essay but the points the father of psychoanalysis makes about the tension between individual identity and the structures of what we know as a society are far more prescient than some of his more outdated ideas about sexuality. There are some deep existential themes hidden beneath some of his more outlandish conclusions.

books.title: Simulacra and Simulation
books.author: Jean Baudrillard
books.blurb: Do you ever have an intense emotional experience and think, “Wow, I feel like I’m in a movie?” The bizarre dynamic between media and reality is the key focus of this French postmodernist’s musings. How has technology corrupted (our understanding of) reality? Is reality even a viable concept anymore? Baudrillard has more recently fallen out of favor amongst academics — it didn’t help that the Wachowskis completely misunderstood his ideas when they made The Matrix films — but his critiques about the omnipresence of television, cinema, and the early internet are more prescient than ever in the age of social media.

books.title: Philosophy in the Bedroom
books.author: Marquis De Sade
books.blurb: What does philosophy have to do with sex? The Marquis De Sade is one of history’s cruelest villains but his questions about the nature of pleasure remain pertinent to this day. Sade ultimately concludes that we owe no one kindness and that the greatest pleasures are derived from crime and violence. You might not agree, but his explorations of brutality and pure hedonism are necessary for disturbing key beliefs you might hold about the inherent values of goodness.

books.title: Plato's Writings
books.author: Plato
books.blurb: Four texts bundled as one entry because they form a complete argument: what philosophy is for, what it costs, and what kind of city would allow it to flourish. The death of Socrates sequence — Apology, Crito, Phaedo — covers his trial, his decision to refuse escape, and his final conversation before drinking hemlock, totaling around 100 pages and constituting the most dramatic philosophical document in the Western tradition. The Republic follows at around 360 pages: the foundational argument about justice, the ideal state, and the nature of the soul. The Grube-Reeve Hackett translations are the standard — rigorous without being archaic, and the versions most university courses now use as the baseline text.

books.title: The Shining
books.author: Stephen King
books.blurb: Stephen King has written many times about the ‘bad place,’ but never to more terrifying effect than in the Overlook Hotel. Possibly the most famous location in all of modern horror, it is not simply haunted, but more a battery for evil: a brick-and-mortar manifestation of demonic forces. When the Torrance family agrees to caretake the hotel over the winter, we know long before them that it will not turn out well. There will always be debate about the relative merits of Kubrick’s adaptation, but however much you appreciate his film, it has none of the tragedy or the warmth—and therefore none of the true terror—that King makes us feel for the Torrances. As the winter closes in and the hotel wakes up, King kneads the reader’s emotions like dough, showing us how much these people love each other, despite their underlying resentments. A final moment between Jack and his son elevates the book beyond anything Kubrick’s cold vision can offer. In future decades, when readers consider the enduring classics of the genre, The Shining will stand out as the perfect fusion of human drama and supernatural menace.

books.title: Beloved
books.author: Toni Morrison
books.blurb: A single chapter of Beloved contains more pain than most novels can manage from first page to last. That scene, in which Sethe murders her baby to spare her from a life of enslavement, is horribly, appallingly based in fact. Everything that follows is an attempt to bear the weight of personal and national trauma in fiction. The ghost story, it turns out, is the perfect vehicle. When a young woman appears bearing the name of Sethe’s dead infant, she seems to be a blessing. Soon, however, she begins to consume Sethe’s life, and tears open psychological wounds that the freed characters are desperately trying to hold closed. Morrison’s novel is lyrical and fragmentary (terms that tend to suggest an emphasis on style rather than satisfactory story), but Beloved offers both. It is a truly Great American Novel, both a literary testament to the suffering of millions and one of the most emotionally profound ghost stories ever composed.

books.title: The Haunting of Hill House
books.author: Shirley Jackson
books.blurb: novel opens with the greatest introduction to haunted architecture ever written: “Hill House, not sane, stood by itself against its hills, holding darkness within … and whatever walked there, walked alone.” It is an epochal moment in horror, the transition from a haunted house as a site of re-enacted trauma to a place that is inherently ill-intentioned. The ghosts of Hill House don’t make sense; “ghost” may not even be the correct word for whatever walks there. When Eleanor Vance joins a group of paranormal investigators interested in Hill House’s benighted reputation, there is the sense that she is not so much the victim of what occurs as the cause. In one novel, Jackson moved the ghost story from the realm of the moral and historical into the psychological. Over half a century later, The Haunting of Hill House remains as elusive as ever. It is still the benchmark by which all modern stories of the supernatural must be judged.

books.title: Experimental Film
books.author: Gemma Files
books.blurb: with her son’s autism diagnosis and axed from her teaching job, Lois Cairns’ life takes a turn for the worse when she becomes obsessed with a snippet of silent film that may hold the key to a century-old mystery. Lois believes the film proves that an eccentric socialite, who vanished under mysterious circumstances early in the 20th century, was in fact a pioneering female filmmaker. Lois’ all-consuming investigation into the mystery revitalizes her career, but puts hers and her family’s lives on the line, because the past doesn’t want to stay dead. Suspenseful and thrilling, Experimental Film meshes old world folklore and modern filmmaking to argue that every movie is a ghost story.

books.title: Mexican Gothic
books.author: Silvia Moreno-Garcia
books.blurb: Set in Mexico circa the 1950s, Mexican Gothic opens with an alarming letter: newlywed Catalina writes in desperation to her cousin Noemí, claiming that her husband is poisoning her, and that “fleshless things will not let me go.” Glamorous and tough Noemí travels to High Place, the countryside home of Catalina’s new husband, Virgil Doyle, to investigate. There she encounters the “essentially macabre” Doyle family: English aristocrats who colonized the mining town where High Place is situated, and their frightening patriarch, a dastardly eugenicist. Plagued by frightening visions of ghosts and violence, Noemí plots to make her escape with Catalina, but High Place won’t let them go so easily. In this dreadful and spellbinding novel, Moreno Garcia delivers Gothic horror at its finest, with a brilliant layer about the scourges of racism and colonialism.

books.title: Lincoln in the Bardo
books.author: George Saunders
books.blurb: One night in February 1862, as the Civil War ravaged the United States, Abraham Lincoln snuck into a tomb at Georgetown Cemetery to cradle the body of his 11-year-old son, recently dead of typhoid fever. This historical fact was the catalyst for Saunders’ miraculous imagination, turned loose on a fictive landscape both supernatural and historical. After his death, Willie Lincoln awakens in the bardo, a spiritual limbo between death and rebirth, where he encounters a veritable Greek chorus of spirits. Trapped in the bardo by his father’s grief, a confused and uncertain Willie is counseled by the spirits, who share their stories of love, death, and remembrance. Saunders links the overwhelming grief of one historically important man to the suffering and salvation of all in this polyphonic story of our shared humanity.

books.title: The Third Hotel
books.author: Laura vanden Berg
books.blurb: When Clare arrives in Havana to attend a horror film festival, she finds her husband Richard there, dressed in a white linen suit she’s never before seen. There’s one other problem: Richard was killed in a hit-and-run months ago. Grief-stricken and astonished, Clare follows Richard through the bustling streets of Havana, slipping into a dissociative state that sends her spiraling backward into the past. “Maybe a person became even more themselves when away, liberated from their usual present tense,” Clare wonders. In this slippery novel of liminal spaces and second selves, van den Berg weaves a lyric story about tourism, marriage, and grief.

books.title: Infidel
books.author: Pornsak Pichetshote
books.blurb: and Aaron Campbell In a run-down apartment building, Aisha, a Muslim woman living with her white fiancé and his daughter, begins having strange dreams about the building’s past. Not too long ago, a Muslim neighbor hoarding explosives in his apartment caused a catastrophic accident, leading to a rise in Islamophobia among the building’s multiracial residents. The explosion awakened hateful spirits that feed off xenophobia; now, Aisha must turn to her neighbors to defeat the ghosts tormenting her. In this modern reimagining of the haunted house trope, the authors illuminate chilling truths about the monsters that live within and without humanity.

books.title: The Removed
books.author: Brandon Hobson
books.blurb: Each year, the Echota family gathers for a bonfire to mark the Cherokee National Holiday and the memory of their son Ray-Ray, a teenager killed in a police shooting. On the fifteenth anniversary of Ray-Ray’s death, the annual bonfire sees the family members’ private grief transform into something elemental and new. As reality and the spirit world blur, Hobson braids the Echotas’ loss with the traumas of their heritage, ceding parts of the story to an ancestor named Tsala. Tsala recounts his own murder for his refusal to be removed from his homeland, while thousands of other Indigenous people forcibly walked the Trail of Tears. Steeped in magical realism and Cherokee lore, Hobson’s mystical story of injustices old and new is a poignant act of reclamation.

books.title: Horrorstor
books.author: Grady Hendrix
books.blurb: Who says ghosts have to live in creaky Victorian houses? In Hendrix’s wildly inventive Horrorstor, the scene is set at ORSK, an IKEA-esque furniture superstore. When strange acts of vandalism start occurring, three employees form an overnight patrol to investigate, but what they find defies belief: wannabe ghostbusters, an unhoused man living secretly in the store, and yes, real ghosts. As these scrappy patrollers square off against the sinister ghosts who want to imprison them in the showroom forever, Hendrix delivers both a palm-sweating horror story and a laugh-out-loud satire of retail. If you’ve ever wished an eternal curse on IKEA while constructing their furniture (who among us hasn’t?), then Horrorstor is the novel for you.

lists.title: 10 Great Books You Can Read in

books.title: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
books.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
books.blurb: wrote his famous novella in three days, burned it in despair, then rewrote it just as quickly. Something of that frenzy can still be felt in the pages after all these years. Despite the starched Victorian language, Jekyll and Hyde is a tale of gleeful depravity, unfettered urges, and extreme violence, even against a child. The story of transformation and duality is so famous that the title has entered our vocabulary, but the book is about far more than a mad scientist’s hubris. Stevenson’s novella comments on class, theology, and substance abuse, as well as the Freudian concept of the divided mind. No work of fiction has been adapted more often, and few have burrowed so deeply into the public consciousness.

books.title: The Old Man and the Sea
books.author: Ernest Hemingway
books.blurb: When you first read this book, you were much too young. Back then, you were worried about getting an A on your essay and where you would go to college and who you would ask to prom. This time around, don't search for themes or ponder the significance of colors — as Hemingway himself said, the sea is just the sea, the sharks are just sharks, and, "All the symbolism that people say is shit." Let the plight of the old fisherman, who finds his once-in-a-lifetime marlin torn to nothing, echo around your head. Know that it was Hemingway's last novel published in his lifetime, and enjoy that finality. Praised by just above everyone from critics to competitors, it was viewed by Hemingway himself as his finest work. It's a short book, and one that appears in many all-time novel lists (despite the fact that it's technically a novella). But as a reintroduction to Hemingway, there are few of his works that require as little a commitment, nor are there many that will stay with you as long.

books.title: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
books.author: Neil Gaiman
books.blurb: OK, at about 180 pages (in the hardcover edition), you will probably have to get up to relieve yourself and/or get a snack while reading The Ocean at the End of the Lane, so maybe one sitting is a bit of a stretch, but most readers will easily polish this book off in one day. The book is something of a fairy take for adults, though told through a child’s eyes. It would be easy to spoil this book’s twists by speaking much on the plot or characters, so suffice it to say the writing is lyrical and evocative, creating vivid images in the reader’s mind.

books.title: Train Dreams
books.author: Denis Johnson
books.blurb: Train Dreams is a strange book. Its prose is crisp and clear and easy to understand, and the protagonist, Robert Grainer, is a rather simple man who lacks any profound sense of curiosity or wonder. Yet the story is nonetheless gripping and mysterious and the journey of the Grainer that of the proverbial hero nonetheless. Set in the American West near the turn of the last century, the landscapes of the novel are at times bleak, at times lurid, and the book feels at times like a raw and real portrait of a time gone by, like dark, unsettling fantasy.

books.title: Slaughterhouse-Five
books.author: Kurt Vonnegut
books.blurb: If you have never read Vonnegut, start with this book. If you read it in one sitting, immediately move on to Cat’s Cradle, Mother Night, God Bless You, Mr. Rosewater, and keep on cruising through this hilarious, odd, and eminently readable writer’s oeuvre. If you don’t like Slaughterhouse Five , then Vonnegut just isn’t for you, and that’s OK. His style is at times playful, often macabre, sometimes puerile, and always well-paced. Like many Vonnegut books, Slaughterhouse-Five tells its story in fragments, hopping from place to place and time to time, and veering in and out of reality. Like only a handful of his books , this one was largely inspired by the horrors he saw first hand as a soldier in WWII. At a bit over 200 pages, it’s the longest on our list, but having read it three or four times already, and once on a single flight, it deserves its spot.

books.title: The Great Gatsby
books.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
books.blurb: The Disenchanted and The Crack Up are both about the fall of F. Scott Fitzgerald, one from the first person perspective and the other from the fictional eyes of a friend watching his hero fall to pieces — just like the story of Gatsby itself. The Crack Up is a collection of essays, many of which are off-topic, but they had to be — a person cannot look so directly and honestly on their own broken soul without turning away at times. Fitzgerald’s Crack Up has always been illustrative to me and it’s something I’ve thought a lot about. I call it the Second Act Fallacy, and you pity and feel for a man with so much talent and wisdom who was helpless to apply it to himself. Liber medicina animi — a book is the soul’s medicine.One of the iconic classics of American literature about wealth, desire, and disillusionment in the Jazz Age.

books.title: Fahrenheit 451
books.author: Ray Bradbury
books.blurb: The third of the great mid-century dystopian novels, and the most American. Guy Montag is a fireman — in the world of this novel, firemen start fires rather than extinguish them, burning books in a society that has decided that literature causes unhappiness. Bradbury wrote it in nine days on a rented typewriter in the basement of a library, paying ten cents per half hour, and the urgency of that composition is on every page. It is the shortest and most emotionally direct of the three great dystopias, and the one most explicitly about what is lost when a society stops reading.

books.title: Of Mice and Men
books.author: John Steinbeck
books.blurb: Maybe you were scared off after measuring the thickness of Grapes of Wrath. Start here. Or maybe you're a longtime Steinbeck fan and know his bibliography inside and out. Still start here. While the author published 33 books over his life, many, including Mice, were in novella form, which falls in length somewhere between a long short story and a short novel. Published in 1937, the story follows George Milton and Lennie Small, two out-of-work drifters during the Great Depression looking for work in the agriculturally rich area of Central California. It's sympathetic to its luckless characters and tender with their hopeful outlook, despite the fact that all the cards stacked against them. Steinbeck is, as always, rooting for the little man. Beyond its elucidation of themes and sympathies that remain the author's life and work, the book has been adapted to theater, TV, and cinema, making it a must-read.

books.title: The Stranger
books.author: Albert Camus
books.blurb: Meursault attends his mother's funeral, feels nothing, shoots an Arab on a beach four days later, and is sentenced to death less for the killing than for his failure to grieve properly. At 123 pages, this is the entry point for a reader who has never encountered world fiction — short enough to read in one sitting, strange enough to stay considerably longer. Camus was arguing that the universe is indifferent to human suffering and that the only honest response is to live without illusion, which is either liberating or terrifying depending on your starting position. Note: Camus is arguing a case from an absurdist-atheist position. The short entry on this list and the canonical one. Cross-references to the Books on Death & How to Face It list, where the same territory is covered from different angles.

books.title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
books.author: Leo Tolstoy
books.blurb: Tolstoy's 1886 novella follows a Russian judge who discovers he is dying and spends his final weeks confronting the specific emptiness of a well-lived conventional life — the career advanced, the correct marriage made, the correct furniture purchased, and none of it any use at all in the room where he is dying alone. Around 86 pages and the fiction entry on this list: the existentialist confrontation with death rendered in the most concentrated literary form available, written by a man who spent the second half of his own life in genuine terror of dying. The AoM reader who has never read Tolstoy should start here — it costs two hours and produces the specific uncomfortable question of whether the life you are building is the life you would want to have lived. Man's Search for Meaning is the philosophical companion that provides the answer Tolstoy's Ivan never finds.

books.title: Shoeless Joe
books.author: W.P. Kinsella
books.blurb: The novel that became Field of Dreams. An Iowa farmer hears a voice telling him to build a baseball diamond in his cornfield, and he does it. What follows is a story about baseball and magic and fathers and sons and the specifically American belief that the past is never entirely gone — that the things and the people you loved are still out there somewhere in the summer dark, waiting to play one more inning. Late summer, corn as far as you can see, baseball in the pennant stretch: this is the book that belongs at the end of August more than any other.

books.title: Babe: The Legend Comes to Life
books.author: Robert Creamer
books.blurb: The gold standard of baseball biography and the standard by which every subsequent Ruth account is measured and found wanting. Creamer covered baseball for Sports Illustrated for decades and spent years on this, published in 1974.
