books.blurb: A gleeful romp this is not, but mercifully, it’s only essay-length and gets right down to business answering a question Virginia Woolf once posed: “How are we to prevent war?” You’ll wonder, after reading it, how you ever looked at war photography before. —Kelly Stout

books.title: A River Runs Through It
books.author: Norman Maclean
books.blurb: Around 104 pages covering Maclean's Montana childhood, his relationship with his brother, and the specific beauty of fly fishing on the Blackfoot River — and the most celebrated account of craft as a way of life in American literature. The short entry and the unexpected angle simultaneously: a book that looks like a fishing story and turns out to be one of the great American meditations on the relationship between skill, love, and loss. The University of Chicago Press rejected it — its director told Maclean they didn't publish fiction by people over seventy. He was wrong on both counts. John Gierach's Trout Bum covers a life organized around fly fishing at around 192 pages and is the right companion for the reader who wants the craft documented at length rather than distilled to its essence. Cross-seeds with the Hunting & Fishing reading on this project.

books.title: The Fellowship of the Ring
books.author: J.R.R. Tolkien
books.blurb: These four books are making the list as one, because they’re really a single, epic story. You’ve no doubt seen the movies, which are great, but the books are even better. Follow Frodo Baggins and his trustworthy friend Samwise Gamgee and learn about friendship, loyalty, dedication to a good cause, and many other manly virtues. You’ll also find one of the wisest characters in literature in Gandalf. J.R.R. Tolkien had one of the greatest imaginations in the history of literature and created an entire universe, complete with new languages, maps of various lands, and even histories of how these lands came to be. No other author has come close to the world-making capabilities of Tolkien, which alone makes the series worth reading. A small fellowship bears a corrupting ring toward Mordor; loyalty and sacrifice drive the quest.

books.title: The Two Towers
books.author: J.R.R. Tolkien
books.blurb: These four books are making the list as one, because they’re really a single, epic story. You’ve no doubt seen the movies, which are great, but the books are even better. Follow Frodo Baggins and his trustworthy friend Samwise Gamgee and learn about friendship, loyalty, dedication to a good cause, and many other manly virtues. You’ll also find one of the wisest characters in literature in Gandalf. J.R.R. Tolkien had one of the greatest imaginations in the history of literature and created an entire universe, complete with new languages, maps of various lands, and even histories of how these lands came to be. No other author has come close to the world-making capabilities of Tolkien, which alone makes the series worth reading. A small fellowship bears a corrupting ring toward Mordor; loyalty and sacrifice drive the quest.

books.title: The Return of the King
books.author: J.R.R. Tolkien
books.blurb: These four books are making the list as one, because they’re really a single, epic story. You’ve no doubt seen the movies, which are great, but the books are even better. Follow Frodo Baggins and his trustworthy friend Samwise Gamgee and learn about friendship, loyalty, dedication to a good cause, and many other manly virtues. You’ll also find one of the wisest characters in literature in Gandalf. J.R.R. Tolkien had one of the greatest imaginations in the history of literature and created an entire universe, complete with new languages, maps of various lands, and even histories of how these lands came to be. No other author has come close to the world-making capabilities of Tolkien, which alone makes the series worth reading. A small fellowship bears a corrupting ring toward Mordor; loyalty and sacrifice drive the quest.

books.title: Moby-Dick
books.author: Herman Melville
books.blurb: Melville published this in 1851 to commercial failure and died thinking it a minor work. It is the greatest American novel and one of the most demanding: Captain Ahab pursues the white whale across three oceans with a monomania that destroys everyone around him, and Melville uses the pursuit to examine obsession, fate, masculinity, God, and the specific American tendency to mistake personal vengeance for cosmic destiny. The whale chapters — eighty pages of cetology, anatomy, and commercial whaling — are the price of admission, not a flaw: they are what makes the Pequod feel like a real ship and the ocean feel like a real ocean. Around 600 pages. The difficult canonical entry on this list. The reader who finishes it will understand why it was worth the effort; the reader who doesn't will have a nagging sense of unfinished business for the rest of his life.

books.title: Charlotte's Web
books.author: E.B. White
books.blurb: Wilbur the pig is going to be slaughtered in the autumn and Charlotte the spider decides to save him by weaving words into her web. She does save him. Then she dies, because spiders do. White published this in 1952 and it remains the most honest account of death and friendship in children's literature — not softened, not explained away, just documented with the precision of a man who loved both the farm and the truth about what happens on farms. Around 184 pages. The book that teaches children what friendship costs before the lesson becomes necessary in real life.

books.title: In Cold Blood
books.author: Truman Capote
books.blurb: In November 1959, two men drove to a farmhouse in Holcomb, Kansas and killed the four members of the Clutter family for $40 and a radio. Capote spent six years reporting the story — the crime, the investigation, the killers' backgrounds, and the execution — and published it in 1966 as the book that invented literary true crime. The prose is as controlled as fiction, the portrait of Perry Smith is one of the most empathetic accounts of a killer ever written, and the moral argument about capital punishment runs underneath every page without ever surfacing as editorializing. Around 343 pages and the anchor entry on this list. Cross-seeds with the Halloween list. The reader who finishes this and wants more Capote goes to Music for Chameleons; the reader who wants more literary true crime starts with everything else on this list.

books.title: Frankenstein
books.author: Mary Shelley
books.blurb: there any more pivotal story in the English-speaking world than Frankenstein? The Iliad and Hamlet might make their claim, but neither of those are still read as often, or remain as readable, as Mary Shelley’s immortal novel. Even its origins have become iconic—the result of a ghost story competition between bored poets in the ‘year without a summer’ of 1816. Much is made of Frankenstein as the first modern work of science fiction. That’s true, but it doesn’t do to overlook the raw horror at work in the miscreation, malformation, and murderous loneliness of Frankenstein’s monster. There are few revelations in all of horror that match Frankenstein’s reaction, “when, by the glimmer of the half-extinguished light, I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open,” or the monster’s chill promise that “I will be with you on your wedding night.” Of course, those who have not read the novel may think Frankenstein is about man versus monster. In truth, it’s the story of a neglected child and a cruel father. It is a violent tragedy that can still stir the soul to pity two hundred years later.

books.title: Beloved
books.author: Toni Morrison
books.blurb: A single chapter of Beloved contains more pain than most novels can manage from first page to last. That scene, in which Sethe murders her baby to spare her from a life of enslavement, is horribly, appallingly based in fact. Everything that follows is an attempt to bear the weight of personal and national trauma in fiction. The ghost story, it turns out, is the perfect vehicle. When a young woman appears bearing the name of Sethe’s dead infant, she seems to be a blessing. Soon, however, she begins to consume Sethe’s life, and tears open psychological wounds that the freed characters are desperately trying to hold closed. Morrison’s novel is lyrical and fragmentary (terms that tend to suggest an emphasis on style rather than satisfactory story), but Beloved offers both. It is a truly Great American Novel, both a literary testament to the suffering of millions and one of the most emotionally profound ghost stories ever composed.

books.title: Leaves of Grass
books.author: Walt Whitman
books.blurb: Whitman published the first edition in 1855 and spent the rest of his life revising and expanding it — the book grew with him from a slim pamphlet into the most comprehensive act of American self-invention in the literary tradition. Song of Myself alone covers the full range: the body, the democracy, the specific democratic faith that every American life is worth the full attention of a serious poet. Whitman is the canonical entry on this list and the most accessible of the great American poets — there is nothing obscure in the language, no apparatus required, only attention. The reader who thinks he does not like poetry has almost certainly not read Whitman. The complete Leaves of Grass runs around 500 pages; the reader who wants an entry point goes to the Library of America selected poems at around 170 pages.

books.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
books.author: Gabriel Garcia Marquez
books.blurb: Seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional Colombian town of Macondo — from its founding through a banana company massacre and a final apocalypse that was written into the family's fate before the first page. García Márquez invented magical realism for this novel and the effect is precise: the miraculous and the historical occupy the same sentence without friction, which turns out to be the most accurate way to describe Latin American history ever found. Around 400 pages and the most important novel written in Spanish in the twentieth century. The AoM reader who finds the first fifty pages unfamiliar rather than difficult should continue — the novel rewards patience in a way very few books on this list do, and what it gives back is unlike anything else in this project.

books.title: The Warmth of Other Suns
books.author: Isabel Wilkerson
books.blurb: Between 1915 and 1970, six million Black Americans left the South. Wilkerson followed three of them: Ida Mae Brandon Gladney, who left Mississippi for Chicago in 1937; George Starling, who left Florida for New York in 1945; Robert Foster, who left Louisiana for Los Angeles in 1953. The Great Migration reshaped American cities, American politics, and American music — and Wilkerson reconstructed it through three individual lives rather than statistics. The most complete account of why Black Southerners left, what the leaving cost, and what it produced. Cross-references to the US History list for the political context, and to the Books About Cities list, where the cities these migrants transformed are documented from the receiving end. The reader who wants the companion structural analysis should read The Mind of the South on this list first.

books.title: Fun Home: A Family Tragicomic
books.author: Alison Bechdel
books.blurb: This groundbreaking and bestselling graphic memoir from Alison Bechdel is the story of her unpleasant and damaged relationship with her late father, Bruce. Bruce Bechdel worked as both an English teacher and funeral home in town, a place Alison and her family dubbed “the Fun Home.” Not long after Alison came out as a lesbian, she discovers her father is gay, and a few weeks after this revelation, Bruce passes away. The award-winning Fun Home took seven years to make, in part because of Bechdel’s fascinating artistic process. She photographs herself in poses for each human figure before drawing the panel.

books.title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
books.author: Zora Neale Hurston
books.blurb: Janie Crawford grows up in an all-Black Florida town, marries three times, and arrives at something that functions as wisdom — or at least as knowledge of her own preferences, which turns out to be rarer. Hurston was an anthropologist who went into the field collecting Black Southern folklore before she wrote novels, and the prose carries that research: the dialogue is phonetically Southern in a way that initially slows the reader and then becomes the texture of the experience. Written in 1937 and ignored until Alice Walker rediscovered it in 1975. The fiction entry for the Black South section of this list. Cross-references to the American Fiction Classics list. The reader who wants the companion nonfiction should go to Hurston's own Dust Tracks on a Road, her autobiography, which covers the same Florida geography in a different register.

books.title: Giovanni’s Room
books.author: James Baldwin
books.blurb: In this short, seminal novel by the great James Baldwin, David, an American expat living in Paris circa the 1950s, wrestles with his identity and his sexuality as his lover awaits the guillotine. In a heartbreaking study of character, Baldwin lays bare David’s denial and self-deception, illuminating how his inability to live authentically bears fatal consequences for the alluring and vulnerable Giovanni. Before the novel was published in 1956, Baldwin’s publisher encouraged him to burn the draft, fearing that he would alienate his readership with a story of gay love. Today, Giovanni’s Room is widely recognized as one of the best LGBTQ+ novels of all time—a one-sitting must-read for anyone seeking to understand the pain and power of love under threat.

books.title: Little Women
books.author: Louisa May Alcott
books.blurb: The four March sisters — Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy — navigate the Civil War years with their father away at the front and their mother holding everything together. Jo is one of the great characters in American fiction: ambitious, funny, and perpetually at war with the conventions that try to contain her. Around 449 pages and the daughters entry on this list. The dad who reads this with his daughter is introducing her to a book that has shaped what American women think about ambition and independence for 150 years. Beth's illness and death in the second half should not be prepared for in advance.

books.title: The Yellow Wallpaper
books.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
books.blurb: Published in 1892, The Yellow Wallpaper is another classic of early-modern gothic horror, though it emphasizes psychological distress over some of the more fantastic elements embraced by Gilman’s peers. The tale of a woman who is confined to her bedroom as part of a rest cure for her so-called hysteria, as the narrator slips into madness she becomes increasingly enamored by the yellow color of her room. Considered a cornerstone of early American feminist writing, its commentary on the oppressive impact of patriarchy remains relevant to this day.

books.title: Middlemarch
books.author: George Eliot
books.blurb: Set against the fictitious town of Middlemarch, author Mary Ann Evans builds a morbid yet oddly modern and dense story about a marriage between two incompatible people that never gets better. During a time when Victorian female authors were pigeonholed into writing romance fantasy, Evans decided to write under the male name, George Eliot, and keep her un-happy ending. Real and really good. In a quote: “If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel’s heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence.”

books.title: Anna Karenina
books.author: Leo Tolstoy
books.blurb: It’s unfortunate that old Leo chose a woman’s name for the title of this masterwork and the heftier-sounding War and Peace for his more inferior (you heard me) novel, because we suspect it’s put men off it since the 1870s. What a shame, because Anna Karenina is perhaps the best book ever written. You’re in this book and so is your best friend, your dad, your boss, your enemy, the girl you first loved, and your neighbor. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry, and it won’t be anywhere near as hard as War and Peace. For best results, we recommend the translation by Richard Peavar and Larissa Volokhonsky. —Kelly Stout

books.title: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao
books.author: Junot Díaz
books.blurb: Oscar is a fat Dominican-American sci-fi nerd from New Jersey who has never been kissed and desperately wants to be a writer. Díaz uses his story as the container for the entire history of the Dominican Republic under the Trujillo dictatorship — delivered partly in footnotes that are more gripping than most history books — and the result won the Pulitzer Prize in 2008 and reads unlike anything else in American fiction. Funny, profane, structurally original, and underneath all of it, genuinely devastating. The AoM reader who thinks he is reading about a loser from New Jersey will find himself, without warning, holding a book about what political terror does to a family across three generations. One of the great American novels of the last twenty years.

books.title: The Age of Innocence
books.author: Edith Wharton
books.blurb: Newland Archer is engaged to the right woman, from the right family, in Gilded Age New York, and falls in love with her unconventional cousin Ellen Olenska, who has left a bad European marriage and returned to a society that cannot decide whether to accept or destroy her. Wharton won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921 and the novel is the most precise dissection of social conformity in American fiction — not a women's novel but a novel about what masculine paralysis looks like when a man chooses the safe life over the real one and spends the rest of his days wondering. Around 360 pages. The AoM reader who approaches this skeptically will find by the final chapter that Archer's choice — and what it costs him — is the most honest portrait of a certain kind of masculine failure available in the canon.

books.title: Sense and Sensibility
books.author: Jane Austen
books.blurb: Austen's best book, and like so many of her others, an exploration of gender politics and female independence at a time in which the freedoms of women were intimately, and often tragically, constrained by the ways in which they depended on males for economic assistance and security. Sounds like sad stuff, but Austen, as always, approaches these and other issues with an acute sensitivity and ear for comedy that elevates an explication of the frustrating social and economic constraints of one half of the population to a work of art.

books.title: Just Kids
books.author: Patti Smith
books.blurb: Smith arrived in New York in 1967 with no money and nowhere to stay and met Robert Mapplethorpe on her second day. They spent the next decade building themselves into artists — living in the Chelsea Hotel, haunting Max's Kansas City, watching Warhol's Factory operate at close range — and the memoir Smith wrote about those years is the best literary account of bohemian New York at its last genuinely broke-and-ambitious moment. Smith writes better than most novelists and she knows it. The literary entry on this list: less about drugs specifically than about the culture that drug use was embedded in, and what it felt like to be young and serious about art in a city that was simultaneously the center of the world and burning down. National Book Award, 2010. Cross-references to the Artists & Writers Bios list.

books.title: Redefining Realness
books.author: Janet Mock
books.blurb: Most people today know Janet Mock through her work on the hit show Pose, but I fell in love with her through her first memoir. The book follows her coming-of-age as a multiracial trans woman growing up in Honolulu, to moving to New York and landing a job at People magazine. With vivid prose that immerses you in her world, Mock offers candid, deeply-felt reflections about her experiences with her family, her friendships, her romantic life, her relationship to gender and class and privilege, and what she had to do to survive. I’m especially inspired by the care and grace with which she renders everyone in her story. There are no one-note characters here. Just as in life, the people we meet in her book are complicated, nuanced, and always beautifully human. —Edgar Gomez

books.title: Harriet the Spy
books.author: Louise Fitzhugh
books.blurb: Harriet carries a notebook everywhere and writes down exactly what she observes about every person she knows — her classmates, her neighbors, her nanny Ole Golly — with a specificity that is frequently unkind and always accurate. When the notebook is found and read, everything falls apart. Around 298 pages and the humor and observation entry on this list. Published in 1964 and still the best book available about what it costs a girl to be smarter and more honest than the people around her, and what she does with that cost.

books.title: As I Lay Dying
books.author: William Faulkner
books.blurb: The Bundren family transports the corpse of their matriarch Addie across Mississippi in August heat to bury her in the town she came from, and fifteen different narrators take turns describing the journey from inside their own damaged consciousness. Faulkner published this in 1930 and it remains the most formally audacious American novel of its era: each narrator sees the same events differently, none of them fully understands what is happening, and the accumulation of partial perspectives produces something more complete than any single reliable narrator could achieve. The difficult entry on this list — not as demanding as The Sound and the Fury, which is the right next step for the reader who finishes this and wants more. Around 267 pages. The reader who expects difficulty and leans into it will find Faulkner funny, which is the thing most first-time readers miss.

books.title: A Thousand Years Of Good Prayers
books.author: Yiyun Li
books.blurb: From one of our finest writers comes a staggering collection of stories about Chinese and Chinese American individuals, all of them located in engrossing and singular settings ranging from the barren wastelands of Mongolia to a fast-food establishment in Chicago. In these powerful stories about the private vagaries of the human heart, Li illuminates something transcendent about the power of culture and place.

books.title: Slouching Towards Bethlehem
books.author: Joan Didion
books.blurb: Didion spent the late 1960s watching California come apart — the Haight-Ashbury at the peak of the Summer of Love, the specific unreality of the Los Angeles entertainment industry, the center of American culture failing to hold — and wrote about it with a coldness that made the essays feel like dispatches from a war zone rather than cultural criticism. The title essay on Haight-Ashbury is the best piece of American journalism of the 1960s and the most accurate account of what the counterculture actually looked like from inside rather than from the mythology that replaced it. Around 238 pages. The AoM reader who assumes Didion is a women's list writer will find she is a diagnostician of American self-delusion who happens to be a woman, which is a different thing entirely.

books.title: Autobiography of Red
books.author: Anne Carson
books.blurb: In this stunning novel in verse, mythology and reality collide in the volcanic story of Geryon, a winged red monster killed by Herakles in Greek legend but reimagined in Carson’s telling as a tormented teenage monster smitten by Herakles the drifter, who becomes the subject of his photography before leaving without a backward look. Years later, Herakles and Geryon collide again, forcing Geryon to confront the pain of their parting and the return of his muse. At once a poignant exploration of love, loss, and loneliness, so too is this novel an ode to the long and winding journey of an artist’s becoming. Strange and sexy, with glimmeringly sharp edges, Autobiography of Red is a singular reading experience that could only come from a mind as singular as Carson’s.

books.title: Things Fall Apart
books.author: Chinua Achebe
books.blurb: Okonkwo is an Igbo warrior in late 19th century Nigeria — strong, disciplined, feared — who has built everything through the force of his will. When British colonialism arrives, it dismantles not just the political structure but the entire system of values that made his identity coherent, and Okonkwo's response is the only one available to a man who does not know how to adapt. Achebe wrote this in 1958, the year before Nigerian independence, and produced the foundational African novel in English — the book that demonstrated Africa had a literary tradition that predated the missionaries. The canonical entry in the African section, 200 pages. Cross-references to the African History list, where the colonialism Okonkwo faces is documented without the fiction.

books.title: Ragtime
books.author: E.L. Doctorow
books.blurb: Three families — a white upper-middle-class family in New Rochelle, a Jewish immigrant named Tateh and his daughter, and the Black ragtime musician Coalhouse Walker — intersect with historical figures including Harry Houdini, Emma Goldman, J.P. Morgan, and Henry Ford in the New York of 1906 to 1912. Doctorow published this in 1975 and invented a form that nobody else has successfully imitated: a novel that moves with the momentum of popular fiction and the ambition of serious literature, using invented characters alongside real ones to reconstruct the specific texture of American life at the moment it became modern. Around 320 pages and the historical fiction entry on this list. The reader who wants to understand the Progressive Era will find Doctorow more useful than most histories.

books.title: Parting the Waters: America in the King Years 1954-63
books.author: Taylor Branch
books.blurb: Branch's Pulitzer Prize-winning trilogy is the definitive narrative history of the civil rights movement — three volumes, roughly 2,800 pages, covering the years from 1954 to King's assassination in 1968 in extraordinary depth. Branch writes it the way David McCullough writes American history: you are inside the room, inside the decision, inside the moment. If you are going to read only one volume, start with Parting the Waters, which covers Montgomery through the March on Washington and is the most accessible entry point. But fair warning — it will be very hard to stop there. This is the serious long-term investment on this list, the one you come back to across multiple years, and the one you'll reference for the rest of your life.

books.title: The Leopard
books.author: Tomasi di Lampedusa Giuseppe
books.blurb: Tomasi di Lampedusa was a Sicilian prince who died in 1957, leaving behind an unpublished novel—the only one he ever wrote. It's a masterpiece. Set during the unification of Italy, it's about one of the prince's forebears, a wry nobleman who struggles to keep his household afloat while a new order rises. The book's most famous line is spoken by the prince's savvy, gold-digging nephew, Tancredi: "If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change." In this age of "disruption," as the revolutions keep coming, it seems even more apt.

books.title: Jane Eyre
books.author: Charlotte Bronte
books.blurb: Part Bildungsroman part Gothic horror story, featuring then-radical opinions on religion, social class, and gender, Jane Eyre revolutionized the novel. Plus, the struggle to strike a balance between love and freedom never gets old.

books.title: Song of Solomon
books.author: Toni Morrison
books.blurb: My favorite of Toni Morrison's books, and better than Beloved, this 1977 masterpiece is possibly the most powerful and moving contemporary American meditation on family, grace, masculinity, and humiliations of American history.

books.title: Birds of America
books.author: Lorrie Moore
books.blurb: If you're not in love with Lorrie Moore, I worry for you. You will hear people speak differently after reading this book, as if you've been in need of a hearing aid for years and you didn't know it. "People Like That Are The Only People Here" is worth the price of admission alone, as it's one of the most powerful and important short stories (about love and loneliness and motherhood and death) of this century.

books.title: The Round House
books.author: Louise Erdrich
books.blurb: A young man grapples with his mother's rape in a most unexpected, powerful and haunting coming of age story.

books.title: The Best Of Everything
books.author: Rona Jaffe
books.blurb: Before The Group, before Valley of the Dolls, and way before Sex and the City, there was this iconic novel about ambitious career women in New York City. For kicks, read it and then watch the Mad Men pilot. You will be amazed. And later in season one, see if you can catch Don reading this book in an effort to better understand the desires of young American women. Ashley Ford, @iSmashFizzle Contributor to BuzzFeed, ELLE, and others.

books.title: The God of Small Things
books.author: Arundhati Roy
books.blurb: and pierced with tragedy, this book is a blow to the heart. And then another. And then another. But not in the Cormac McCarthy way. The God of Small Things reveals the beauty and grace possible in the darkness like no other novel I have ever read. I both envy and pity the early editors and reviewers who had the task of describing this novel for the first time. If forced to boil it down, I'd say this is a novel about having a family at all, about the motivations within the structured microcosm of society that is a family. Just that.

books.title: Underworld
books.author: Don DeLillo
books.blurb: The story of one man and one family that is also the story of what happened to America in the second half of the 20th century. Selected Stories Of Alice Munro Piercing, prismatic tales about the lives of girls and women that possess the amplitude of novels, and the emotional precision of Chekhov.

books.title: Madame Bovary
books.author: Gustave Flaubert
books.blurb: She's French but she doesn't have to be. She is any reality-challenged newlywed. This first novel (Flaubert really knocked it out of the park) is an absolute masterpiece about what happens when humans feel bored and trapped, when they emotionally chew off their own shapely legs. Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage by Alice Munro Alice Munro is a national treasure, and technically that nation is Canada, but philosophically it's The People's Republic of Everybody. It's therefore difficult to pick out her strongest collection or to have the gall to pick, but I'd go with this one. They are about aging and love and marriage and life itself. I can't envision a reader who wouldn't be changed for the better by reading Alice Munro. The Collected Stories of Katherine Mansfield Katherine Mansfield is not required reading to be a person—but passion and point of view are—and since Mansfield is one of my personal favorites, I am going to foist her on you. She's a bit like a New Zealand Edith Wharton with a sprinkling of Jane Austen and John Cheever. But clever. "The Doll's House" is one of my favorite short stories of all time and just to prove it, I named the heroine of my first novel after a character in that story.

books.title: The Liars' Club
books.author: Mary Karr
books.blurb: This book was a bestseller for a reason. One of the most brutal, elegant, and yes, funniest memoirs of the late 20th century, Mary Karr's The Liars Club is an important work that is at turns personal and political, the story of a Texas childhood marked by anguish, adventure, and a potent combination of toxic masculinity, alcoholism and thwarted artistic ambitions.

books.title: The Group
books.author: Mary McCarthy
books.blurb: you have to read a novel with a character named "Priss" to be a better person? Kind of, yeah. The Group is a seminal, massively vital book written ahead of its time (it was banned here and there) and yet very much of its time, focusing on gender politics, friendship, socioeconomic status and influencing whole genres of contemporary fiction — all while being a total blast to read. Every woman should read it to know themselves; every man should read it to know who they're dealing with.

books.title: To the Lighthouse
books.author: Virginia Woolf
books.blurb: A book about an accomplished London family on vacation in the Scottish Hebrides who plan to make a trip to a nearby lighthouse. But it's by Virginia Woolf, so it's really about life, consciousness, and the problem of rendering them in art. And the obliterating forces of war, death, and time—and what comes after.

books.title: See You Tomorrow
books.author: William Maxwell
books.blurb: This novel has the most stunning architecture, a structure that, the longer one looks at it, the more powerful and moving it becomes. The story is about loss and grief, and is told through the repeated reimagining of a murder the narrator knew of as a boy.

books.title: Forgotten Country
books.author: Catherine Chung
books.blurb: In her debut novel, Catherine Chung writes of a displaced family, a sister harboring the kind of secret too many girls know too well, and another sister who tries to mend the fractures in her family before it's too late.

books.title: Balm
books.author: Dolen Perkins-Valdez
books.blurb: I am always looking for interesting and, more importantly, original stories about slavery. In this gorgeously written novel, Perkins-Valdez writes of life after slavery and the Civil War as a man tries to find his beloved wife, a woman seeks a life for herself away from the mother and aunts who didn't know how to see her, and a widow who can speak to the dead searches for solace. NW, by Zadie Smith Whenever Smith writes London, I forget time and place. That is no different in NW, an ambitious and audacious novel about four people as they grow up beyond the confines of the council estate where they were raised. It's thrilling to see how fearless Smith is, taking all kinds of narrative risks throughout while also telling an unforgettable story about identity.

books.title: Ceremony
books.author: Leslie Marmon Silko
books.blurb: Ceremony is one of the great (and under appreciated) American novels. Silko writes with tremendous power, rage, and range of violence, Pueblo myth and a veteran's recovery. The Collected Stories of Grace Paley Under the seductive, crisp and funny voice of Grace Paley, there burns a great indignation and condemnation of the way the powerful prey on the weak in society.

books.title: The Chronology of Water
books.author: Lidia Yuknavitch
books.blurb: You've never read a memoir quite like this. Yuknavitch's prose is stunning and vibrant, even as she tackles tough moments, and the uglier facts of life.

books.title: Silver Sparrow
books.author: Tayari Jones
books.blurb: This gorgeous novel provides a gracious look into the not-so-distant past, and gives us a full view into life, love, and secrets that ultimately define our lives.

books.title: The Color Purple
books.author: Alice Walker
books.blurb: This is a necessary read. If you've never read The Color Purple, you're missing out on some of the greatest literature of our time, not to mention a uniquely black look at poverty, beauty, and what we mean when we say "sister."

books.title: An Untamed State
books.author: Roxane Gay
books.blurb: This novel is brutal in its telling, and forces empathy and understanding for those who have experienced trauma, especially women. This isn't another sad story. It makes every emotion you already experience a little more real.

books.title: Shadowshaper
books.author: Daniel José Older
books.blurb: The existence of a young adult novel with an afro-latina teen girl for a protagonist is already reason to cheer, but when you add the fantastical elements from authoer Older's imagination, you have a masterpiece that defies the status quo in surprising and pioneering ways.

books.title: Bastard Out Of Carolina
books.author: Dorothy Allison
books.blurb: This semi-autobiographical first novel was a bestseller and finalist for the National Book Award. A story about family violence and incest, it's understandably intense and surprisingly funny. Read it because Allison is a rare and special talent. If you've never had the pleasure of hearing her speak about writing or literature, do yourself a favor and watch any interview with her on YouTube. You will be moved and reminded of why you like books in the first place.

books.title: Play It As It Lays
books.author: Joan Didion
books.blurb: If there is a consummate Los Angeles novel, this would be it but then, as with all her writing, Didion takes things further, to a complex and dark place where a woman's choices are painfully constrained by the whims of men.

books.title: The White Album
books.author: Joan Didion
books.blurb: We tell ourselves stories in order to live, begins this 1979 collection of Joan Didion essays. Though less-celebrated than 1968's Slouching Towards Bethlehem, The White Album harnesses Didion's skill at capturing the tensions and obsessions of mid-to-late 20th century California and amps up the existential ennui another notch as she tries to make sense of the chaos of everything from politics to contemporary consumer culture. "The center cannot hold," Didion wrote, quoting Yeats, in "Bethlehem." In "Album," the essayist and critic chronicles what life felt like after the center fell apart.

books.title: Bad Behavior
books.author: Mary Gaitskill
books.blurb: writes about the abhorrent things men and women do to each other, about sex, addiction, and masochism—without ever moralizing—better than Gaitskill. It started with this debut short-story collection and has continued in all her work thereafter.

books.title: The Lover
books.author: Marguerite Duras
books.blurb: There are few novels more sensuous and troubling and magnetic than The Lover. Duras is simply exquisite from the first word to the last. She imbues her prose with the damp heat of Indochina and the fraught tension of forbidden love and never forgets how beautiful words can be when arranged just so. Lizzie Widdicombe, @widdikombe

books.title: Housekeeping
books.author: Marilynne Robinson
books.blurb: Twenty-five years before Marilynne Robinson won a Pulitzer Prize for Gilead (and acquired a superfan named Barack Obama), she wrote this short, strange novel about two orphaned sisters being raised by a "drifter" aunt in a forgotten town called Fingerbone. A hypnotic meditation on the transience of life and love, it rings in your ears. We're all drifters.

books.title: Heartburn
books.author: Nora Ephron
books.blurb: Moby Dick it ain't, but don't go through life without reading Heartburn. To the list of great narrators we have to add Rachel Samstat, Ephron's wisecracking cookbook author, who is seven months pregnant when her husband informs her that he's in love with another woman. Lemons become lemon soufflé. The whole book is funny, but the scene where Rachel's therapy group gets held up by a mugger is one of the most pants-peeingly hilarious in American literature.

books.title: Mason & Dixon
books.author: Thomas Pynchon
books.blurb: A buddy movie starring the British surveyors who mapped the boundary between North and South in pre-Revolutionary America and a dazzling post-modernist confection that emerges as the author's most affecting novel yet. The Stories Of Vladimir Nabokov A glittering collection of tales animated by the author's fascination with the magical transactions of art and the indelible losses of exile.

books.title: Sula
books.author: Toni Morrison
books.blurb: The renowned story of convention in direct opposition to independence, friendship, and what women are routinely asked to carry in their bodies and on their backs.

books.title: Tristram Shandy
books.author: Laurence Sterne
books.blurb: This was one of the first modern novels ever written, and remains one of the funniest and most experimental: there is almost nothing in the most out-there of modern prose that Sterne didn't do first. Sloane Crosley, @askanyone Novelist, essayist, and one of 2015's biggest success stories.

books.title: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
books.author: Muriel Spark
books.blurb: Miss Jean Brodie, of the Marcia Blaine School for Girls, has some unorthodox teaching methods. Putting aside the official curriculum, she tutors a hand-picked group of students on important topics like her love life, the fact that she is in her "prime" (whatever that means), Renaissance painting, and the finer points of Fascism. Spark assumes a God-like voice, occasionally fast-forwarding to the girls' futures: fiery deaths, disappointing marriages, etc. As you laugh at Miss Brodie's outrageous dictums, the petty intrigues of the faculty, and the students' adolescent excesses, you may be surprised to notice a lump forming in your throat. How can a book so savagely funny be so wrenchingly, heartbreakingly sad?

books.title: The Complete Poems
books.author: Emily Dickinson
books.blurb: Dickinson's poems are sharp, wild, implosive things. She will always be relentlessly modern, and is one of the parents of modern American poetry.

books.title: Walk Two Moons
books.author: Sharon Creech Say
books.blurb: what you want about literature meant for children, but the way this book deals with girlhood, womanhood, and grief is more nuanced than most books meant for adults. If you allow it to blow your mind, it will.

books.title: Citizen
books.author: Claudia Rankine Rankine
books.blurb: defies genre and writes honestly and relentlessly about being black in modern America. This book is necessary in every sense of the word.

books.title: Uncle Tom's Cabin
books.author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
books.blurb: It has obvious flaws and must be considered in context by the modern reader (James Baldwin's essays make an excellent critical companion), but I don't think we should entirely dismiss the novel that helped fuel the Civil War by making the political personal.

books.title: The Boys of My Youth
books.author: Jo Ann Beard
books.blurb: In this one collection, I found the rhyme and reason for why I choose to write in this genre. "The Fourth State of Matter," just one of these essays, is utterly life-changing.

books.title: Possessing the Secret of Joy
books.author: Alice Walker
books.blurb: Alice Walker manages to take on the very political issue of female genital mutilation while never losing sight of the power of fierce, deeply engaged storytelling.

books.title: The Ballad Of The Sad Café
books.author: Carson McCullers
books.blurb: The go-to McCullers is usually The Heart is a Lonely Hunter, but Ballad depicts the irrational nature of love and an ill-fated love triangle better than any story I've ever read. Also: it's quite possibly the best-titled novella of all time.

books.title: Stone Butch Blues
books.author: Leslie Feinberg
books.blurb: In this moving novel, Feinberg explores the life of Jess Goldberg, a butch lesbian trying to make a way through the world in a body few people are interested in understanding. In addition to tackling sexuality and gender identity, this novel also reveals hard truths about working class America at the mid-century. Few books have stayed with me more.

books.title: Memoirs of Hadrian
books.author: Marguerite Yourcenar
books.blurb: What's the world's greatest love story? Most people, pressed to answer this question, would probably not point to a fifty-eight-year-old Roman emperor's passion for a Greek boy, circa 175 A.D. Certainly not most French women writing in the 1950s. And yet, with The Memoirs of Hadrian, Yourcenar made exactly that case. And more: She collapsed time, showing how a man who lived 2,000 years ago thought and felt just as deeply as we do about big and little subjects, from diet to governance. Anna Holmes, @annaholmes

books.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
books.author: Harper Lee
books.blurb: Atticus Finch defends a Black man falsely accused of rape in 1930s Alabama, seen through the eyes of his daughter Scout. The most-assigned novel in American high schools and the most persistently underestimated: the legal argument Finch makes — methodical, patient, aimed at facts the jury already knows and chooses to ignore — is as good a model of courtroom advocacy as anything in the nonfiction entries on this list. Cross-references to the Fathers and Sons Fiction and Coming-of-Age Fiction lists, where this book appears as a primary entry. The canonical American courtroom novel. The reader who thinks they remember it from school will find it different on a second reading, when the ending is no longer a surprise and what remains is the architecture.

books.title: Moby-Dick
books.author: Herman Melville
books.blurb: Melville published this in 1851 to commercial failure and died thinking it a minor work. It is the greatest American novel and one of the most demanding: Captain Ahab pursues the white whale across three oceans with a monomania that destroys everyone around him, and Melville uses the pursuit to examine obsession, fate, masculinity, God, and the specific American tendency to mistake personal vengeance for cosmic destiny. The whale chapters — eighty pages of cetology, anatomy, and commercial whaling — are the price of admission, not a flaw: they are what makes the Pequod feel like a real ship and the ocean feel like a real ocean. Around 600 pages. The difficult canonical entry on this list. The reader who finishes it will understand why it was worth the effort; the reader who doesn't will have a nagging sense of unfinished business for the rest of his life.

books.title: A Wrinkle in Time
books.author: Madeleine L’Engle
books.blurb: Warmer than typical sci-fi, touching on the battle between good and evil without being heavy-handed, A Wrinkle in Time is an unique book that easily won a place in the hearts of kids everywhere. Charles Wallace and Meg Murry are a brother and sister who have special gifts but are written off by others. Together with neighbor Calvin O’Keefe, and aided by three angelic beings, they go in search of their missing father who has been trapped on an alien planet controlled by an evil, disembodied brain. An interesting enough plot to keep a younger boy reading, enough symbolism and allegory to keep an older boy thinking.

books.title: Pride and Prejudice
books.author: Jane Austen
books.blurb: You probably already have a copy of this from school lying around somewhere. You may have even read it in high school. Either way, we highly suggest returning to it, no matter how dog-eared your copy is. Austen was a genius for dozens of different reasons, and Pride and Prejudice shines still today because of how the story unfolds. People would have you believe 19th-century literature is proper and dry, but Austen’s work reads like delicious, juicy gossip that’s as fresh as ever. After you finish the book, take a break and watch the stunning 2005 movie adaptation. In a quote: “I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading! How much sooner one tires of any thing other than of a book! When I have a house of my own, I shall be miserable if I have not an excellent library.”

books.title: Dark Star Safari
books.author: Paul Theroux
books.blurb: In 2001, Theroux traveled overland from Cairo to Cape Town — by train, bus, ferry, and foot — through Egypt, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and South Africa. He was 60 years old, deeply skeptical of the aid industry, contemptuous of Western do-gooderism, and completely honest about what he saw. The result is the funniest and most politically direct travel book ever written about Africa — Theroux does not moralize, does not perform guilt, and does not pretend the Africa he encounters is either Heart of Darkness or the Lion King. He describes it with precision, wit, and genuine respect for the people who live there. The book that ties the continental scope of this list together from ground level, written by a man who has been going to Africa for forty years and never stopped being surprised by it.

books.title: Long Walk to Freedom
books.author: Nelson Mandela
books.blurb: Mandela wrote this autobiography while imprisoned on Robben Island, smuggled the manuscript out page by page, and published it in 1994 after his release and election as South Africa's first post-apartheid president. It covers his Xhosa childhood, his legal career in Johannesburg, the founding of the ANC's armed wing, his arrest, 27 years in prison, and the negotiated transition to democracy — one of the most extraordinary political lives of the 20th century, told in the man's own words with complete clarity and without self-pity. The reader who wants to understand apartheid, the Boer legacy, and the South African transition gets all of it here from the perspective of the man at the center of it. One of the great political memoirs in any language.

books.title: Half of a Yellow Sun
books.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
books.blurb: In 1967, the Igbo people of southeastern Nigeria declared independence as the Republic of Biafra. The Nigerian federal government blockaded the region, and over the next three years between one and three million people died, most of them from starvation. Adichie — whose own family lived through the war — tells the story through three characters whose lives are dismantled by the conflict, and the result is the finest novel ever written about post-colonial African political violence. The historical research is meticulous, the emotional intelligence is extraordinary, and the portrait of a educated, sophisticated African society being destroyed from within carries a specific moral weight that no non-fiction account of the Biafran War has matched. Things Fall Apart explains what colonialism cost West Africa. This book explains what independence cost.

books.title: Dancing in the Glory of Monsters
books.author: Jason Stearns
books.blurb: Between 1996 and 2003, a war in the Democratic Republic of Congo drew in nine African nations, spawned more than twenty armed factions, and killed an estimated 5.4 million people — the deadliest conflict since World War II. Almost no one in the Western world knows it happened. Stearns spent years in eastern Congo as a UN investigator, interviewed generals, warlords, refugees, and child soldiers, and produced the only comprehensive popular account of a war so complex that most journalists gave up trying to explain it. The title comes from a Congolese phrase for dancing at funerals — grief and joy inseparable — and Stearns uses it to capture something true about a continent the rest of the world has consistently failed to pay attention to. The most important contemporary entry on this list.

books.title: King Leopold's Ghost
books.author: Adam Hochschild
books.blurb: Between 1885 and 1908, King Leopold II of Belgium ran the Congo Free State as his personal rubber plantation, extracting profit through a system of hostage-taking, mutilation, and mass murder that killed between 8 and 10 million people. Hochschild's 1998 book brought this history back into public consciousness after a century of deliberate institutional forgetting, and it remains the essential account of what the Scramble for Africa actually produced on the ground. The writing is clear and furious without tipping into polemic, and the cast of characters — Leopold, the shipping clerk E.D. Morel who exposed the system, Roger Casement who documented it, Joseph Conrad who fictionalized it — is as extraordinary as any fiction. One of the great works of popular history of the last thirty years.

books.title: Cleopatra: A Life
books.author: Stacy Schiff
books.blurb: The last ruler of an independent Egypt spoke nine languages, commanded armies, administered the wealthiest nation in the Mediterranean world, and kept Rome at bay for two decades through a combination of genuine political genius and two of the most consequential romantic alliances in history. Schiff won the Pulitzer Prize for this biography and the achievement is stripping away two thousand years of mythology — the seductress, the asp, the passive object of Caesar and Antony's attention — and rebuilding Cleopatra as the most capable ruler of her era, operating in a political environment that would have destroyed most men. The entry point for African history that the AoM reader will actually pick up, and the book that makes ancient Egypt feel inhabited rather than excavated.

books.title: A Long Way Gone
books.author: Ishmael Beah
books.blurb: In 1993, when Beah was twelve years old, rebels attacked his village in Sierra Leone and he spent the next year wandering through a war zone before being conscripted into the government army at thirteen. By the time UNICEF found him at fifteen he had been a soldier for two years. This memoir covers his conscription, his rehabilitation, and his eventual escape to the United States with the directness of a man who has decided that the only way to tell this story is to tell it plainly. There is no self-pity and no performance of trauma. The portrait of how a child becomes a killer — the specific process, the drugs, the violence that eventually feels ordinary — is one of the most important documents to emerge from the West African conflicts of the 1990s.

books.title: The Slave Ship
books.author: Marcus Rediker
books.blurb: Between the 16th and 19th centuries, approximately 12 million Africans were loaded onto ships on the West African coast and transported across the Atlantic under conditions designed to maximize cargo and minimize cost. Rediker reconstructs the Middle Passage through the ship itself — the physical layout, the crew hierarchy, the captains who ran tight operations and those who didn't, and the specific daily experience of the people chained below decks — using logbooks, court records, insurance claims, and abolitionist testimony. The result is the most viscerally immediate account of how the slave trade actually functioned as a human enterprise. Not a political argument but a piece of historical reconstruction so precise and so unflinching that it permanently changes the reader's understanding of what the trade was.

books.title: Shaka Zulu
books.author: E.A. Ritter
books.blurb: In less than a decade, Shaka kaSenzangakhona transformed the Zulu from a minor clan into the most formidable military power in southern Africa — standardizing weapons, revolutionizing infantry tactics with the chest-and-horns formation, creating a military discipline that professional European armies would have recognized as their own, and building a nation from nothing through a combination of strategic genius and absolute ruthlessness. Ritter's biography draws on oral tradition and historical record, and the portrait that emerges is one of the most extraordinary military minds in African history. The Zulu movie covers the battle at Rorke's Drift. This book covers the civilization and the man who built the army that fought it. There is no more dramatic or more underread subject in African military history.

books.title: The Zanzibar Chest
books.author: Aidan Hartley
books.blurb: Hartley grew up in East Africa as the son of a British colonial civil servant, became a war correspondent, covered the Somali famine of 1992-93, and reported on the Rwandan genocide. The Zanzibar Chest is his memoir — framed around the discovery of his father's letters from colonial East Africa — and it covers more of the continent's modern history in one book than most histories manage in three. The Somalia chapters are among the most harrowing pieces of war journalism ever written. The Rwanda chapters are quieter and more devastating. The Africa Hartley documents — beautiful, violent, ancient, and catastrophically mismanaged by the outside world — is the Africa that most Americans have no framework for, and this book provides it with the authority of a man who spent his entire adult life there.

books.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
books.author: Gabriel Garcia Marquez
books.blurb: Seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional Colombian town of Macondo — from its founding through a banana company massacre and a final apocalypse that was written into the family's fate before the first page. García Márquez invented magical realism for this novel and the effect is precise: the miraculous and the historical occupy the same sentence without friction, which turns out to be the most accurate way to describe Latin American history ever found. Around 400 pages and the most important novel written in Spanish in the twentieth century. The AoM reader who finds the first fifty pages unfamiliar rather than difficult should continue — the novel rewards patience in a way very few books on this list do, and what it gives back is unlike anything else in this project.

books.title: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao
books.author: Junot Díaz
books.blurb: Oscar is a fat Dominican-American sci-fi nerd from New Jersey who has never been kissed and desperately wants to be a writer. Díaz uses his story as the container for the entire history of the Dominican Republic under the Trujillo dictatorship — delivered partly in footnotes that are more gripping than most history books — and the result won the Pulitzer Prize in 2008 and reads unlike anything else in American fiction. Funny, profane, structurally original, and underneath all of it, genuinely devastating. The AoM reader who thinks he is reading about a loser from New Jersey will find himself, without warning, holding a book about what political terror does to a family across three generations. One of the great American novels of the last twenty years.

books.title: In Patagonia
books.author: Bruce Chatwin
books.blurb: Chatwin traveled to the southernmost tip of South America in the 1970s following a fragment of what his grandmother claimed was brontosaurus skin — a piece of hide she kept in a cabinet that had fascinated him since childhood. The journey through one of the emptiest landscapes on earth produces a book that is simultaneously travel writing, biography, natural history, and something genuinely unclassifiable. The Welsh colony in Chubut, the outlaws who fled south at the end of their careers — Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid spent their last years in Patagonia — and the specific quality of light at the end of the world. W.H. Hudson's Far Away and Long Ago, written in 1918 about an Argentine pampas childhood in the 1840s, is the older and quieter companion piece for the reader who wants the continent before the twentieth century touched it.

books.title: The River of Doubt
books.author: Candice Millard
books.blurb: In 1913 Theodore Roosevelt — post-presidency, post-defeat, restless and looking for something worth dying for — joined a Brazilian expedition to map an unmapped tributary of the Amazon. What followed was one of the most harrowing survival stories in exploration history: disease, starvation, a murder within the expedition party, and Roosevelt himself nearly dying of a leg infection deep in the jungle with no extraction possible. Millard covers the physical reality of the Amazon, the Brazilian interior, and the specific quality of determination that kept Roosevelt alive when lesser men would have quit. Cross-seeds with the Explorers & Adventurers biography list — Roosevelt belongs on both. Around 350 pages and the perfect entry point to the Amazon through a figure the AoM reader already knows and the jungle he had no business surviving.

books.title: Our Man in Havana
books.author: Graham Greene
books.blurb: A vacuum cleaner salesman in pre-revolutionary Havana is recruited by British intelligence and, having nothing to report and needing the money, begins inventing his agents and fabricating his intelligence. The intelligence services, delighted with his product, begin acting on it — and suddenly his invented agents start getting assassinated. Greene wrote it as a farce about the absurdity of the spy world and was more right than he knew: the novel was published in 1958 and the CIA spent the next thirty years running almost exactly this kind of operation in Cuba and Latin America with almost exactly these results. The funniest Cold War novel ever written, a perfect tonal counterweight to everything else on this list, and a book that becomes more accurate with every passing decade.

books.title: Black Robe
books.author: Brian Moore
books.blurb: In the 1630s, a French Jesuit priest travels deep into the interior of New France with a Huron escort, attempting to reach a distant mission and baptize a people who have no framework for understanding what he is offering them or why. Moore's novel is 250 pages of sustained moral and physical discomfort — a portrait of two cultures colliding with genuine respect for both and illusions about neither. The violence is real, the cold is real, and the theological arguments between the priest and his Huron guides are some of the most interesting in historical fiction. The best short entry point for the French colonial period in North America and the book that makes you understand why New France failed on its own terms.

books.title: The War of 1812
books.author: Pierre Berton
books.blurb: The war that Canadians remember as the moment they decided they weren't Americans, and Americans mostly don't remember at all. The British burned the White House. American invasions of Upper Canada were repelled repeatedly by a combination of British regulars, Canadian militia, and Indigenous warriors whose role in the defense Berton documents more honestly than most accounts on either side of the border. Berton writes it as Canadians understand it: not as a sideshow to the Napoleonic Wars but as the crucible in which a distinct national identity — cautious, anti-republican, stubbornly itself — was forged. Essential reading for any American who wants to understand why their northern neighbor sees shared history so differently.

books.title: Bolívar: American Liberator
books.author: Marie Arana
books.blurb: Simón Bolívar liberated six countries from Spanish rule — Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and Panama — through a combination of military genius, personal magnetism, and a refusal to accept defeat that borders on the pathological. The campaigns across the Andes are among the most extraordinary military achievements in history: crossing mountain passes that killed horses and men alike to attack armies that thought themselves unreachable. Arana is a Peruvian-American writer who treats Bolívar as a fully human figure — the liberator, the autocrat, the lover, the dying man on a Colombian coast watching everything he built fragment around him. Around 400 pages and the founding story of an entire continent given the account it deserves. García Márquez's The General in His Labyrinth imagines Bolívar's final river journey as a novel and is the right companion piece for the reader who wants the myth alongside the history.

books.title: The Power of the Dog
books.author: Don Winslow
books.blurb: The definitive novel about the Mexican drug war — a trilogy opener covering the DEA, the Sinaloa cartel, the Catholic Church, and the Mexican government across thirty years of escalating violence from the 1970s onward. Winslow spent a decade researching it and the result is as factually dense as any non-fiction entry on this list while reading like the fastest thriller you've ever picked up. The cartel structure, the corruption chain, the American demand driving all of it — Winslow maps the entire system without losing the human beings inside it. The AoM reader who saw Sicario and wanted to understand what was actually true now has the book. The sequels, The Cartel and The Border, are equally good. Start here.

books.title: The National Dream
books.author: Pierre Berton
books.blurb: Canada's founding myth isn't a revolution or a civil war — it's a railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway connected the country coast to coast in 1885 and Berton's two-volume history of its construction is the closest thing Canadian popular history has to Shelby Foote: sprawling, human, politically honest, and completely gripping. The graft, the engineering, the Chinese laborers who died building it, the near-collapses of political will that almost killed the project twice — Berton covers all of it without losing the narrative thread. Published as two volumes but reads as one continuous story. The entry point for anyone who wants to understand how Canada actually became a country rather than a collection of British territories that never quite unified.

books.title: The Last Spike
books.author: Pierre Berton
books.blurb: Canada's founding myth isn't a revolution or a civil war — it's a railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway connected the country coast to coast in 1885 and Berton's two-volume history of its construction is the closest thing Canadian popular history has to Shelby Foote: sprawling, human, politically honest, and completely gripping. The graft, the engineering, the Chinese laborers who died building it, the near-collapses of political will that almost killed the project twice — Berton covers all of it without losing the narrative thread. Published as two volumes but reads as one continuous story. The entry point for anyone who wants to understand how Canada actually became a country rather than a collection of British territories that never quite unified.

books.title: Tango: The Art History of Love
books.author: Robert Farris Thompson
books.blurb: Yale art historian Robert Farris Thompson traces the origins of the tango in the African-influenced slums of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late nineteenth century — the specific combination of European immigrant longing and African rhythmic sensibility that produced a dance neither culture could have created alone. The tango moved from the brothels of the Río de la Plata to the ballrooms of Paris and back again, each time changed by what it encountered, and Thompson covers the full cultural arc with the precision of a scholar and the enthusiasm of a man who has clearly danced it himself. Around 300 pages and the most unexpected entry in this section. For the reader who wants Buenos Aires as a complete civilization — the tango, the literature, the architecture, the specific melancholy the Argentines call nostalgia — this is the door.

books.title: El Narco
books.author: Ioan Grillo
books.blurb: Grillo has spent twenty years reporting from Mexico for Time and the BBC, and this is his account of how the cartels went from regional drug smugglers to fully militarized insurgent organizations capable of challenging the Mexican state. Where The Power of the Dog gives you the immersive narrative experience, El Narco gives you the factual architecture underneath it — the economics, the recruitment, the political corruption, the American demand that funds all of it, and the immigration crisis that flows directly from the violence. For the AoM reader who finished Winslow and wants to understand what's actually happening on the border and why it isn't going to resolve cleanly, this is the book. Grillo writes without condescension and without easy answers.

books.title: The Conquest of New Spain
books.author: Bernal Díaz del Castillo
books.blurb: Díaz was a foot soldier in Cortés's conquest of Mexico and wrote this account in his eighties, furious at the official historians who were getting the story wrong. The result is the most vivid first-person account of the conquest of the Americas — the march to Tenochtitlán, the first sight of the Aztec capital rising from its lake, the Noche Triste massacre, the final siege — written by a man who was there and who had no interest in making it sound dignified or inevitable. There is no more direct window into what it felt like to be present at one of history's great hinge moments. It reads faster than most modern thrillers and arrives with the authority of someone who was actually swinging a sword.

books.title: The Black Jacobins
books.author: C.L.R. James
books.blurb: The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 is the only successful slave revolt in history — enslaved people who rose up, defeated Napoleon's army, and established the first Black republic in the Western Hemisphere. James wrote this history in 1938 and it has never been surpassed. Toussaint L'Ouverture — the self-educated former slave who led the revolution, outmaneuvered every European power that came at him, and was finally captured by treachery and imprisoned in a French mountain fortress where he died — is one of the great figures in the history of human freedom, and James gives him the biography he deserves. The reader who hasn't encountered this story will find it astonishing that it isn't taught everywhere. It should be.

books.title: Cuba: An American History
books.author: Ada Ferrer
books.blurb: Four centuries of Cuban history told from the Cuban perspective rather than Washington's — from colonial rule through the Ten Years' War through the revolution through the missile crisis through the present day. Ferrer is a Cuban-American historian at NYU whose family lived the history she's writing, and the authority shows. The revolutionary chapters are genuinely thrilling: Che in the mountains, the Bay of Pigs disaster told from the beach, the specific Cuban machismo of the Castro era documented without nostalgia and without the reflexive American contempt that distorts most English-language accounts. The AoM reader who wants to understand Cuba — not the talking points from either direction but the actual country and its actual history — starts here.

books.title: The Art of Political Murder
books.author: Francisco Goldman
books.blurb: In April 1998, Bishop Juan Gerardi presented a four-volume report documenting military atrocities committed during Guatemala's 36-year civil war. Two days later he was beaten to death with a concrete block in his garage. Goldman — an American novelist and journalist of Guatemalan descent — spent years investigating the murder and the subsequent cover-up, during which witnesses were killed and prosecutors fled the country, and produced one of the great works of narrative journalism of the last twenty years. It is a murder mystery, a political thriller, and a portrait of a country whose institutions are so thoroughly compromised that justice is not merely difficult but genuinely dangerous to pursue. Reads faster than most thrillers and every word of it is true.

books.title: Under the Black Flag
books.author: David Cordingly
books.blurb: The definitive history of Caribbean piracy — Blackbeard, Calico Jack, Anne Bonny, the real Port Royal, the naval campaigns that finally ended it — written by the former curator of the National Maritime Museum in Greenwich, which is not nearly as dry as that sounds. The golden age of Caribbean piracy lasted roughly 1650 to 1730 and was simultaneously one of the most violent and one of the most socially radical periods in maritime history: many pirate ships operated as rough democracies, with elected captains and written articles of conduct, at a time when the entire world around them did not. Cordingly separates myth from historical record without killing the fun in the process and the characters he documents are genuinely extraordinary.

books.title: The Path Between the Seas
books.author: David McCullough
books.blurb: The history of the construction of the Panama Canal — a story about ambition, engineering, politics, yellow fever, and death on a massive scale that also happens to be the moment the United States announced itself as a global power capable of remaking geography. The French attempt that preceded the American one killed 22,000 workers and bankrupted a country. McCullough handles the disease campaign, the political maneuvering to acquire the Canal Zone by methods that were not entirely legal, and the sheer physical scale of the excavation with the same narrative command as 1776 and John Adams. One of the great American engineering stories, the right closing entry for this section, and a book that makes you look at a map differently afterward.

books.title: Killing Pablo
books.author: Mark Bowden
books.blurb: Pablo Escobar at his peak was the seventh-richest man in the world, ran an organization responsible for 80 percent of the cocaine entering the United States, and was conducting a private war against the Colombian state that included bombing a commercial airliner, assassinating a presidential candidate, and offering to pay off the national debt in exchange for immunity. Bowden — same author as Black Hawk Down — covers the eighteen-month manhunt that ended with Escobar's death on a Medellín rooftop in December 1993, drawing on Colombian police files, DEA records, and interviews with the men who hunted him. Around 300 pages and the definitive account of the most extraordinary criminal career in the history of the drug war. The Power of the Dog in the Mexico section covers the Sinaloa cartel; this covers its predecessor and in some ways its model.

books.title: Overthrow
books.author: Stephen Kinzer
books.blurb: In fourteen countries across the 20th century, the United States overthrew governments it found inconvenient — Guatemala in 1954, Iran in 1953, Chile in 1973, Nicaragua through the 1980s, and on down a list that gets more uncomfortable the longer it runs. Kinzer was the New York Times bureau chief in Central America and writes clean, propulsive narrative history without ideological editorializing. The value of this book for the AoM reader isn't any single coup — it's the pattern, which explains more about why the region distrusts Washington, why the migration flows exist, and why Central American politics remain unstable than any amount of current events coverage. Understanding the pattern is understanding the present. The most useful book in this section.

books.title: The Inconvenient Indian
books.author: Thomas King
books.blurb: King is a Cherokee-Greek-American-Canadian academic who decided to write the history of Indigenous peoples in North America the way a very smart, very tired man who has been explaining the same thing for fifty years would explain it — with devastating wit and zero patience for comfortable mythology. The book moves between history, polemic, and personal essay without warning, and the tonal control is extraordinary. It is funny in the way that only genuine outrage, perfectly channeled, can be funny. King doesn't ask you to feel guilty. He asks you to pay attention, which turns out to be considerably more demanding. The most honest book in this section and the one most likely to stay with you.

books.title: Sunshine Sketches of a Little Town
books.author: Stephen Leacock
books.blurb: Once the most widely read English-language humorist in the world and now largely forgotten outside Canada, Leacock wrote a series of linked sketches in 1912 about the fictional small Ontario town of Mariposa — its pompous citizens, its failing businesses, its local politics conducted with magnificent self-importance, and its complete conviction that it occupies the center of the universe. The satire is gentle enough to be funny and sharp enough to draw blood, and the portrait of small-town civic life it produces is recognizable a century later. It reads the way Mark Twain would read if Twain had been Canadian — slightly more apologetic and no less accurate. The most purely enjoyable book in this section.

books.title: Blood of Brothers
books.author: Stephen Kinzer
books.blurb: Kinzer was the New York Times bureau chief in Managua through the 1980s, which put him at ground level for the Sandinista revolution, the Contra war, and the American-backed campaign to destabilize a government Washington didn't like. This is his on-the-ground account — journalism at its best, reported from both sides of the conflict without the ideological commitments that distort most books written about Nicaragua from either direction. The AoM reader who wants to understand the Sandinistas without reading a manifesto or a hit piece now has the book. Kinzer covered the same ground for Overthrow from a historical distance; here he's in the middle of it, and the difference shows on every page.

books.title: The Golden Spruce
books.author: John Vaillant
books.blurb: In January 1997, a former logger named Grant Hadwin — a man of extraordinary physical capability and deteriorating mental stability — swam across a freezing British Columbia channel in the middle of the night and chainsaw'd down a 300-year-old golden Sitka spruce sacred to the Haida people and unique in the natural world. Then he disappeared trying to reach his own trial by kayak and was never seen again. Vaillant uses the act as the entry point for a book about the BC logging industry, Haida culture, and the specific madness that the wilderness produces in men who spend too long alone in it. Same author as The Tiger. One of the most underread books in this entire project.

books.title: Open Veins of Latin America
books.author: Eduardo Galeano
books.blurb: Uruguayan journalist Eduardo Galeano wrote this in 1971 as the definitive account of how Latin America was systematically underdeveloped — the silver of Potosí that funded the Spanish Empire while impoverishing Bolivia, the rubber boom that enslaved the Amazon, the banana republics run by United Fruit, and the specific mechanism by which extraordinary natural resource wealth produced poverty rather than development across an entire continent. Hugo Chávez gave Barack Obama a copy at a summit in 2009 and it became a bestseller overnight, which tells you something about both the book and the summit. The political perspective is explicitly noted — Galeano is arguing a case from the left — but the historical evidence is real and the argument is the essential counterweight to every triumphalist account of Western expansion on this project. Read Kinzer's Overthrow in the Central America section alongside it.

books.title: Prisoner Without a Name, Cell Without a Number
books.author: Jacobo Timerman
books.blurb: Argentine newspaper editor Jacobo Timerman was arrested by the military junta in 1977, held for two and a half years in secret prisons, and tortured with the specific systematic patience of a state that had decided disappearance was an administrative tool. His account of the imprisonment — the techniques used to break people, the virulent anti-Semitism running through the officer class, and the Argentine intellectual culture that either collaborated with or stayed silent during the 30,000 disappearances — is one of the most important political testimonies of the twentieth century. Around 180 pages and the shortest entry on this list. The book that explains from the inside what the dirty war actually was. Robert Farris Thompson's Tango covers the Buenos Aires that existed before and after the junta — the African-influenced music that became Argentina's defining cultural export — as the essential cultural companion to this one.

books.title: Insurgent Mexico
books.author: John Reed
books.blurb: Reed was 26 years old when he rode with Pancho Villa's División del Norte in 1913 and wrote the dispatches that made Villa famous in the American press. This is the book that invented the embedded war correspondent genre — raw, immediate, and written with the barely-contained excitement of a young man who couldn't believe his luck. Villa comes across as simultaneously terrifying and magnetic, which is exactly right.
