Where most first-contact stories feature a seismic clash between cultures, the Strugatskys present something dark and different: They envision unfeeling aliens who think so little of us that they simply pass our planet by—and leave their garbage behind. Roadside Picnic pushed the genre forward by questioning our perceived centrality in the universe—and insisting that we learn to live with our own insignificance.

books.title: The Calculating Stars
books.author: Mary Robinette Kowal
books.blurb: Mary Robinette Kowal’s outstanding alt-history series Lady Astronaut begins with a disaster: When a meteorite hits the eastern seaboard in 1952, millions of people are killed, including the president and most other government officials. Mathematician and pilot Elma York calculates that the resulting climate shift will wipe out life on Earth in a matter of decades, meaning that the only solution is to establish a colony on Mars. Elma longs to become an astronaut, but because of the sexism, racism, and antisemitism of the time, she and other women are benched as “human computers.” Against the thrilling backdrop of this burgeoning space race, Elma and her colleagues wage an increasingly public war against discrimination, fighting for their right to become astronauts. Textured with strong scientific research and achingly real characters,

books.title: The Sirens of Titan
books.author: Kurt Vonnegut
books.blurb: Perhaps you expected to see Slaughterhouse-Five on this list instead, but bear with us. The Sirens of Titans takes Slaughterhouse’s science fiction slant and leans into it full throttle, making for something even more spectacular, strange, and sidesplittingly funny. Malachi Constant, the richest man on a future Earth, hopscotches across the solar system, suffering the slings and arrows of fortune at every turn. Constant has come into the crosshairs of Winston Niles Rumfoord, a malevolent space traveler who’s become “chrono-synclastic infundibulated” by his voyage. Now, like a vindictive god, Rumfoord is determined to teach the entire human race a lesson by pitting it against the belligerent Martians. Pulpy and surprisingly poignant, The Sirens of Titan trafficks gracefully in some of sci-fi’s most enduring questions about fate, free will, and predestination.

books.title: This Is How You Lose the Time War
books.author: Amal El-Mohtar
books.blurb: and Max Gladstone Structured as a poetic correspondence between two time-traveling spies, this forbidden romance puts the “distance” in “long-distance relationship.” As Agents Red and Blue hopscotch through the multiverse, altering history on behalf of their respective military superpowers, they leave behind secret messages for one another—first taunting, then flirtatious, then flowering with love and devotion. “There’s a kind of time travel in letters, isn’t there?” Blue muses. “Letters are structures, not events,” Red replies. “Yours give me a place to live inside.” Amid the dangerous chaos of their circumstances, Red and Blue find constants in one another. Playful and imaginative, told with lyrical grace, this is a dazzling puzzle box of a novella.

books.title: The Children of Men
books.author: P.D. James
books.blurb: Before it was a grim Alfonso Cuarón film, The Children of Men was a grim, remarkable novel. The year is 2021: With all men inexplicably sterile, no child has been born for 25 years, and the human race faces extinction. England is ruled by the Warden, a despotic leader who prizes the youngest generation above all others. Theo Faren, the Warden’s estranged cousin, sleepwalks through life as an Oxford historian until he receives a visit from a group of dissidents, whose company includes a pregnant woman. Packed with prescient insight about politics, power, and tyranny,

books.title: The Three-Body Problem
books.author: Cixin Liu
books.blurb: One of China’s most acclaimed science fiction writers opens his Hugo Award-winning Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy with The Three-Body Problem, a gripping first-contact thriller set against the backdrop of China’s Cultural Revolution. When a young physicist comes to work at the government’s secretive Red Coast Base, she soon learns that frontier scientists are communicating with extraterrestrials—and they’re planning to make a hostile visit. Enormous in scope, rich in both twisty-turny mysteries and big ideas about progress, The Three Body-Problem marks the ascension of a writer bound to become every bit as canonical as Arthur C. Clarke or Isaac Asimov. This book is now a Netflix series from Game of Thrones showrunners

books.title: The Claw of the Conciliator
books.author: Gene Wolfe
books.blurb: Revered as “the Melville of science fiction” by Ursula K. Le Guin, Gene Wolfe wrote dense and heady books that aren’t for the faint of heart. But for serious sci-fi readers, there are immense rewards to penetrating Wolfe’s baroque prose and visionary imagination. His best-known work is The Book of the New Sun, a dazzling tetralogy about Severian, a torturer exiled for showing mercy to a prisoner. Our favorite volume is The Claw of the Conciliator, the second installment in the series, wherein Severian heads to the city of his exile, only to be waylaid along the journey by love, fantastical creatures, and a mysterious artifact with ancient powers. Erudite and intricate, this series is a colossus of imagination and language—a must-read for any serious student of the genre.

books.title: 1Q84
books.author: Haruki Murakami
books.blurb: This epic descendent of George Orwell’s 1984 covers that fateful year in two storylines—one fictional, one “real.” Bridging that gap are two long-lost lovers: Aomame, an assassin targeting domestic abusers, and Tengo, an aspiring novelist ghostwriting a dyslexic teenager’s bestseller. When Aomame discovers that the world is not what it seems and works to take down a dangerous cult leader, she and Tengo are drawn into a distorted reality, searching for one another across the chasm. It’s often said that a novel should contain the world; in 1Q84, Haruki Murakami makes good on that promise, weaving everything from recipes to music into this mammoth tale of love and longing in a contemporary

books.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
books.author: Philip K. Dick
books.blurb: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? famously became the basis for Blade Runner, but if you’re a movie fan who hasn’t read the novel, you’re in for something new, as it’s more of a complement than a faithful adaptation. Some of the familiar bones are here, like bounty hunter Rick Deckard and his mission to retire rogue androids, but you won’t find the term “blade runner” anywhere. Set in an abandoned San Francisco after World War Terminus’s radioactive fallout has destroyed the Earth, this short gut-punch of a novel finds its central theme in empathy. Can androids experience it? Are humans who lack it any better than machines? Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? asks more questions than it answers, reveling in ambiguity about just what separates man from machine. Like all the best science fiction, its weighty foray into what makes us human will linger with you for a long time.

books.title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy
books.author: Douglas Adams
books.blurb: Few science fiction novels can claim to have inspired their own holiday, but The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy isn’t your ordinary science fiction novel. (The holiday is Towel Day, if you must know.) Douglas Adams’s signature work has cast a long shadow over popular culture, and for good reason. This absurdist comedy is the story of Arthur Dent, a hapless everyman who wanders the universe after Earth is destroyed to make way for the galactic highway. As he romps through space with alien travel writer Ford Prefect and a crew of android oddballs, Dent has adventures that illuminate how “utterly insignificant” our “little blue green planet” truly is. In the face of absurdity, Adams reminds us, what else can we do but laugh?

books.title: Brave New World
books.author: Aldous Huxley
books.blurb: Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World is an original banned book, getting kicked off of shelves almost as soon as it was published. The dystopian novel is set in 2540, in a futuristic world known as the “World State,” wherein advanced science and technologies are shaping utopia by producing genetically modified babies. The cuddly little machine-made humans are also conditioned in metal utero with specific moral values to be subsequently raised in strict social castes. The powers that be keep people in these social striations by encouraging regular and casual sex and consuming an opioid-like upper called soma. The novel was first banned in Ireland in 1932 for obvious reasons, and it was quickly followed up by the Aussies in the same. The U.S. did its part with eight states filing for censorship of Huxley’s blasphemous book that dared to ask about the trade-off between happiness and freedom.

books.title: The Time Machine
books.author: H.G. Wells
books.blurb: Published way back in 1895, The Time Machine was one small step for H.G. Wells but one giant leap for science fiction. The novel popularized the concept of time travel by vehicle, lighting the way for everything from Back to the Future to Doctor Who. The Time Machine is the story of the Traveler’s journey 800,000 years into the future, where he discovers that mankind has evolved into two races: the ethereal Eloi and the predatory Morlocks. Through the Traveler’s exciting, nail-biting adventure, we see an entire generation’s fin de siècle anxieties about industrialization and the future of humanity. This short, seminal book is a must-read for any sci-fi fan.

books.title: Hyperion
books.author: Dan Simmons
books.blurb: Simmons structured his masterpiece after Chaucer's Canterbury Tales: seven pilgrims traveling to the world of Hyperion each tell the story of why they are there, and each story is a different subgenre of science fiction — military SF, horror, detective fiction, literary fiction, romance — woven into a single cosmological narrative of extraordinary ambition. The Shrike — a creature of blades and time that impales its victims on a tree of thorns — is the most terrifying villain in science fiction. The first two volumes form a complete story and should be read back to back. Few reading experiences in the genre are as immersive or as rewarding.

books.title: The Fall of Hyperion
books.author: Dan Simmons
books.blurb: Simmons structured his masterpiece after Chaucer's Canterbury Tales: seven pilgrims traveling to the world of Hyperion each tell the story of why they are there, and each story is a different subgenre of science fiction — military SF, horror, detective fiction, literary fiction, romance — woven into a single cosmological narrative of extraordinary ambition. The Shrike — a creature of blades and time that impales its victims on a tree of thorns — is the most terrifying villain in science fiction. The first two volumes form a complete story and should be read back to back. Few reading experiences in the genre are as immersive or as rewarding.

books.title: Contact
books.author: Carl Sagan
books.blurb: The great Carl Sagan wrote dozens of works of nonfiction but just one novel: Contact, a 1985 bestseller that later became a Jodie Foster flick. Sagan’s preoccupations with intelligent life come into view through Dr. Ellie Arroway, a principled astronomer who detects and decrypts a deep-space transmission from a planetary system far, far away. At the transmission’s urging, the nations of the world race to build a mysterious machine, but faith leaders call the enterprise (and the rationality of science) into question. Through this thoughtful, layered story, Sagan plumbs the often antagonistic relationship between science and religion, asking if perhaps both are seeking contact in different forms. After all, disciples from each camp can agree on one thing: “The universe is a pretty big place. If it's just us, seems like an awful waste of space.”

books.title: Snow Crash
books.author: Neal Stephenson
books.blurb: Stephenson invented the word "metaverse" in this novel in 1992 and predicted avatar-based virtual reality social spaces, corporate nation-states, and the weaponization of information systems with an accuracy that reads less like speculation and more like prophecy. Hiro Protagonist — pizza delivery driver for the Mafia and the greatest sword fighter in the Metaverse — is one of the great SF heroes. The novel is also genuinely funny, written with a kinetic energy that makes its 500 pages disappear, and the central premise — that language itself can be a virus, a hack, a weapon — is one of the most original ideas in the genre. It has never been more relevant.

books.title: A Canticle for Leibowitz
books.author: Walter M. Miller Jr.
books.blurb: After World War III, Earth has fallen into a new Dark Age; most of the United States is a radioactive wasteland, and civilization is in tatters. While violent packs of survivors burn books and slaughter those who can read, the monks of St. Leibowitz preserve the heritage of the past by smuggling important volumes into their monastery. As the novel progresses through the centuries and a new Renaissance gives way to a second space age, so much about modern life changes, but at the monastery, much remains the same. Walter M. Miller Jr.’s ambitious sci-fi classic captures the human tendency for self-destruction, as viewed through the cyclical rise and fall of civilization, but it’s not all doom, gloom, and nuclear warfare: A Canticle for Leibowitz is a moving paean to the power of knowledge and hope.

books.title: The Martian Chronicles
books.author: Ray Bradbury
books.blurb: If you expected to see Fahrenheit 451 on this list, then you haven’t spent enough time with The Martian Chronicles, undoubtedly Ray Bradbury’s masterpiece. Radically poetic and rich with metaphor, it was an astonishing leap forward for a genre until then not considered sufficiently “literary.” Bradbury’s linked stories open on an Earth ravaged by nuclear warfare. In search of a new beginning, Americans pack up their manifest destiny and blast off to conquer Mars, but little do they know, the red planet will conquer them in return. Bradbury’s Mars is a dreamlike landscape of wasted cities, populated by a dwindling race of ancient, unknowable beings. In glimmering stories that swing from dark tragedy to pure comedy, he showcases mankind’s exploration and desolation of Mars, all while dismantling midcentury mythologies of American exceptionalism. Told in language at once elegiac and sinister, fantastical and fable-like,

books.title: What Mad Universe
books.author: Fredric Brown
books.blurb: Published in 1949 during the waning glory of science fiction’s golden age, What Mad Universe is a dazzling high-wire performance—at once a cheeky satire of classic pulp magazines and an excellent pulp tale in its own right. In a near-future setting, pulp magazine editor Keith Winton is transported to a parallel universe through a freak rocket launch accident. This alternate reality looks just like home, but with some key differences: Here, everything from Keith’s magazines is a fact of daily life, from interstellar travel to war with extraterrestrials. Soon enough, Keith becomes a fugitive on the run in New York City, desperate to get back to his own timeline. What Mad Universe is packed with daffy, self-referential details for the devoted sci-fi reader; for instance, in Fredric Brown’s alternate universe, H.G. Wells never wrote a novel about a Martian invasion of Earth, but rather a political manifesto condemning the human colonization of Mars. Campy and comical, this novel is both an homage and a send-up, not to be missed.

lists.title: Best Wellness Books for All You

books.title: Bliss Brain: The Neuroscience of Remodeling Your Brain for Resilience, Creativity, and Joy
books.author: Dawson Church
books.blurb: In this fascinating exploration of meditation, Church, a natural storyteller, takes us through a harrowing personal experience with the page-turning dramatic touch of an expert novelist. His story demonstrates that even when unimaginable shit goes down and you think there's no way to overcome it, there is an answer. Meditation can be discouraging because it’s so damn difficult, but Church takes us off the hook, or at least reframes our resistance. “The difficulty has nothing to do with willpower or intention,” he writes. “It’s simply due to the design of the human brain.” Church maps out how, through meditation, the brain can be remodeled. Be sure not to miss the companion meditations that come with the book.

books.title: Sleep Smarter: 21 Essential Strategies to Sleep Your Way to A Better Body, Better Health, and Bigger Success
books.author: Shawn Stevenson
books.blurb: Sleep writes Shawn Stevenson, “suffers from a PR problem and desperately needs rebranding. Sleep isn’t sexy.” Sure, it’s essential, but we often don’t value it as a key component of health and wellness, which it most certainly is. Stevenson’s book is a well-informed tool backed by scientific data, complete with action steps at the end of each chapter. He provides applicable, not theoretical help. Stevenson’s prose is conversational, he’s got a great sense of humor and leaves the reader knowing that a good night’s sleep is not only possible, but attainable.

books.title: Limitless: Upgrade Your Brain, Learn Anything Faster, and Unlock Your Exceptional Life
books.author: Jim Kwik
books.blurb: When he was in kindergarten, Jim Kwik suffered a brain injury in a classroom accident. “I’m so stupid,” “I don’t understand,” and “I’m too dumb to learn” became his mantras. He thought he would forever need to work harder, but in his powerful and constructive book, he illustrates that working harder does not necessarily mean working smarter. In this hopeful, challenging, and probing work, Kwik shows us how we arrive at our limitations, and deconstructs preconceived notions like: intelligence is fixed; mistakes are failures; and genius is born. Smartly structured, full of thoughtful questions and exercises, Kwik reassures the reader that we are capable of so much more than we believe. Limitless provides an engaging roadmap to self-empowerment.

books.title: Wonder Drug: 7 Scientifically Proven Ways That Serving Others Is the Best Medicine for Yourself
books.author: Stephen Trzeciak
books.blurb: and Anthony Mazzarelli Take a look at any selection of self-help books and you'll find many arguing that in order to achieve health and happiness, you need to look inward. Stephen Trzeciak and Anthony Mazzarelli’s captivating new book, Wonder Drug, claims the exact opposite. In fact, it’s by looking outside ourselves—by serving others—that health and happiness are found. “When you connect with other people,” they write, “you get hits of reward-center hormones—endorphins, dopamine, oxytocin, and serotonin—that make you feel good.” They have a prescription for how to get started, and remind us that doing just a little bit is enough to make a big difference.

books.title: The Telomere Effect: A Revolutionary Approach to Living Younger, Healthier, Longer
books.author: Elizabeth Blackburn
books.blurb: and Elissa Epel For those of you with a taste for more science-heavy work, look no further than this riveting study by a molecular biologist (Blackburn) and a health psychologist (Epel), who bring wellness down to the cellular level. They explain, “Telomeres are repeating segments of non coding DNA that live at the ends of your chromosomes.” So what does that mean? It means that our health and longevity are affected by the length of our telomeres. And wouldn’t you know it, their length depends on how we live, sleep, and eat, as well as our environment, relationships, and history. Amazingly, telomeres are impacted by the way we think and feel, too. The authors illustrate how we can affect our telomeres and live a longer, healthier life. They succeed in bringing a highly specialized topic previously relegated to medical journals to a wider audience. The book is dense, studious, comprehensive, and completely absorbing.

books.title: Resilient: How to Grow an Unshakable Core of Calm, Strength, and Happiness
books.author: Rick Hanson
books.blurb: In our current climate, resilience is needed more than ever. But how do you build it? Is it just a matter of sheer grit? In this engrossing and accessible guide, Hanson writes, “Mental resources like determination, self-worth, and kindness are what makes us resilient: able to cope with adversity and push through challenges in the pursuit of opportunities. The key is knowing how to turn passing experiences into lasting inner resources built into your brain.” Hanson breaks down the components of resilience and offers a process on how to develop resilience beyond the notion of grit. As a writer, Hanson goes down smoothly. The chapters—on topics such as courage, confidence, intimacy, and calm—are all easy to follow, making this a necessary and valuable tool.

books.title: Us: Getting Past You and Me to Build a More Loving Relationship
books.author: Terrence Real
books.blurb: Our culture embraces individualism, yet when it comes to intimacy—and making our relationships work—individualism is poison. That’s how Terry Real, a couples therapist from Boston and founder of Relational Life Therapy, sees it. He believes in the power of togetherness not individuality. “Us is the seat of closeness,” he writes. “You and me is the seat of adversarial contest.” Which might be good when confronting a tiger, but not so much with your partner. In his enveloping and insightful book, enlivened by examples from his practice, Real lays out how the patriarchal construct of relationships imprisons both men and women. Real implores us, no matter what type of relationship we’re in, to give up the position of winning vs. losing and right vs. wrong. Power and dominance are the death of connection. Real is a natural storyteller, pointed, jovial, and funny. If you’re struggling in your relationship and are open to hard truths, delivered with compassion and zero wasted time, Real is the ticket.

books.title: Loving What Is: Four Questions That Can Change Your Life
books.author: Byron Katie
books.blurb: The genius of Katie’s most celebrated book is its daring simplicity. Her methodology for mental and emotional wellness is based on asking ourselves four questions, no matter the situation: 1) Is it True?; 2) Can you absolutely know that it is true?; 3) How do you react, what happens, when you believe that thought?; 4) Who or what would you be without the thought? “These questions,” writes Katie, “will burn up anything that isn’t true for you.” These questions help disarm and dismantle the stream of non-truths that play over in our minds. By asking ourselves these questions, it’s possible to transform our thinking. Katie’s vital guide brims with wisdom and provides the reader with hope and relief. You’ll walk away with a different perspective and feel a whole lot lighter.

books.title: Walking Through Anger: A New Design for Confronting Conflict in an Emotionally Charged World
books.author: Christian Conte
books.blurb: Ah another favorite universal theme—anger. This isn’t a fun one. Especially when you’re dealing with other people’s anger, which can be invasive, threatening, and completely overwhelming. Christian Conte, PhD, an Anger Management Specialist who has logged over 20,000 hours working with violent criminals, introduces us to his Yield Theory. Conte’s approach isn’t just instructing how to diffuse someone’s anger, but how to yield to it. To meet people where they are, which seems about the last thing you want to do when someone is furious and you’d rather take cover. We do this by listening on a deeper level, says Conte. Not through our mind’s eye, but from the other person’s perspective. Instead of insisting people see things our way—what Conte describes as our “cartoon world”—instead, through humility and open curiosity, we ask the person: show me what you’re seeing that I’m not seeing. This book is a gem, and it serves us well as we navigate rough terrain with the people in our lives.

books.title: Meditation for Fidgety Skeptics: A 10% Happier How-to Book
books.author: Dan Harris
books.blurb: You may know Dan Harris as a former anchor on ABC News, or as the author of the New York Times bestseller 10% Happier, which has become Harris’s signature platform (including a podcast, newsletter, and app). His 2017 book, Meditation for Fidgety Skeptics, also falls under the 10% Happier brand, and is a relatable, instructive, and incredibly useful guide that also happens to be extremely funny. Harris delineates the challenges and benefits of meditation through his own experience. While he is hilarious, his sense of humor never undermines his enlightening message and direction.

books.title: A New Earth: Awakening to Your Life's Purpose
books.author: Eckhart Tolle
books.blurb: Tolle delivers a masterpiece on awakening to consciousness. Oprah Winfrey called this “the most important book I’ve ever read,” and co-hosted a podcast with Tolle devoted to each chapter. The author has a calming presence, but don’t confuse his calm for a lack of conviction. Consciousness is about being in the present, dropping our stories, and creating space between our thoughts and who we really are. When I feel off-center, I can pick up A New Earth and find myself realigned in no time.

books.title: The Way of Integrity: Finding the Path to Your True Self
books.author: Martha Beck
books.blurb: Beck is my kind of writer: smart, funny, and no-bullshit. In this hit-you-between-the-eyes book, she shows us how easily we fall out of integrity even in small ways, like why we often say “yes” when we mean “no.” In an effort to fit into the confines of social constructs—family, work, culture—we subvert our integrity in the name of love, security, and acceptance. I had no idea how out-of-integrity I am in certain areas of my life. Beck’s book has empowered me to take ownership and action.

books.title: Dare: The New Way to End Anxiety and Stop Panic Attacks
books.author: Barry McDonagh
books.blurb: If you have anxiety, this book is ideal. McDonagh, who had quite a wrestle with anxiety himself, has developed specific and doable steps on how to approach anxiety: Diffuse, Allow, Run Toward It, Engage. He’s quick to argue that anxiety is not our fault. “In the United States alone,” McDonagh writes, “approximately 40 million American adults aged 18 and older are estimated to have an anxiety disorder. So if you suffer from anxiety, you’re actually quite normal.” This is an informative instruction on a complicated, overwhelming topic. Having experienced anxiety at different points of my life, this is hands-down my favorite book for how to move through and release anxiety, knowing it won’t hold me hostage.

books.title: Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience
books.author: Brené Brown
books.blurb: The latest from Brené Brown is a lavishly produced, graphically rich coffee table book, written in her inimitable style. She’s witty, vulnerable, and frank. She’s also brilliant. Atlas of the Heart—which has a companion HBO series—is devoted to finding language for our emotions. “To form meaningful connections with others,” Brown writes, “we must first connect with ourselves, but to do either, we must first establish a common understanding of the language of emotion and human experience.” As with everything Brown publishes, this is must-read material.

books.title: The Biology of Belief: Unleashing the Power of Consciousness, Matter & Miracles
books.author: Bruce H. Lipton
books.blurb: even bother trying to feel well if we have no control over our genes, good or bad? In case you missed Bruce Lipton’s 2005 masterpiece, The Biology of Belief, here’s the good news: we are not powerless to affect the expression of our genes. He writes, “When we change our beliefs, we change the blood’s neurochemical composition, which then initiates a complementary change in the body’s cells.” This is just the tip of the iceberg in understanding how our beliefs shape our biology. Though Lipton’s concepts are rooted in empirical research, you don’t need to be a scientist to understand what he’s saying. He seamlessly weaves data together with fascinating examples, and brings a great sense of humor to the table, too. This is an intriguing and extraordinary work.

books.title: The Power of Now: A Guide to Spiritual Enlightenment
books.author: Eckhart Tolle
books.blurb: Tolle’s sterling debut, 1997’s The Power of Now, posits a daringly simple truth: when we are in the now, the present moment, there are no problems. WTF? Our quest to avoid the now is what leads to suffering. Tolle teaches us how to step back from our thoughts and observe them instead of being ruled by them. His approach is gentle yet unapologetically direct. Having a tough moment? Turn to any page and Tolle will bring you back to the present. This book is now considered a classic, and a copy has been on my night table for decades. The companion volume, Practicing the Power of Now, sits right beside it.

books.title: The Anatomy of Anxiety: Understanding and Overcoming the Body's Fear Response
books.author: Ellen Vora
books.blurb: Vora makes an illuminating distinction between “false anxiety” and “true anxiety." “False anxiety” is an anxiety response brought on by a physical imbalance; but most importantly, it’s avoidable. And wouldn’t you know, many of the things we reach for to feel better actually make anxiety worse. Thankfully, though it's not easy, if we stop boozing, jacking ourselves up with caffeine and sugar, and prioritize sleep, amongst other things, we can quell some, if not all, of the discomfort. If you've addressed all physical components to anxiety but are still suffering, this is what Vora calls “true anxiety.” We think anxiety is so awful that it should be avoided at all costs, but Vora introduces an enlightening concept—anxiety is an opportunity to take stock of your life and see where things aren’t working for you. “Instead of asking, How can I stop feeling so anxious?,” she writes, “we should be asking, What is my anxiety telling me?” Might you be saying yes when you mean no? Are you in a job you hate? Do you have community? Vora, board certified in psychiatry and integrative holistic medicine, an acupuncturist and yoga teacher, considers the whole system, mind and body. Change is daunting, but Vora’s approach is brilliant, encouraging, and compassionate. This essential book reminds us that anxiety can be a messenger for positive change.

books.title: Mating in Captivity: Unlocking Erotic Intelligence
books.author: Esther Perel
books.blurb: Sex is the elephant in the room in a lot of long-term relationships. In her invaluable 2006 study, Mating in Captivity, Belgian psychotherapist Esther Perel challenges the myth of the “sexless marriage” and offers couples a foundation to keep erotic awareness and connectivity alive. Perel gives us compelling examples from her practice and forces us to reckon with our inherited assumptions about sex. This can be a painful read in how it forces the reader to examine their own relationship to sex, but Perel is encouraging and optimistic. She does not mince words or sugar-coat anything.

books.title: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art
books.author: James Nestor
books.blurb: Breathing: nothing more essential, right? In a stressful situation, we say, "Just breathe.” And yet, as we learn in James Nestor’s smart examination, many of us don’t know how to breathe effectively. Or at least, many of us don’t breathe in an optimal way. “No matter what we eat,” writes Nestor, “how much we exercise, how resilient our genes are, how skinny or young or wise we are—none of it will matter unless we’re breathing properly. The missing pillar of health is breath.” The book’s strength is in its helpfulness. Nestor provides practical applications of breathing exercises, addressing both how and why they help. Breath is a fantastic tool that provides huge insight into ourselves and our most inalienable right.

books.title: Connecting with Crystals: Crystal Wisdom and Stone Healing for Body, Mind, and Spirit
books.author: Laurelle Rethke Stay
books.blurb: with me here, because if you’re not already into crystals, they may initially seem ridiculously woo woo, but I am totally into them. I like being able to hold something in my hand, knowing it’s having a positive effect on me. Crystals are everywhere these days, but where to begin? Laurelle Rethke’s beautifully-designed guide is a comprehensive reference ideal for beginners and seasoned enthusiasts alike. We learn how crystals work and what to use them for, as well as how to choose them, care for them, clean them, etc. The book is as aesthetically attractive as it is informative. You may also want to consider The Crystal Healer, one of many fabulous books on the subject by Philip Permutt.

books.title: Set Boundaries, Find Peace: A Guide to Reclaiming Yourself
books.author: Nedra Glover Tawwab
books.blurb: It’s no revelation that having healthy boundaries is crucial to our overall well-being. That said, some of us would rather put darts in our eyes than set them. We all seem to have someone in our life with whom it feels impossible to set boundaries. Help arrives in Tawwab’s enlightening book, full of relatable examples from her therapeutic practice. She encourages the reader to set boundaries even when it's uncomfortable, as it’s ultimately a path to protect ourselves and feel better.

books.title: The Tapping Solution: A Revolutionary System for Stress-Free Living
books.author: Nick Ortner
books.blurb: Wait—you’re telling me that if I have physical or emotional pain, all I need to do is tap on specific acupressure points and that will help me feel better? According to Nick Ortner, the answer is yes. Emotional Freedom Technique (EFT), also known as tapping, combines ancient Chinese acupressure and modern psychology; when practiced, a message is sent to the amygdala—the emotional center of the brain—which activates a calming response. EFT is my go-to when emotions get too big and difficult. The most appealing thing about this modality is that it can be learned in minutes, as you’ll discover in Ortner’s indispensable guide. He shares how he personally benefited from EFT, includes the history and science behind tapping in sharp detail, and provides user-friendly descriptions of the practice. Ortner is amusing, articulate, and very real. While you’re at it, consider Peta Stapleton’s excellent book, The Science of Tapping.

books.title: The Science of Stuck
books.author: Britt Frank
books.blurb: We all experience feeling stuck at different points in our lives. We know what to do, Britt Frank writes in her winning and revelatory book, yet we’re unable to bridge the gap between desire and action. Frank delves into the science behind why we get stymied, and it’s a relief to learn it’s not because we’re lazy or unmotivated. “Lazy is a moral judgment,” writes Frank, “not a biological reality.” There are legitimate reasons why we get stuck. And then there’s the sobering, dirty truth: we actually can benefit from being stuck. Whaaat? Yes: if we don’t try, we can’t fail, lose money, or be shamed—for starters. Frank provides a clear understanding of what’s happening in the brain when we’re stuck and offers practical solutions. She writes in a lively and conversational style, peppered with pop culture references. Understanding that stuck is a function of the brain and not who we are frees us from judgement and paves the way forward.

books.title: Dying to Be Me: My Journey from Cancer, to Near Death, to True Healing
books.author: Anita Moorjani
books.blurb: Anita Moorjani was about to die. She slipped into a coma after a four-year battle with cancer, and during her near death experience, she learned a radical truth: self-love is the answer. Upon her return from the near death experience, she shifted to living from a place of love, not fear. Moorjani is an evocative writer, which makes her personal story even more dramatic and compelling. The bright side is that you don’t need a near-death experience to embrace her life-changing principles. I can’t count how many times I’ve read this book. I’m endlessly inspired.

books.title: Move The Body, Heal The Mind: Overcome Anxiety, Depression, and Dementia and Improve Focus, Creativity, and Sleep
books.author: Jennifer Heisz
books.blurb: It comes as no surprise that there's a connection between exercise and good mental health. “Regular exercises tones the stress response,” writes Heisz, “making us less reactive to psychological stressors, and this promotes optimism, even amidst the most seemingly uncontrollable situations.” What’s refreshing about Heisz’s approach to exercise is her understanding that everyone’s threshold is different. The goal is to find the sweet spot between doing too little and too much. Heisz champions the low-and-slow approach and provides custom regimens for different afflictions, like addiction, poor sleep, and anxiety. This is especially appealing for those of us that have a hard time getting started—and Heisz addresses that, too. By turns, empathetic, personal, and practical, this is a smart, terrific resource.

books.title: Living Untethered: Beyond the Human Predicament
books.author: Michael A. Singer
books.blurb: Singer author of the classic self-help book the untethered soul, is back with his latest—a brilliant, observant, no-nonsense bit of good mental health. Singer wastes no time putting things in perspective. “It took 13.8 billion years for this moment to get here, and every single thing had to happen exactly as it did—but I don’t like it,” we like to complain. “That’s funny,” Singer continues, “it’s like saying that you don’t like that Saturn has rings.” If we can surrender what we think we want, we can have a more peaceful and harmonious life. “Remember,” cautions Singer, “you are not surrendering life; you are surrendering your resistance to life.” Put this on your summer reading list.

books.title: The Power of Regret: How Looking Backward Moves Us Forward
books.author: Daniel H. Pink
books.blurb: When someone says they have no regrets, you know immediately they’re full of it. Everyone can find an example of when they wish they’d handled something differently. You don’t have to be a regretful person; it can just be that one nagging regret that’s been stinging you for decades. But what if regret teaches us how to make better decisions in the future? That’s the animating idea of Daniel Pink’s heavily-researched and entertainingly written work. Regret, he argues, can be transformative. You know—manure into marigolds! “Self-compassion reframes the regret as a human imperfection rather than an incapacitating flaw,” writes Pink. I never imagined something as heavy and painful as regret could be a well to draw from. Intelligent, approachable, and liberating.

books.title: The Universe Has Your Back: Transform Fear to Faith
books.author: Gabrielle Bernstein
books.blurb: This 2016 bestseller from Gabrielle Bernstein will transform your life. We try to control our lives, insisting things go as we desire, but this insistence is often based in fear. Turning fear into love is Bernstein’s central message. Instead of demanding things go our way, she argues that “when we surrender to the power of the Universe we will always be guided to exactly what we need.” Bernstein shares intimate stories about how she’s taken her hands off the steering wheel, knowing the universe has her back.

books.title: Judgment Detox: Release the Beliefs That Hold You Back from Living A Better Life
books.author: Gabrielle Bernstein
books.blurb: Judgment. We judge ourselves, we judge others, we judge ourselves for judging others. Judging can be a destructive and insidious force—one that's hard to reel in. As Gabrielle Bernstein points out in her transformative book, judgment “is a form of emotional pain that you want to relieve.” Judging is a deflection from the true pain beneath the surface. In a six-step interactive process built on spiritual practices such as Emotional Freedom Technique (EFT), meditation, and prayer, Bernstein offers an invaluable roadmap to help break these habits, all told in her approachable manner with vivid, intimate detail.

books.title: When Things Fall Apart: Heart Advice for Difficult Times
books.author: Pema Ch”dr”n
books.blurb: Pema Ch”dr”n is a pioneer and legend of American Buddhism. Her teachings are rooted equally in sobering truth and gentle compassion. You can’t go wrong with any of her books or teachings, but I love her 1997 classic, When Things Fall Apart. It’s a natural inclination to avoid uncomfortable feelings, but avoidance perpetuates suffering. “If we’re willing to give up hope that insecurity and pain can be exterminated,” Ch”dr”n writes, “then we can have the courage to relax with the groundlessness of our situation.” When we don’t resist, she argues, we discover the jewels in our circumstances. Obstacles are friends, not enemies, and the path is always the goal. She will lead the way.

books.title: The Little Book of Breathwork
books.author: Catherine Carrigan
books.blurb: Catherine Carrigan’s 2019 jewel, packed with insight and instruction, is anything but little. “Your breath is your power,” she writes. “Whether you realize it or not, you derive all of your personal power from your breath.” This book is filled with specialized breathwork techniques for many common ailments, including anxiety, depression, asthma, and fatigue. Carrigan also provides breathing exercises to improve energy and happiness, as well as clearing emotions and the mind. Carrigan is so accomplished—she’s a medical intuitive, yoga instructor, kinesiologist, holistic lifestyle coach—that you don’t quite know how she has time to breathe. Carrigan is the author of numerous books, and this one is a gift that keeps giving.

books.title: Unfu*k Yourself: Get Out of Your Head and into Your Life
books.author: Gary John Bishop
books.blurb: At first blush, you can’t be blamed if you’re resistant to take Gary John Bishop’s less-than-delicately titled Unfu*k Yourself seriously (never mind Love Unfu*ked and Stop Doing That Sh*t). But this neat, trim volume is just the kick in the ass you need. Bishop is blunt without being a jerk. He’s a realist who encourages us to skip our excuses and face our true resistance. What are we willing and unwilling to do? This is where our truth lives, he argues. This brisk, unapologetic book challenges us to take more agency over our lives, circumstances, and desires. It was exactly what I needed to hear.

books.title: Forest Bathing: How Trees Can Help You Find Health and Happiness
books.author: Qing Li
books.blurb: You don’t have to be Henry David Thoreau or Rachel Carson to appreciate that being in nature is good for the mind, body, and spirit. But too often our concept of being outdoors is to be active—hiking, climbing, biking, etc. The beauty of Forest Bathing (a fast-growing healing modality), as Dr. Quing Li explains, is that we can simply be still in the forest amongst the trees and feel better. This elegantly designed book will show you how and why being in the forest is replenishing, restorative, and healing. Good and good for ya.

books.title: The Joy of True Meditation: Words of Encouragement for Tired Minds and Wild Hearts
books.author: Jeff Foster
books.blurb: “Stress is the tension between this moment and your mental image of how this moment should be,” writes Jeff Foster in this beautiful, demystifying appreciation of meditation. This isn’t an instructional book—it doesn’t offer exercises, but rather it's a series of essays on the practice, like a meditation on meditation. Foster writes from the gut, and his authenticity is off the charts. This is a book I want to give to everyone I know. If you saw my heavily underlined, highlighted, and dog-eared copy of this compact but powerful volume, you’d understand why.

books.title: The Happiness Trap: How to Stop Struggling and Start Living: A Guide to ACT
books.author: Russ Harris
books.blurb: does the pursuit of happiness often result in anything but feeling happy? Maybe because we confuse happiness with gratification. In this neatly-organized examination, Harris outlines how we fall into the happiness trap—and how to pull ourselves out. He employs Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a program based on six principles that concentrate on mindfulness, values, and action. The ACT program is not spiritual or religious, Harris points out. It’s not meditation or a path to enlightenment. “ACT is a scientifically based program for creating a meaningful life through accepting our internal experience, staying present, and acting on our values,” he writes. Sensible and hands-on, it works.

lists.title: Books A Man Should Have Read by

books.title: War And Peace
books.author: Leo Tolstoy
books.blurb: Much of this epic tome is not set in conflict at all, but don’t worry, even the “peace” parts of War and Peace are plenty enjoyable. The scenes Tolstoy sets during Russia’s epic struggles against Napoleon’s forces in the early 19th century have some of the finest moments ever wrought on paper. You see in this novel heroism but also have myriad examples of the utter stupidity of warfare, and often Tolstoy manages to entwine these two aspects masterfully, such as when Prince Andrey Bolkonsky rises up after an injury and charges back into battle with a mighty “Hurrah!” At first, your heart surges and you charge alongside him, but in seconds you’re thinking: “Actually … what the hell are you doing?”

books.title: The Long Walk
books.author: Slavomir Rawicz
books.blurb: Potential Spoiler Alert: there have been allegations that much of this memoir is exaggerated, if not outright fabricated. It is the story of a Polish officer’s epic journey from captivity in a WWII-era Soviet prison camp to freedom in British India, a journey of thousands of miles… all conducted on foot. If the story is 100% true it ranks as one of history’s the greatest tales of escape and perseverance. If it’s even partially sort of accurate, it’s still an amazing epic. Put aside the notions of truth and fiction and simply enjoy the book, as whether it’s more fact or more fiction, it is still a raw yet elegant tale of manly perseverance.

books.title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
books.author: Ernest Hemingway
books.blurb: Many mistakenly believe Hemingway to be a war veteran, but in reality, the closest he came to combat was being insignificantly wounded while volunteering as a Red Cross ambulance driver during the First World War. However lacking in firsthand experience, he would continue to revisit mortal conflict in both his fiction and his nonfiction. Like another book later in this list, Bell does have some basis in reality. It was researched by Hem himself while working as a war correspondent during the Spanish Civil War and going behind enemy lines to meet a man very much like his protagonist, Robert Jordan. The theme of one man against long odds not only betrays the writer's admiration for the trait but also for the cause itself, and he, like the late photographer Robert Capa and many others, deeply sympathized with the Second Spanish Republic's doomed fight against fascism. Its antagonists would prove a durable enemy, as the rise of the Nazi Germans during World War II would play a role in both Hemingway's own life and in that of his fiction.

books.title: The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay
books.author: Michael Chabon
books.blurb: Two cousins — Joe Kavalier, who escaped Prague on the last train before the Nazis sealed the border; Sam Clay, a Brooklyn kid who has never been anywhere — build a comic book empire in 1940s Manhattan. The city is the specific possibility space of American immigrant ambition: the place where someone with nothing but talent and desperation can, briefly, make something. Pulitzer Prize, 2000. The novel does what the best New York fiction does — treats the city not as a backdrop but as a condition, the density and proximity of Manhattan as the precondition for a collaboration that would have been impossible anywhere else. Cross-references to the American Fiction Classics list. Nothing on this list captures the promise of the American city at its mid-century peak with comparable warmth or narrative momentum.

books.title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
books.author: Jane Jacobs
books.blurb: Jacobs was not a planner, not an architect, and not an academic, which is why she could see what all three were missing. Her argument — that cities work when streets are busy, blocks are short, buildings are mixed in age and use, and density is high; and that urban renewal was doing the opposite of all four — demolished the postwar planning consensus and has not been successfully refuted since. The canonical entry on this list and the book that everything else here is in conversation with, whether the author knows it or not. Cross-references to the Political History & Power list for the Robert Moses dimension, and to The Power Broker on the US History list, which documents what happened to New York because the planners rejected everything Jacobs argued for.

books.title: Paris: The Biography of a City
books.author: Colin Jones
books.blurb: Paris has been continuously inhabited for 2,000 years, has twice been the center of the Western world, and has been deliberately demolished and rebuilt at least once — Haussmann's 1860s demolitions cleared out the working-class neighborhoods that had staged three revolutions in forty years and replaced them with the boulevards tourists now photograph. Jones moves from Roman Lutetia through the medieval city to the present, making clear at every stage that a city's current form is always a political choice made by someone with power and a purpose. The city biography entry for the European half of this list. Cross-references to the French History list for the political history underlying the urban decisions Jones is documenting. Read alongside Istanbul for what it looks like when the political choice is melancholy rather than triumphant.

books.title: The Fountainhead
books.author: Ayn Rand
books.blurb: Howard Roark is an architect who refuses to compromise his designs for clients, committees, or critics, and the novel is the sustained argument that this refusal is morally correct. Set largely in New York, the city functions as the arena where individual vision confronts institutional mediocrity — the newspapers, the architectural establishment, the public housing bureaucracy. Note: Rand is arguing a case from an Objectivist perspective and the novel is her philosophical manifesto; the architecture is the vehicle, not the subject. At 700 pages the longest fiction entry on this list. Cross-references to the American Fiction Classics and Political History & Power lists. The reader who wants the architectural argument without the ideology should read Learning from Las Vegas and The Architecture of Happiness instead; the reader drawn to the ideology should know Atlas Shrugged makes the same argument with more scope.

books.title: Up in the Old Hotel
books.author: Joseph Mitchell
books.blurb: Mitchell wrote about New York for The New Yorker from 1938 to 1964 — the waterfront bars, the oyster cellars, the old men who still remembered the city before electricity, the characters of the Fulton Fish Market — and produced the most complete portrait of a city in the process of disappearing while still fully present. The deep cut on this list: serious readers of New York treat it as scripture; the general reader has rarely been pointed toward it. Mitchell stopped writing after 1964 and spent the last thirty years of his career walking into The New Yorker every day and producing nothing — the most mythologized writer's block in American journalism. Cross-references to the Essays & Longform Journalism list. Read Here Is New York first for the compressed version of what Mitchell spent four decades documenting.

books.title: City of Quartz
books.author: Mike Davis
books.blurb: Los Angeles, Davis argues, is a city engineered to keep its poor invisible — gated communities, privatized public space, police architecture designed to make sleeping outdoors physically painful, zoning laws that concentrate poverty in places the freeways bypass. Davis is not producing a polemic; he is making a documented case with aerial photographs, city planning documents, and police statistics. Note: arguing from a hard-left urban studies perspective and the case is sustained and specific. The most uncomfortable entry on this list and the one most likely to produce anger — at Davis, at Los Angeles, at American urban policy as a category. Cross-references to the Political History & Power list. The reader who wants the counterargument should read Joel Kotkin's The City: A Global History, which covers the same urban patterns from a diametrically opposed political position.

books.title: The Corner
books.author: David Simon & Ed Burns
books.blurb: Simon and Burns spent a year on the corner of Monroe and Fayette in West Baltimore in 1993, documenting the drug economy in real time — the hierarchy of the corner, the economics of the package, the specific daily lives of the people who worked and used there. The material became the empirical foundation for The Wire, but the book is not a companion to the show. It is the primary source account of how the American drug war looks from inside the community it claims to be protecting: the costs measured not in arrests and seizures but in the people whose lives organized themselves around a corner that should not have existed. Cross-references to the True Crime list. The reader who has watched The Wire will find the book darker and more specific; the reader who hasn't should read this first.

books.title: Tokyo Vice
books.author: Jake Adelstein
books.blurb: Adelstein was the first non-Japanese staff reporter at a major Japanese daily, covered the Tokyo Metropolitan Police beat for twelve years, got too close to the yakuza, and was told to either drop a story or be killed. The account he wrote is the best portrait of Tokyo available to a Western reader — not the temples and cherry blossoms but the hostess bars, the organized crime economy, the police who made deals they shouldn't have, and the specific texture of a megalopolis of fourteen million people operating under a system of social obligation that produces both extraordinary order and extraordinary corruption. Cross-references to the True Crime and East Asian History lists. The primary source entry for Japan on this list and the one most likely to permanently alter how a Western reader thinks about what Tokyo actually is.

books.title: Here Is New York
books.author: E.B. White
books.blurb: White rented a hotel room on East 48th Street in the summer of 1948 and spent several days writing what he saw from the window and remembered from his years in the city. The fifty pages that resulted are the most precise account of what New York is and why it matters ever written — the three New Yorks (the one of the native, the one of the commuter, the one of the person who came seeking something), the specific loneliness of eight million people living in voluntary proximity, the city as the destination of everyone who finds everywhere else too small. The short entry on this list. Cross-references to Up in the Old Hotel on this list, which documents the same city four decades earlier at full length, and to the Essays & Longform Journalism list.

books.title: Gotham: A History of New York City to 1898
books.author: Edwin G. Burrows & Mike Wallace
books.blurb: From the Lenape to the consolidation of the five boroughs in 1898 — 1,400 pages of the most consequential city in the Western world, reconstructed from ships' logs, court records, newspapers, and contemporary accounts that most historians hadn't touched. The Pulitzer Prize committee called it the definitive history of New York and no serious challenge to that assessment has been mounted since. At 1,400 pages it is the largest commitment on this list, but it is organized into digestible sections and written for general readers rather than specialists. The comprehensive city biography entry. For the story of what New York became after 1898, Robert Caro's The Power Broker on the US History and Political History & Power lists covers the Moses years with comparable authority and considerably more anger.

books.title: Low Life
books.author: Luc Sante
books.blurb: Sante documented New York's criminal underworld from 1840 to 1919 — the dive bars of the Bowery, the opium dens of Chinatown, the gangs with names like the Whyos and the Hudson Dusters, the confidence men, the pickpockets, the street culture of a city simultaneously building its greatest monuments and running on vice and violence at every level below the surface. The research is archival — period photographs, court records, newspaper morgues — and the writing is that of a man who loves what he is documenting and knows it is entirely gone. The deepest cut on this list and its best-kept secret: the reader who thinks they know New York's history will find here everything the official version omitted. Cross-references to the Outlaws & Rogues Bios and True Crime lists.

books.title: Triumph of the City
books.author: Edward Glaeser
books.blurb: Glaeser's argument is direct: cities are the most successful human invention in history, and the policies designed to help people escape them — mortgage interest deductions, highway subsidies, zoning laws enforcing low density — have made both cities and suburbs worse while damaging the economy and the environment. The overview entry on this list and the accessible counterweight to Jacobs: where she explains how cities work from street level, Glaeser explains why they matter from altitude. Note: arguing a case from a market-oriented economics perspective. The reader who finishes this and wants the policy debate should go directly to The Death and Life; the reader who wants the deeper urban economics should read Alain Bertaud's Order Without Design, which covers the planning mechanics Glaeser summarizes.

books.title: Evicted
books.author: Matthew Desmond
books.blurb: Desmond embedded in Milwaukee's poorest neighborhoods in 2008 and followed eight families and two landlords through a year of eviction proceedings — a process in which eviction is not an emergency but a routine, landlords extracting maximum rent from people with no alternatives while courts process hundreds of cases per day. Pulitzer Prize, 2016. Note: Desmond is arguing a case from a left-progressive policy perspective and the book builds toward a specific housing policy recommendation. The journalism is primary-source regardless of the politics, and the reporting is thorough. The uncomfortable entry on this list. Cross-references to the Political History & Power and Economics & How the World Works lists for the policy dimensions. The reader who wants the complementary street-level account should go to The Corner on this list.

books.title: Midnight's Children
books.author: Salman Rushdie
books.blurb: Saleem Sinai is born at the exact moment of Indian independence — midnight, August 15, 1947 — and his life is entangled with his nation's from that instant forward. The city is Bombay, now Mumbai, and Rushdie uses it the way Dickens used London: as a character that is simultaneously the setting, the subject, and the condition of possibility for everything that happens. The most ambitious fictional portrait of a non-Western city in English-language literature. Booker Prize, 1981; voted the best Booker winner of the prize's first twenty-five years. Cross-references to the World Fiction in Translation list and the South Asian History list, where the Independence and Partition context is documented without the magic realism. Read alongside Istanbul for the comparison between two cities whose relationship to their own former greatness defines their inhabitants' psychology.

books.title: Gang Leader for a Day
books.author: Sudhir Venkatesh
books.blurb: Venkatesh arrived in the Robert Taylor Homes housing project in Chicago in 1989 with a clipboard and a survey asking residents to rate their experience of poverty on a scale from 1 to 10. The gang leader who found him found the survey amusing and spent the next decade letting Venkatesh observe his operation. The result is the most complete account of how an urban economy at the bottom actually functions — the informal markets, the protection payments, the rational organizational structure of operations entirely outside the legal system. Venkatesh is honest about his own ethical compromises in obtaining the access. Cross-references to The Corner on this list, which covers the same economic reality from the street level in Baltimore; and to the Political History & Power list for the institutional context that makes these economies both necessary and permanent.

books.title: The Image of the City
books.author: Kevin Lynch
books.blurb: Lynch sent researchers into Boston, Jersey City, and Los Angeles with instructions to ask residents to draw maps of their cities from memory. The maps were wildly inconsistent — what some remembered vividly, others couldn't locate — and Lynch used them to develop a theory of how people navigate urban space through five elements: paths, edges, districts, nodes, and landmarks. The deep cut on this list: every city planner and urban designer has read it; almost nobody else has, despite the fact that it explains why some cities feel coherent and others feel impossible to navigate. Under 200 pages. Cross-references to The Architecture of Happiness on this list for the psychological complement to Lynch's spatial theory, and to The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces for the behavioral complement.

books.title: Boss: Richard J. Daley of Chicago
books.author: Mike Royko
books.blurb: Daley ran Chicago from 1955 to 1976 and built the last great American urban political machine — precinct captains who delivered votes in exchange for city jobs, contracts routed to loyalists, and the 1968 Democratic Convention managed with police violence when the situation required it. Royko covered Daley for the Chicago Daily News and produced the definitive portrait of American machine politics: funny, precise, and more honest about how the system actually delivered services to working-class neighborhoods than most reformers were willing to admit. The humor entry on this list — Royko was the best newspaper columnist in Chicago, which was always saying something. Cross-references to the Political History & Power list. The reader who wants Chicago's racial geography should follow this with Arnold Hirsch's Making the Second Ghetto.

books.title: London: The Biography
books.author: Peter Ackroyd
books.blurb: Ackroyd treats London as a living organism with a continuous personality across 2,000 years of occupation. He organizes the book thematically rather than chronologically — chapters on noise, on rats, on the Thames, on fog, on the specific light of the city at different seasons, on districts that have housed the same trades and characters for centuries despite everyone inside them changing. At 800 pages it is not a quick read, but it can be entered anywhere without losing the thread. The artsy entry for the city biography section, and the one that reads most unlike conventional urban history. Cross-references to the British History list for the straightforward chronological account this book deliberately refuses to provide. The reader who wants Ackroyd at shorter length should try his biography of Dickens, which covers the same city through a single life.

books.title: Down and Out in Paris and London
books.author: George Orwell
books.blurb: Orwell spent time in both cities poor enough to work as a dishwasher in hotel kitchens — plongeur in the Paris argot — and documented what the city looks like from the bottom with the precision of a man who had chosen to be there rather than fallen there accidentally. The specific arithmetic of poverty, the way the city reveals different aspects of itself to people who have enough money and to people who don't, the invisible economy of the street — all of it exact. The unexpected-angle entry on this list: approaches the city through the experience of being invisible in it. Under 250 pages. Cross-references to the Essays & Longform Journalism list, where Orwell's essays appear as a primary entry. Read alongside Gang Leader for a Day for the American equivalent of what Orwell was documenting in 1930s London and Paris.

books.title: Manhattan Transfer
books.author: John Dos Passos
books.blurb: New York from 1890 to the 1920s, told through a dozen characters — a ferry captain's daughter, a labor organizer, an actress, a newly arrived immigrant — whose lives intersect and separate across three decades of the city's transformation from a walking city to a metropolitan machine. Dos Passos invented the polyphonic urban novel technique that Döblin, Steinbeck, and a generation of novelists borrowed, and used New York as the subject because it was the first city in the world where the overwhelming fact of modern life — that millions of strangers press their lives against yours without either of you choosing it — had become the central condition of existence. The historical fiction entry on this list and its deepest fiction cut. Cross-references to the American Fiction Classics list.

books.title: The Architecture of Happiness
books.author: Alain de Botton
books.blurb: De Botton's argument is that the spaces we inhabit affect how we feel and think — not metaphorically but causally — and that architecture is therefore a moral practice rather than merely an aesthetic one. He moves through the history of Western architecture examining what each style was trying to achieve for the people inside it, and why some buildings make their occupants feel capable and others make them feel diminished. The artsy entry for the architecture half of this list and the most accessible book on the built environment for a reader who hasn't thought much about it. Under 280 pages. Cross-references to The Image of the City and Learning from Las Vegas on this list, which approach the same questions through empirical observation and provocation rather than through philosophy.

books.title: Istanbul: Memories and the City
books.author: Orhan Pamuk
books.blurb: Pamuk grew up in an Istanbul that knew it had once been the capital of the Ottoman Empire and could not decide how to feel about it. The Turkish word hüzün — collective melancholy, the grief of a city watching itself become provincial — is the book's organizing concept, and Pamuk builds his memoir around it: black-and-white photographs of the Bosphorus, the ruins of waterfront mansions, the last Ottoman writers who mourned what the city had lost. Nobel Prize, 2006. The literary city memoir on this list: part autobiography, part city biography, part essay on memory and place. Cross-references to the World Fiction in Translation and Middle East and Islam History lists. Read alongside Paris for the contrast between a city that razed its past and a city that cannot stop mourning it.

books.title: Invisible Cities
books.author: Italo Calvino
books.blurb: Marco Polo describes fifty-five cities to Kublai Khan, seated across from each other in the palace garden. Each city is a meditation — on memory, desire, signs, the dead, the continuous present, the impossible future. None of the cities exists. Calvino published this in 1972 and it remains the purest literary argument for why cities matter at all: not as physical infrastructure but as shared fictions that make collective life possible, the agreements between strangers that allow millions of people to live pressed against each other. Under 175 pages. Cross-references to the World Fiction in Translation list. The reader who wants a conventional novel about a city should go to Manhattan Transfer on this list; the reader who wants to understand cities as a philosophical proposition should start here and work outward.

books.title: Learning from Las Vegas
books.author: Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown & Steven Izenour
books.blurb: In 1972, three architects argued that Las Vegas was the most architecturally significant city in America — not because it was beautiful but because it was honest about what it was: a landscape of signs designed to communicate to people in cars at 35 miles per hour. The argument demolished the modernist consensus that good architecture should be silent and pure, and established that the commercial vernacular — the strip, the billboard, the decorated shed — was worth taking seriously as a subject. The deep cut on this list: essential reading in architecture schools, almost unknown outside them, despite explaining more about how American commercial space looks than any other book written. Under 200 pages. Cross-references to The Architecture of Happiness for the philosophical complement and Boss for what the people driving through those signs were voting for.

books.title: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
books.author: William H. Whyte
books.blurb: Whyte mounted time-lapse cameras on New York office buildings in the 1970s and spent years watching what people actually did on plazas and sidewalks when nobody was designing their behavior. What he found contradicted everything planners assumed: formal seating and open space drove people away; crowding, street food vendors, and ledges at sitting height brought them in. The empirical entry on this list and its most surprising short read — under 125 pages, almost entirely observation, every page counterintuitive. The unexpected-angle entry: approaches city design through behavioral science rather than aesthetics or ideology. Cross-references to The Image of the City, which covers how people cognitively map urban space; this covers how they physically occupy it. The reader who finishes it will never walk through a plaza without reading it differently.

books.title: Kitchen Confidential
books.author: Anthony Bourdain
books.blurb: Bourdain spent twenty-five years in professional kitchens and this account covers the specific brutality of restaurant work — the knife skills and station discipline that separate competent cooks from professionals, the specific culture of people who choose to work with fire and sharp metal in hundred-degree rooms for twelve hours a day. Around 312 pages and the most readable professional craft memoir available. The book that looks like culinary gossip and turns out to be one of the most precise accounts of what professional mastery looks and feels like from the inside — the physical skill, the mental organization, the specific pride of work done under pressure. Michael Ruhlman's The Soul of a Chef covers the same world from the training side at around 352 pages and is the serious companion for the reader who wants the full professional arc.

books.title: The Art of Eating
books.author: M.F.K. Fisher
books.blurb: Fisher wrote about food during WWII rationing, during her years alone in Provence, during poverty and grief and pleasure, and what she produced was not recipes but the argument that eating well is a moral and intellectual practice available to anyone willing to pay attention. The five books collected here — How to Cook a Wolf, The Gastronomical Me, Consider the Oyster, and two others — established the vocabulary that all American food writing since has used. The artsy entry on this list and the literary anchor: the reader who finds food writing frivolous will find Fisher's refusal to apologize for the subject both bracing and instructive. W.H. Auden said she was one of the best prose writers in America. He was right. Cross-references to the Essays & Longform list.

books.title: Heat
books.author: Mike Lupica
books.blurb: Knowing that boys love sports, there are children’s authors who churn out one cookie cutter sports story after another. And then there is Mike Lupica. Lupica gives the kind of vivid play by play details that every good sports book needs, while also filling out his characters and their stories off the field with enough interest and realism to make the reader care. Heat’s plot is of the Law & Order ripped from the headlines variety; Cuban-American Michael Arroyo is a star pitcher who’s chances of leading his team to the Little League World Series are jeopardized when he is accused of being older than 12. Not only that, but Arroyo’s parents are dead and he must keep social services from finding out. Sounds schmaltzy, but Lupica manages to keep it topical and relevant without being heavy handed. If your boy digs it, be sure to check out the myriad of Lupica’s other sports-themed offerings.

books.title: The Man Who Ate Everything
books.author: Jeffrey Steingarten
books.blurb: Steingarten was appointed food critic of Vogue and decided to take the job seriously enough to conquer his food phobias — kimchi, Indian desserts, Greek cuisine, clams — by eating them repeatedly until he liked them. The resulting book is the humor entry on this list: a man applying rigorous scientific methodology to the question of why he irrationally dislikes certain foods, and documenting his findings with the precision of someone who knows the comedy is in the methodology rather than the subject. Steingarten is also genuinely expert, which makes the humor land differently than food writing that tries to be charming without knowing anything. Under 400 pages. Cross-references to the Psychology & the Mind list for the behavioral science of food preference he keeps stumbling into.

books.title: The Apprentice
books.author: Jacques Pépin
books.blurb: Pépin began his kitchen career at thirteen in his mother's restaurant in Lyon, cooked for three French heads of state including de Gaulle, arrived in America in 1959, and turned down a position as White House chef to cook alongside Julia Child instead. The memoir he wrote covers all of it — the brigade system of French professional cooking before it was romanticized, the physical standards that produced the greatest generation of French chefs, and what it meant to bring that tradition to a country that didn't know it needed it. The biography entry on this list and its deepest cut: almost everyone knows Bourdain and almost nobody has read this. Cross-references to the Artists & Writers Bios list for the craft dimension.

books.title: Salt: A World History
books.author: Mark Kurlansky
books.blurb: Salt preserved the fish that fed medieval Europe, financed the construction of Rome's roads, caused the American Civil War's supply crisis, and gave Gandhi his most effective political weapon against British imperial rule. Kurlansky traces the mineral's role in human history from ancient China through the French salt tax that helped trigger the Revolution to the American salt industry's role in the Civil War, and the accumulation of evidence that a condiment shaped civilization is genuinely surprising. The unexpected-angle entry on this list — it approaches food history through a single ingredient and demonstrates that the history of what humans eat is the history of everything else. Under 500 pages and reads faster than that. Cross-references to the World History list.

books.title: Blood Bones & Butter
books.author: Gabrielle Hamilton
books.blurb: Hamilton grew up in a family that fell apart, worked in professional kitchens from her teens through her twenties, opened Prune on a shoestring in Manhattan's Lower East Side, and wrote the most honest chef memoir since Bourdain — hungrier, stranger, and more literary than Kitchen Confidential. Where Bourdain wrote about the kitchen as a place of belonging for the misfit, Hamilton writes about it as a place of survival for someone who had no other plan. The prose is exact and the self-examination is uncomfortable in ways that make the book linger. The deep cut on this list: the food world considers it essential and it has never found the audience Kitchen Confidential did. Cross-references to the Coming-of-Age Fiction list for the bildungsroman dimension.

books.title: Fast Food Nation
books.author: Eric Schlosser
books.blurb: Schlosser spent three years reporting on the American fast food industry — the feedlots, the slaughterhouses, the flavor laboratories in New Jersey that synthesize the smell of cooking food for use in processed products, the franchise system that transfers wealth upward while appearing to distribute it — and produced the most rigorous account of how industrial food works available to a general reader. Note: Schlosser is arguing a case from a left-progressive consumer-advocacy position and the book is a sustained polemic. Include it because the reporting is thorough and primary sources are identified, and because the AoM reader should know what he is eating and where it came from before deciding how he feels about it. Cross-references to the Omnivore's Dilemma, which covers adjacent ground with less anger and more systems thinking.

books.title: The Whole Beast: Nose to Tail Eating
books.author: Fergus Henderson
books.blurb: Henderson opened St. John restaurant in a former London smokehouse in 1994 and built his menu around the principle that an animal's death deserves more respect than most restaurants give it: if you kill the pig, you eat the trotters, the ears, the bone marrow, the blood. The book is part cookbook and part philosophical argument, and the argument — that squeamishness about offal is a moral failure masquerading as a preference — is made without moralizing. The primary source entry: Henderson was there for the nose-to-tail movement before it became a trend, and this is the document that started it. Cross-references to the Manual's meat cookbook list, where the practical application of Henderson's philosophy is covered by books that don't also constitute a manifesto.

books.title: The Omnivore's Dilemma
books.author: Michael Pollan
books.blurb: Pollan traced four meals back to their origins: a McDonald's lunch back through the industrial corn system that produced it; an organic supermarket dinner back through its supply chain; a meal from a sustainable farm he worked on himself; a meal he hunted and foraged entirely. The exercise produced the most rigorous account of how Americans actually eat and what that eating costs — environmentally, nutritionally, and morally. Note: Pollan argues a case from a broadly environmental perspective, and the argument is well-evidenced regardless of where you start politically. The uncomfortable entry on this list. Cross-references to the In Defense of Food entry on the Fitness & Physical Culture list, which covers the nutritional dimension; this covers the agricultural and cultural dimension in considerably more depth.

books.title: Consider the Fork
books.author: Bee Wilson
books.blurb: Every tool in a kitchen — the pot, the knife, the stove, the refrigerator, the fork itself — has a history that reflects how the people who used it thought about cooking, eating, and the relationship between them. Wilson moves through those tools chronologically and geographically, and what emerges is a history of human ingenuity applied to the most fundamental daily problem: how to feed yourself and the people around you.
