books.blurb: Richards has been a member of the Rolling Stones for sixty years and spent approximately thirty of them in a state that should have been incompatible with playing guitar at that level. The memoir he wrote with James Fox at seventy is the humor entry on this list: Richards is funny the way very old men who have survived everything are funny — with the equanimity of someone who stopped keeping score. The chapters on the early Stones are primary source documents of how a specific counterculture got made from the ground up, by broke kids in South London who loved Black American music and had no reason to believe they would succeed. Cross-references to the Books About Music list. For the darker account of the same period from closer to the chaos, Tony Sanchez's Up and Down with the Rolling Stones — written by the Stones' personal drug dealer — covers the same years from a different vantage point.

books.title: The Sixties
books.author: Todd Gitlin
books.blurb: Gitlin was president of Students for a Democratic Society in 1963 and spent the decade at the center of the movement before spending the following twenty years trying to understand what went wrong. The book he produced is the most honest reckoning with the counterculture written by someone who was inside it: the strategic failures, the ideological self-destruction, the specific ways the movement's excesses handed its opponents exactly the ammunition they needed. Note: Gitlin is arguing a case from a left-liberal perspective and the book is simultaneously a history and a confession. The aftermath entry on this list — the one that asks what the counterculture actually accomplished and what it destroyed in the process. Cross-references to the Political History & Power list. The reader who wants the conservative counterargument should read Allan Bloom's The Closing of the American Mind, published the same year.

books.title: Please Kill Me
books.author: Legs McNeil & Gillian McCain
books.blurb: McNeil and McCain conducted hundreds of interviews with the Stooges, the Velvet Underground, the New York Dolls, the Ramones, Television, Blondie, the Sex Pistols, and everyone connected to all of them, then assembled the transcripts into an oral history that reads as fast as the music sounds. The result is the most complete account of how punk was made — not the mythology but the specific people, the specific venues, the specific decisions about what to play and how loud to play it. The rock culture entry on this list and arguably the best book here: the voices are irreplaceable and McNeil knew everyone. Cross-references to the Books About Music list. The reader who wants the British equivalent should read Jon Savage's England's Dreaming, which covers the Sex Pistols and the UK punk moment at comparable depth with a more analytical framework.

books.title: Trainspotting
books.author: Irvine Welsh
books.blurb: Edinburgh heroin addicts in the 1980s choose, in Welsh's formulation, life — or they choose heroin, which is the same sentence with different punctuation. Welsh writes in phonetic Scots dialect and the effect is either immersive or impenetrable depending on the reader; most readers find it immersive within twenty pages. The fiction entry on this list and the one that deals most directly with addiction as a subject rather than a lifestyle: the people in this novel are not romanticizing anything, and Welsh is not asking you to. The most honest literary account of what dependency actually looks like from inside it, without the redemptive arc that American addiction narratives typically require. Cross-references to the Noir & Hard-Boiled Crime Fiction list. The reader who wants the American equivalent — same subject, different city, different decade — should read Hubert Selby Jr.'s Requiem for a Dream.

books.title: Storming Heaven
books.author: Jay Stevens
books.blurb: Stevens spent years reconstructing how LSD moved from a Swiss laboratory in 1943 to the center of the American counterculture twenty years later — through the CIA's MKULTRA program, through Cary Grant's psychiatric therapy, through Ken Kesey's Merry Pranksters, through Timothy Leary's Harvard experiments and subsequent expulsion, and finally into Haight-Ashbury in 1967 where it arrived as a sacrament for a movement that was already burning itself out. The uncomfortable entry on this list: the government was both suppressing and distributing the compound simultaneously, and the counterculture's most sacred tool was partly a product of Cold War weapons research. The most comprehensive single account of the LSD moment. Cross-references to the Political History & Power list for the MKULTRA dimension. Read The Doors of Perception first for Huxley's framework; this is the history of what happened when that framework met the American 1960s.

books.title: Junky
books.author: William Burroughs
books.blurb: Burroughs wrote this in 1952 as a factual account of heroin addiction in New York, New Orleans, and Mexico City — the buying, the using, the withdrawal, the specific economics of supporting a habit in 1940s America. No redemption arc. No insight about what it means. The writing is deliberately flat, journalistic, and unadorned, which makes it more disturbing than any heightened prose style could. It is the better Burroughs entry point for the reader who has been told to read Naked Lunch and bounced off the first page: the same man, the same material, the same refusal of conventional narrative, at one-third the difficulty. Under 200 pages. Cross-references to the New Journalism & Literary Nonfiction list for the immersion reporting method. The reader who gets through Junky and wants more should attempt Naked Lunch knowing what they're walking into.

books.title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
books.author: Hunter S. Thompson
books.blurb: Thompson and his attorney drive to Las Vegas in 1971 loaded with every controlled substance available to assess the American Dream at the moment of its final failure. The novel version — different from the journalism elsewhere — uses the drug intake as a diagnostic instrument: the more extreme the behavior required to feel anything, the more clearly something has gone wrong with the culture that produced the need. Thompson was writing the obituary for the 1960s, and he knew it. "We had all the momentum; we were riding the crest of a high and beautiful wave." The wave broke. Cross-references to the Essays & Longform Journalism list, where Fear and Loathing on the Campaign Trail '72 appears as a primary entry, and to the Motorcycles list, where Hell's Angels covers the earlier Thompson. This is the one to read last, after you know what he was mourning.

books.title: The Doors of Perception
books.author: Aldous Huxley
books.blurb: Huxley took four-tenths of a gram of mescaline on a May morning in 1953, sat in his Los Angeles study, and spent eight hours perceiving the ordinary world as though he had never seen it. He wrote this account immediately afterward, and it became the intellectual framework for the entire psychedelic movement: Leary read it, the Grateful Dead read it, every serious thinker who followed the 1960s counterculture into mysticism read it first. The argument Huxley makes — that the brain is a reducing valve, filtering out most of experience for practical reasons, and that certain substances briefly remove the filter — is either the most important insight about consciousness in the 20th century or a rationalization for recreational drug use. He does not resolve this question. Under 100 pages. Cross-references to the Religion & Faith list for the mystical experience dimension.

books.title: Howl and Other Poems
books.author: Allen Ginsberg
books.blurb: Ginsberg read this at the Six Gallery in San Francisco in October 1955 to an audience of about 150 people. It begins: "I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness, starving hysterical naked." The poem ran to 112 lines and took about forty minutes to read aloud and changed American poetry permanently. City Lights published it the following year; customs officials seized copies at the border as obscene; a trial followed; Ginsberg won. The primary source entry on this list: before the Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test, before Fear and Loathing, this is where the argument began — that conformist America was destroying its own people. Under 75 pages. Cross-references to the Poetry Collections list. The reader who wants the biographical context should go to the Ginsberg biography by Barry Miles, which documents everything the poem alludes to.

books.title: The Haight-Ashbury
books.author: Charles Perry
books.blurb: Perry was a Rolling Stone editor who lived in the Haight during the Summer of Love and wrote the only serious week-by-week account of what actually happened rather than what was later remembered. The mythology collapsed faster than anyone admits: by October 1967, four months after the "Summer of Love" began, the Haight community held a mock funeral for the Death of the Hippie. The drugs had attracted people who were not equipped for them. The community had attracted people who were not equipped for community. Perry documents the arc without nostalgia. The deep cut on this list: known to serious historians of the period and almost nobody else. Cross-references to the Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test on the New Journalism list, which covers the Prankster dimension of the same cultural moment from the road rather than the neighborhood.

books.title: Wild Swans
books.author: Jung Chang
books.blurb: Chang traces three generations of her family across the full arc of twentieth-century China — her grandmother, a warlord's concubine in the final years of imperial China; her mother, a Communist Party official who gave everything to the revolution; and herself, coming of age as a Red Guard during the Cultural Revolution before becoming one of its targets. The Cultural Revolution chapters — where teenage zealots destroyed everything the civilization had built and turned children against parents as a matter of revolutionary duty — are among the most disturbing things on this entire project. Chang writes it as personal history rather than political analysis and the effect is more devastating for it. The book that belongs here rather than the Cold War list because it covers the full Chinese human experience, not just the superpower competition.

books.title: Country Driving
books.author: Peter Hessler
books.blurb: Hessler spent a decade as the New Yorker's China correspondent and wrote the essential account of what the fastest economic transformation in human history actually looks like from the inside. Three acts: driving the length of the Great Wall following a newly paved road, renting a farmhouse in a village north of Beijing and watching it transform as the economy arrives, and embedding in a factory town in Zhejiang province watching young women from rural Sichuan become industrial workers. The Wall sections give this historical depth that complements the dedicated Great Wall entry elsewhere on this list. For the reader who wants China's business disaster comedy alongside the transformation story, Tim Clissold's Mr. China covers losing $400 million in the emerging economy of the 1990s with the darkest possible humor.

books.title: The Chrysanthemum and the Sword
books.author: Ruth Benedict
books.blurb: The US government commissioned this in 1946 to help Americans understand the culture they had just defeated — a culture whose soldiers fought with a ferocity that baffled commanders who had faced every other enemy in the war. Benedict was an anthropologist who had never visited Japan and worked entirely from interviews, documents, and films. The result is the most penetrating account of Japanese culture ever written by an outsider: the distinction between shame culture and guilt culture, the specific Japanese relationship with obligation and hierarchy, the way Bushido was adapted into industrial militarism, and why the same civilization that produced kamikazes also produced the disciplined postwar reconstruction that followed. Written without condescension and without the exoticizing that ruins most Western accounts of Japan. Still the essential book for understanding what the Meiji transformation built and what it eventually became.

books.title: The Great Wall
books.author: John Man
books.blurb: The wall tourists visit today was built by the Ming dynasty in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — a different structure from the earthwork barriers the Qin and Han dynasties built two thousand years earlier, and almost certainly not visible from space. Man covers the full history of wall-building in China across multiple dynasties: what each version was actually trying to accomplish, how effective it was as a defensive barrier, and the specific paradox of a civilization that spent centuries building the largest structure in human history against nomadic peoples it could never quite defeat. Country Driving, elsewhere on this list, opens with Hessler following a road that traces the Ming Wall and gives the modern ground-level view. Man gives you the full 2,000-year story that explains what Hessler is looking at.

books.title: Samurai William
books.author: Giles Milton
books.blurb: In 1600 an English navigator named William Adams became the first Westerner to reach Japan and the first foreigner ever granted the rank of samurai. Tokugawa Ieyasu — in the process of unifying Japan and becoming its shogun — used Adams as a naval advisor and shipbuilder, refused to let him leave for a decade, and gave him a feudal estate and a Japanese wife. Milton covers the collision of Elizabethan England and samurai Japan, the texture of a feudal military culture seen through genuinely foreign eyes, and the question of what happens to a man when the world he was born into becomes permanently unreachable. Around 320 pages and reads like a thriller. James Clavell fictionalized the same story in Shogun if you want 1,200 pages of it; Milton's true account is more interesting.

books.title: Korea: A Walk Through the Land of Miracles
books.author: Simon Winchester
books.blurb: Winchester walks the length of the Korean peninsula in 1988, just before the Seoul Olympics, using the journey to cover Korean history from the Three Kingdoms period through the Japanese occupation and the division. The medieval sections — the Goryeo dynasty that gave Korea its name, the Korean genius for ceramics and printing technology, and the Joseon dynasty's 500-year run as one of the most stable governments in Asian history — are the least covered material in English-language popular history and Winchester handles them with the care of a man who knows he is filling a genuine gap. The Cold War list carries the Korean War story through Halberstam's The Coldest Winter; this list carries everything that came before it and made that war matter.

books.title: When China Ruled the Seas
books.author: Louise Levathes
books.blurb: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming dynasty sent seven massive treasure fleets into the Indian Ocean under Zheng He, a Muslim eunuch admiral whose flagship was four times the size of anything Columbus sailed. The fleets reached East Africa, traded with Arabia, and established Chinese diplomatic presence across Southeast Asia — then the Ming court reversed course, banned oceangoing ships, and burned the records. China deliberately chose isolation at the precise moment Europe was beginning its age of exploration, and the question Levathes raises — what if it hadn't — is one of the most compelling counterfactuals in world history. Around 250 pages, genuinely propulsive, and the best argument this list makes for the specific contingency of Western dominance. The Ming dynasty's full story continues in Country Driving's account of what that civilization eventually became.

books.title: Angkor and the Khmer Civilization
books.author: Michael Coe
books.blurb: The Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat — the largest religious monument ever constructed, a stone temple complex covering 400 acres in the Cambodian jungle — and then disappeared so completely that nineteenth-century European explorers refused to believe Cambodians could have built it. Coe is an archaeologist who covers the full arc of Khmer civilization: the hydraulic engineering that fed a city of a million people, the Hindu-Buddhist religious synthesis expressed in the architecture, the military campaigns that extended the empire across Southeast Asia, and the specific mystery of the collapse in the fifteenth century that archaeologists are still arguing about. Written for general readers rather than specialists and exactly the lost-civilization material that makes history lists worth building. Jon Swain's River of Time covers the ruins as a journalist witnessed them falling to the Khmer Rouge if you want the modern companion.

books.title: Records of the Grand Historian
books.author: Sima Qian, trans. Burton Watson
books.blurb: Sima Qian was China's Herodotus — the court historian who wrote the definitive account of Chinese history from the Yellow Emperor through the Han dynasty around 100 BCE, covering the Warring States period, the First Emperor who ended it, and the full sweep of the civilization that followed. He wrote part of it after the emperor had him castrated for defending a general who surrendered to the Xiongnu — a detail that tells you everything about both men. The Burton Watson translation is the one to get: Watson was a literary translator first, a sinologist second, and the English reads cleanly rather than like a scholarly exercise. The Chinese names require some patience, but Watson minimizes the problem more than anyone else who has attempted this text.

books.title: Hokkaido Highway Blues
books.author: Will Ferguson
books.blurb: Canadian writer Will Ferguson hitchhikes the length of Japan following the cherry blossom front from the southern tip of Kyushu to the northern tip of Hokkaido — a journey of several months through a country whose hitchhiking culture consists entirely of people who cannot believe anyone is hitchhiking. Ferguson is funny in the way that produces insight rather than condescension, and the Japan he encounters — the obsessive politeness, the vending machines selling things that have no business being in vending machines, the salarymen who pour their entire identity into a company that regards them as interchangeable — is the real Japan seen through genuinely curious foreign eyes. The best humor entry point to Japanese culture available, and the right note to end a list that has covered 2,500 years of East Asian history.

books.title: The Art of War / The Book of Five Rings
books.author: Sun Tzu / Miyamoto Musashi
books.blurb: Sun Tzu wrote the Art of War during the Warring States period — 250 years of seven kingdoms fighting for supremacy that also produced Confucius and the first unified Chinese empire. At 60 pages it is the most continuously influential military text ever written; the Victor Mair translation, working from bamboo strip manuscripts discovered in 1972, is the one to get. Miyamoto Musashi wrote The Book of Five Rings in a cave in 1645, distilling a life spent undefeated in over sixty duels — including one fought with a wooden sword carved from an oar on the boat to the island. The William Scott Wilson translation is clean and direct. Two short books, combined reading time of an afternoon, and between them the foundational strategic thinking of two civilizations. Both cross-seed with the Craft, Skill and Mastery list.

books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
books.author: Daniel Kahneman
books.blurb: Kahneman spent fifty years studying how people actually make decisions — as opposed to how economic theory says they should — and this is the summary account of everything he found. Around 499 pages covering System 1 and System 2 thinking, loss aversion, anchoring, the planning fallacy, and the specific cognitive biases that make human beings systematically irrational in predictable and exploitable ways. The behavioral economics entry and the most practically useful book on this list: the reader who finishes it will recognize every bias being deployed against him in every negotiation, advertisement, and political speech for the rest of his life. Richard Thaler's Misbehaving covers the institutional history of behavioral economics — how it fought its way into mainstream economic theory — at around 432 pages and belongs alongside it for the reader who wants the full disciplinary story behind Kahneman's research.

books.title: The Wealth of Nations
books.author: Adam Smith
books.blurb: Smith published this in 1776 — the same year as the Declaration of Independence, which is not a coincidence in terms of what was in the air — and produced the foundational argument for market economics: that the division of labor drives productivity, that prices are information, that free exchange between self-interested parties produces collective prosperity through no one's intention or design. The Penguin Classics abridged edition at around 560 pages is the practical entry point — the full Cannan edition runs to 1,100 pages and most of it is eighteenth-century economic data the argument doesn't require. The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Smith's earlier work arguing that human moral judgment is grounded in sympathy rather than self-interest, is the essential companion that most readers of Smith never reach — and the book that complicates the invisible hand in ways worth understanding.

books.title: The Big Short
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.blurb: Already on the Business list — cross-seeding here as the money and banking entry because it does more than document a financial crisis. Lewis's account of the investors who figured out the mortgage-backed securities market was fraudulent documents the specific ways that financial intermediation disconnects risk from consequence at a systemic level, creating incentives for behavior that is individually rational and collectively catastrophic. Around 266 pages and the most readable account of how financial markets actually work available — not how they're supposed to work, but how they work when the people operating them have every incentive to pretend the difference doesn't exist. The Ascent of Money by Niall Ferguson covers the full history of financial instruments from Babylonian grain futures through hedge funds at around 358 pages and is the essential historical companion.

books.title: The Worldly Philosophers
books.author: Robert Heilbroner
books.blurb: The overview entry and the most readable history of economic thought available — around 365 pages covering the great economists from Adam Smith through Thorstein Veblen and Keynes, explaining what each was trying to solve and why his solution mattered. Heilbroner was an economist who could write, which turns out to be rarer than it should be, and the result is essential context for every other book on this list: the specific historical conditions that produced each theory, the specific problems each thinker was trying to solve, and the specific ways each solution created the problems the next thinker inherited. Read this first if the classical texts feel daunting, or read it after Smith and Hayek and Marx to understand where each fits in the larger argument. Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics covers the analytical principles at around 704 pages for the reader who wants the full framework.

books.title: Grand Pursuit
books.author: Sylvia Nasar
books.blurb: Nasar wrote A Beautiful Mind and brought the same biographical intelligence to this account of eight economists — Marx, Marshall, Beatrice Webb, Fisher, Schumpeter, Keynes, Hayek, Friedman, and Amartya Sen — who spent two centuries trying to answer whether economics could improve the human condition. Around 558 pages and the most readable intellectual biography of the economics profession available: not a history of economic theory but a history of the people who built it, the specific historical circumstances that formed their ideas, and the specific ways their arguments changed how governments and markets operate. The biography entry on this list and the one that makes the rest of the list's arguments feel like they were written by actual human beings rather than by the dismal science.

books.title: Why Nations Fail
books.author: Daron Acemoglu & James Robinson
books.blurb: The answer to the question the rest of this list raises — if markets work, why are most countries poor? Acemoglu and Robinson spent decades on this and the argument at around 529 pages is the most important economics book of the last twenty years: nations fail not because of geography, culture, or ignorance but because of extractive political and economic institutions that concentrate power and block the creative destruction that produces growth. Nations succeed when their institutions are inclusive — when property rights are protected, political power is distributed, and the rule of law applies to everyone including the people making it. The historical range is extraordinary: the same argument explains the divergence between Nogales, Arizona and Nogales, Mexico, between North and South Korea, between Venice at its peak and Venice under the oligarchy that followed. Cross-seeds with the World History reading on this project.

books.title: Resource Curse
books.author: Tom Burgis
books.blurb: Burgis spent years as a Financial Times correspondent documenting how natural resource wealth — oil, diamonds, copper, coltan — systematically corrupts the governance of the countries that have it. Around 320 pages of the most politically pointed resource economics available: the specific mechanisms through which oil revenue funds kleptocracy, through which mining contracts enrich foreign companies and local elites while the population gets nothing, through which the curse operates not through bad luck but through specific institutional failures that extractive industries actively encourage. The political economy entry and the why-it-matters-now entry simultaneously — the argument that explains why the Democratic Republic of Congo, with more mineral wealth than almost any country on earth, has been at war for thirty years. Cross-seeds with the African History reading on this project.

books.title: Debt: The First 5,000 Years
books.author: David Graeber
books.blurb: The unexpected angle entry — and the most intellectually provocative book on this list after Marx. Graeber was an anthropologist who spent years arguing that conventional economic history is wrong about the origins of money: barter economies never existed as a historical reality, money emerged from debt relationships, and the entire moral framework of obligation and repayment underlying modern capitalism is a specific historical construction rather than a natural fact. Around 534 pages. Note the political perspective explicitly: Graeber was an anarchist and his conclusions about debt forgiveness and financial power are radical. Read it for the historical argument about money's origins — which is rigorously documented — and evaluate the political conclusions separately. The reader who finishes this and wants the mainstream counterargument should go directly back to Hayek.

books.title: The Road to Serfdom
books.author: Friedrich Hayek (ed. Bruce Caldwell)
books.blurb: Hayek wrote this in 1944 as a warning to British progressives that central economic planning, however well-intentioned, leads toward totalitarianism — not through malice but through the internal logic of planning itself. The price system, Hayek argues, is an information-processing mechanism of staggering complexity that coordinates the decisions of millions of people without anyone directing it, and any attempt to replace it with central direction destroys the signal while pretending to preserve the system. Note the political perspective: Hayek is arguing a classical liberal case for markets and against state intervention that the AoM reader will find more congenial than the Keynesian alternative. Bruce Caldwell's University of Chicago edition at around 266 pages includes the essential historical context. Milton Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom applies the same argument to specific policy questions at around 230 pages and belongs alongside it.

books.title: The Communist Manifesto
books.author: Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels
books.blurb: The uncomfortable entry — flagged explicitly. Around 50 pages and the most influential political-economic document of the twentieth century: the foundational argument that capitalism contains structural contradictions producing inevitable class conflict, that history is the history of class struggle, and that the bourgeoisie has created the conditions for its own destruction. The AoM demographic will disagree with most of it. They should read it anyway — because this argument shaped every major political event from 1848 through 1991 and understanding why it was so compelling to so many intelligent people is essential to understanding the world it helped create. Note the perspective: Marx is arguing for the abolition of private property and the dictatorship of the proletariat. Das Kapital Volume 1 provides the full economic proof at around 1,000 pages for the reader who wants the machinery behind the declaration.

books.title: Freakonomics
books.author: Steven Levitt & Stephen Dubner
books.blurb: Levitt is a University of Chicago economist who noticed that the most interesting economics questions are never about markets, and Dubner is a journalist who could write, and the collaboration produced the most readable economics book of the last twenty years. Around 242 pages of incentive analysis applied to sumo wrestling, drug dealing, the Ku Klux Klan, and the specific economic factors behind the 1990s crime drop. The humor entry and the gateway drug simultaneously — the book that proves economics is not the study of money but the study of how people respond to incentives, which turns out to be the study of almost everything. The AoM reader who thinks economics is about graphs and GDP will not think so after page twenty. Superfreakonomics covers the same territory a second time at around 270 pages for the reader who wants more of the same method applied to different problems.

books.title: How To Write An Autobiographical Novel
books.author: Alexander Chee
books.blurb: As for essay collections, Page tapped Alexander Chee’s How to Write an Autobiographical Novel. “Ohhhh,” he gushed. “It’s so good.” In this acclaimed collection, Chee takes stock of his life in literature, ruminating on how reading and writing have shaped the way he experiences the world. So, too, does he explore the connections between art and activism, and the many memorable jobs that have supported his writing, from reading Tarot to waiting on William F. Buckley’s table. Compassionate and caring, wistful and generous of spirit, Chee is a writer you’ll love getting lost with.

books.title: In the Dream House
books.author: Carmen Maria Machado Page
books.blurb: In the Dream House is mind-shatteringly impressive. In it, Machado recounts her history with an abusive girlfriend by deploying multiple genres and forms (“Dream House as Noir,” “Dream House as Lesbian Cult Classic,” etc.) to tell the story of the relationship. In so doing, she emphasizes the dearth of common language for narratives of queer domestic abuse, building an unforgettable work of memoir and criticism.

books.title: Split Tooth
books.author: Tanya Tagaq
books.blurb: Rounding out Page’s list is one final novel: Split Tooth, by Tanya Tagaq. “It’s one of the best things I’ve ever read,” he gushed. “Amazing. Amazing. Amazing. The last two pages of her book are just this whole beautiful piece about: I don’t want to forgive. But I forgive myself. I’ll pick it up every once in awhile just to read that.” Written by an acclaimed Inuit throat singer, Split Tooth straddles poetry and prose to tell the story of an Inuit teenager coming of age in the spectral Arctic landscape, where she faces alcoholism, bullying, and teen pregnancy. But no earthly force can keep her down; told in soaring episodes of magical realism, her story is one of spirituality, shamanism, and pure magic.

books.title: Somebody's Daughter
books.author: Ashley C. Ford Page
books.blurb: also described Ashley C. Ford’s award-winning memoir Somebody’s Daughter as “fantastic.” In this searingly honest story, Ford recounts her turbulent coming of age in Indiana, where she was raised by a volcanic and sometimes abusive mother. Her childhood was haunted by the specter of her incarcerated father, whom she idealized as the loving and supportive parent she lacked. When an adult Ford learns that her father will be released after almost thirty years, she is ushered to reckon with the heinous crime he committed. Her vulnerability on the page is an extraordinary feat.

books.title: Real Life
books.author: Brandon Taylor
books.blurb: Though Page describes his literary diet as mostly nonfiction, two novels snuck into his reading list. The first is Brandon Taylor’s Real Life, a sensational debut novel shortlisted for the prestigious Booker Prize. “It’s fantastic,” Page said. “He’s such a phenomenal writer, it just floors you.” Real Life is a poignant, exacting story about Wallace, a biochemistry student at a Midwestern university, whose Blackness and queerness alienate him from his small community of friends. Taylor is an extraordinary cartographer of Wallace’s loneliness, crafting a finely wrought story of academia, intimacy, and identity. Want to get a taste of Taylor’s distinctive style before diving headfirst into Real Life? Read an original story by him here at Esquire.

books.title: Punch Me Up to the Gods
books.author: Brian Broome
books.blurb: memoir that made Page’s list is Brian Broome’s Punch Me Up to the Gods. “That is absolutely one of the best things I’ve ever read,” he said. “Amazing. A. Mazing. Astounding.” In this unflinching debut, Broome explores what it means to be poor, Black, and queer in America through the lens of his own childhood in rural Ohio. Abused by his parents and segregated within his community, Broome writes with breathtaking rawness and vulnerability about how the world he knew as a child shaped the man he became.

books.title: Amateur
books.author: Thomas Page McBee
books.blurb: Page's post-interview pick is Amateur, an illuminating memoir by Thomas Page McBee. “Amateur is a beautiful and powerful book written by the superbly talented Thomas Page McBee, who I was lucky to work with on the new season of Umbrella Academy," Page said. "This memoir is such an important piece of trans literature to support and one that spoke to me deeply.” Amateur is McBee's account of his decision to train as a boxer and become the first transgender man to fight a cisgender man in Madison Square Garden. Through boxing, McBee confronts the violent inheritance of toxic masculinity, while also learning powerful truths about how the boxing ring can bond men together. Lyrical and vulnerable, Amateur asks if violence and maleness must go hand in hand. You can read McBee's account of writing for the third season of The Umbrella Academy here.

books.title: The Power Broker: Robert Moses and the Fall of New York
books.author: Robert A. Caro
books.blurb: Robert Moses never held elected office. He also shaped the physical landscape of New York — and by extension the template for American urban life in the 20th century — more decisively than any elected official in the country's history. Caro spent seven years reporting this book, and the result is the greatest work of American biography ever written and the most thorough examination of how power is actually accumulated and what it does to the man who holds it. At 1,200 pages it is the longest book on this list by a significant margin. It rewards every page. Caro's multi-volume LBJ biography is arguably the superior achievement; start here first, because this is where he figured out what he was doing.

books.title: Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller Sr.
books.author: Ron Chernow
books.blurb: I found Rockefeller to be strangely stoic, incredibly resilient, and, despite his reputation as a robber baron, humble and compassionate. Most people get worse as they get successful, many more get worse as they age. In fact, Rockefeller began tithing his money with his first job and gave more of it away as he became successful. He grew more open‑minded the older he became, more generous, more pious, more dedicated to making a difference. And what made Rockefeller stand apart as a young man was his ability to remain cool‑headed in adversity and grounded in success, always on an even keel, never letting excessive passion and emotion hold sway over him.

books.title: The Fish That Ate the Whale: The Life and Times of America’s Banana King
books.author: Rich Cohen
books.blurb: Zemurray arrived in America as a penniless Russian Jewish immigrant, spotted opportunity in overripe bananas nobody else wanted, built a trading empire from the docks of New Orleans, bought United Fruit when it was failing and ran it better than the Boston Brahmins who'd built it, and overthrew a Central American government when it got in his way. Cohen's biography is around 270 pages — one of the most purely entertaining business biographies of the last twenty years and the entry on this list most likely to be finished in a single sitting. Cross-seeds with the Americas reading on this project.

books.title: The Triumph of the American Imagination
books.author: Neal Gabler
books.blurb: Disney was not the cheerful uncle of the brand but a driven, depressive, often tyrannical man whose imagination was powered by a specific anxiety that never left him — a Kansas City boyhood of poverty and an emotionally withholding father who features recognizably in every Disney villain. Gabler covers the full arc from the early failures through Mickey through the studio strike through Disneyland and the death during EPCOT planning. Around 900 pages and one of the great American biographies — flag it as a long-game read going in and don't let the page count scare you off the best entry on this list.

books.title: Edison
books.author: Edmund Morris
books.blurb: Morris tells the life in reverse chronological order — starting with the deaf, cantankerous, failing old Edison and working back through the War of Currents against Tesla and Westinghouse, through Menlo Park, to the young inventor going deaf on a train platform in Ohio. Around 550 pages and the right combination of awe and skepticism: Edison was the greatest inventor in American history and also one of the most ruthless businessmen — the War of Currents was a campaign of deliberate public misinformation that makes modern tech industry practices look restrained. The structure sounds like a gimmick. It isn't.

books.title: Becoming Steve Jobs
books.author: Brent Schlender & Rick Tetzeli
books.blurb: Schlender knew Jobs for twenty-five years and covered Apple from the inside, and the result corrects the Isaacson biography's central failure — treating Jobs's story as a myth with a hero rather than a life with a man in it. The specific growth from the reckless, destructive genius who got fired from his own company to the something-more-like-wisdom of the NeXT and Pixar years and the second Apple act is the actual story, and Schlender tells it. Around 460 pages. Isaacson's Steve Jobs is the comprehensive myth-version — read Schlender first and Isaacson if you want the footnotes.

books.title: The House of Medici
books.author: Christopher Hibbert
books.blurb: The Medici were merchant bankers who used their money to build Renaissance Florence — commissioning Brunelleschi's dome, Michelangelo's David, Botticelli's Primavera — and then watched the dynasty collapse under the weight of its own success three generations later. The oldest entrepreneurial story on this list and the one with the highest cultural return on investment in human history. Hibbert covers the full arc from Cosimo through Lorenzo the Magnificent through the fall in around 360 pages of readable popular history. April Blood by Lauro Martines covers the Pazzi Conspiracy assassination attempt against Lorenzo in 1478 — one afternoon that nearly ended everything — and is the essential companion read.

books.title: On Her Own Ground
books.author: A'Lelia Bundles
books.blurb: Walker was the first self-made female millionaire in America — built a hair care empire from nothing in the early 1900s, trained hundreds of Black women as commissioned sales agents across the country, and used the money to fund anti-lynching campaigns and civil rights organizing at a time when both required personal courage of a different order than building a business. Bundles is Walker's great-great-granddaughter and had access to family papers unavailable to any other biographer. Around 368 pages and the most remarkable origin story on this list. Cross-seeds with African American history reading on this project.

books.title: Barnum: An American Life
books.author: Robert Wilson
books.blurb: Barnum invented American showmanship — the circus, the museum of curiosities, the manufactured celebrity — and did it with a specific cheerful amorality that makes him the most entertaining and most uncomfortable figure on this list. Wilson's biography is around 300 pages and the most complete account of a man who understood his audience better than anyone in nineteenth-century America. Neil Harris's Humbug makes the sharpest argument about what Barnum was actually doing: convincing audiences to participate in being fooled, which Harris argues is the foundational move of American consumer culture. Read Wilson for the life and Harris for the argument.

books.title: The People's Tycoon
books.author: Steven Watts
books.blurb: Snow's I Invented the Modern Age covers the builder years brilliantly but this list wants full arcs, and Watts delivers one — the specific genius of the assembly line and the five-dollar day, and the specific ugliness of the antisemitism and the Dearborn Independent and the decades of stubborn mismanagement that nearly killed the company Ford's grandson had to rescue. Around 600 pages and the most complete account of the man who reshaped daily American life more than any other industrialist. Ford's own My Life and Work is short, opinionated, and worth reading alongside Watts for the self-image versus the reality.

books.title: The First Tycoon
books.author: T.J. Stiles
books.blurb: Pulitzer Prize, around 720 pages, and the most underread of the great Gilded Age biographies. Vanderbilt built a ferry empire, then a railroad empire, in an era with no regulations, no unions, and no legal constraints worth mentioning — and he did it with a physical intimidation that Rockefeller and Carnegie, who worked through lawyers and accountants, never needed. Stiles covers the full brutal arc without softening the man. The specific nastiness of nineteenth-century American capitalism on full display, and more fun to read than it has any right to be.

books.title: Andrew Carnegie
books.author: David Nasaw
books.blurb: Carnegie came from nothing in Scotland, built the American steel industry, sold it to J.P. Morgan for $480 million in 1901, and spent the rest of his life giving the money away because he genuinely believed dying rich was dying disgraced. Nasaw covers the full arc in around 880 pages without the hagiography Carnegie's own memoir invites: the Homestead Strike massacre of 1892, in which Carnegie's partner Frick broke a union with Pinkerton agents and rifle fire while Carnegie hid in Scotland, gets the full treatment. Meet You in Hell by Les Standiford covers that chapter alone in 300 pages. Cross-seeds with British history reading on this project.

books.title: Howard Hughes: His Life and Madness
books.author: Donald Barlett & James Steele
books.blurb: The cautionary tale. Hughes was the most daring aviator of his generation, built a defense contracting empire, produced Hollywood films, owned Las Vegas casinos, and spent the last fifteen years of his life locked in darkened hotel rooms, injecting codeine, eating nothing but ice cream and chicken, letting his fingernails grow to four inches, and watching Ice Station Zebra on loop. Barlett and Steele are investigative journalists who spent years in the archives — around 600 pages and the most extreme example on this list of what happens when a builder's obsessive intensity consumes everything, including the builder. Cross-seeds with the Explorers & Adventurers reading on this project.

books.title: Made in America
books.author: Sam Walton with John Huey
books.blurb: Walton wrote this in the last year of his life while dying of cancer and it reads like a man who can't quite believe what he built — the specific Arkansas stubbornness, the Saturday morning store meetings at 7 a.m., the refusal to pay a dollar more for anything than he had to, and the genius of a man who understood that retail is a game of pennies played at continental scale. Around 350 pages and the most straightforward success story on this list. The autobiography of a man who died worth $25 billion and drove a 1979 Ford pickup with bird dogs in the back until the end.

books.title: Brunel: The Man Who Built the World
books.author: Steven Brindle
books.blurb: Brunel built the Great Western Railway, the SS Great Britain — the first ocean-going propeller-driven iron ship — the Clifton Suspension Bridge, and the SS Great Eastern, which remained the largest ship ever built for forty years. He did all of it in Victorian England before he was fifty-three, driving himself and everyone around him with a cigar permanently clamped in his mouth and a stovepipe hat he used as a portable filing cabinet. Around 320 pages and the right entry point into the most productive engineer who ever lived. The AoM reader who doesn't know Brunel will not believe the résumé.

books.title: WAR
books.author: Sebastian Junger
books.blurb: Although the war in Afghanistan has been going on for more than a decade, soldiers and cultural pundits alike have often noted how completely removed the vast majority of the American public is from that reality. Journalist Sebastian Junger closes that gap a little by transporting us to a hooch in the Korengal Valley where he spent five months living, sleeping, and coming under fire with the US 2nd Battalion. Junger offers a vivid, page-turning portrait of what it’s like to be in combat, the powerful bond between men who experience it together, the nature of the love and courage born from battle, and why despite its danger and hardships, men are drawn to it again and again. The book is a must-read, however, not simply because of its penetrating observations on war, but for its insight into the very nature of manhood and honor –- stripped to its most basic core.

books.title: Consider the Lobster
books.author: David Foster Wallace
books.blurb: Wallace applies his full intellectual machinery to subjects that don't expect it — the ethics of boiling lobsters alive at the Maine Lobster Festival, the talk radio industry as a political phenomenon, the pornography industry's annual convention in Las Vegas, John McCain's 2000 primary campaign — and the results are the best American literary essays of the decade. Around 343 pages. The lobster essay is famous; the piece on talk radio and the McCain essay are better, and the 100-page essay on usage and language that closes the collection is the most entertaining piece of prescriptive grammar ever written. String Theory, his tennis writing, appears on the Tennis list. This collection covers the rest of the territory. The reader who thinks Wallace is too difficult will find these essays more accessible than the novels and considerably funnier.

books.title: Slouching Towards Bethlehem
books.author: Joan Didion
books.blurb: Didion spent the late 1960s watching California come apart — the Haight-Ashbury at the peak of the Summer of Love, the specific unreality of the Los Angeles entertainment industry, the center of American culture failing to hold — and wrote about it with a coldness that made the essays feel like dispatches from a war zone rather than cultural criticism. The title essay on Haight-Ashbury is the best piece of American journalism of the 1960s and the most accurate account of what the counterculture actually looked like from inside rather than from the mythology that replaced it. Around 238 pages. The AoM reader who assumes Didion is a women's list writer will find she is a diagnostician of American self-delusion who happens to be a woman, which is a different thing entirely.

books.title: Arguably
books.author: Christopher Hitchens
books.blurb: Hitchens published this final collection in 2011, the year he died of esophageal cancer, and it is the fullest demonstration of what he could do: essays on Proust, on Orwell, on the Parthenon marbles, on Islamism, on Trotsky, on the alleged benefits of waterboarding (he tried it), and on a dozen other subjects, all written in prose that is precise, combative, and structurally immaculate. Around 750 pages and the most demanding book on this list — Hitchens assumes the reader has read widely and argues accordingly. Note the political perspective throughout: Hitchens was a former Trotskyist who became a supporter of the Iraq War, and the essays argue positions across the spectrum with equal force. The reader who disagrees with him on every political point will still finish the book having been shown what serious argumentative prose looks like.

books.title: Essays
books.author: George Orwell
books.blurb: Orwell wrote the most important political prose of the twentieth century in these essays — Politics and the English Language, which remains the best account of how dishonest language corrupts honest thought; Shooting an Elephant, about the specific psychology of colonial authority; Why I Write, about the four motives that produce serious prose. He wrote them between 1931 and 1950, while also writing Animal Farm and 1984, while also fighting in Spain, while also dying of tuberculosis. Around 1,400 pages in the full Penguin collection — the reader who wants a shorter entry point goes to the selected Penguin Essays of George Orwell at around 640 pages. The canonical entry on this list: the origin point of the British political essay tradition that Hitchens inherited and the standard against which all subsequent political prose is measured.

books.title: Fear and Loathing on the Campaign Trail '72
books.author: Hunter S. Thompson
books.blurb: Thompson covered the 1972 presidential campaign for Rolling Stone as it happened — filing dispatches from the press bus, the campaign hotels, and the convention floor with the specific combination of chemical impairment and political fury that produced the most honest account of how American presidential campaigns actually work. McGovern loses to Nixon in a landslide; Thompson documents every step of the machinery that produced the result, including the press corps that covered it. Around 506 pages and the political journalism entry on this list. Note the political perspective: Thompson hated Nixon with a specificity that occasionally distorts the reporting and never affects the accuracy of the structural observations. The reader who wants Thompson at his most purely entertaining goes to Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas; this is Thompson at his most useful.

books.title: The Right Stuff
books.author: Tom Wolfe
books.blurb: Wolfe covered the Mercury astronauts in 1979 and invented a way of writing nonfiction that hadn't existed before: the interior monologue of a man strapping himself into a rocket, the specific sociology of test pilot culture, the unspoken code of masculine competence that the astronauts called the right stuff and never defined directly because defining it would have violated it. Around 436 pages and the anchor entry on this list — the book that established what New Journalism could do when a writer with a novelist's toolkit was turned loose on a true story. The reader who finishes this and wants more Wolfe goes to The Kandy-Kolored Tangerine-Flake Streamline Baby for the early magazine work. The reader who wants the same approach applied to war goes to Michael Herr's Dispatches on the Cold War list.

books.title: The Essays of Montaigne
books.author: Michel de Montaigne
books.blurb: Montaigne invented the essay as a form in the 1570s — a French nobleman who retired to a tower, painted a question on the ceiling that read WHAT DO I KNOW?, and spent twenty years writing about cannibals, experience, friendship, idleness, cruelty, and the specific problem of how to live, producing in the process the most direct and honest prose in the European literary tradition before the twentieth century. The Penguin Selected Essays edited by M.A. Screech runs around 400 pages and is the right entry point. The origin point entry on this list: every essay writer since 1580 has been working in Montaigne's form whether they acknowledged it or not. The reader who expects Renaissance philosophy to be difficult will be surprised — Montaigne writes as if he is talking directly to whoever is reading, which is exactly what he intended.

books.title: Me Talk Pretty One Day
books.author: David Sedaris
books.blurb: Sedaris spent his twenties in New York failing to become an artist, moved to France in his forties and failed to become French, and wrote about both experiences with a self-deprecation so precise it reads as a form of autobiography. The humor entry on this list and the funniest book on it: the essays on his father's jazz obsession, his French language classes, his siblings, and his own consistent inability to be competent at anything he attempted are as well-constructed as anything in American comic writing. Around 272 pages. The AoM reader who approaches this skeptically because he has seen Sedaris on NPR will find the written work considerably darker and more structurally rigorous than the public radio persona suggests. The piece about his sister the taxidermist alone justifies the purchase.

books.title: Fame and Obscurity
books.author: Gay Talese
books.blurb: Talese spent his career at Esquire doing something nobody else did as well: spending months with a single subject — Frank Sinatra, Joe DiMaggio, a New York Times pressman, a bridge builder — until the accumulated detail produced a portrait that the subject could not have given in an interview and would probably have preferred not to exist. This collection covers the best of that work. The profile of Sinatra — written without a single interview because Sinatra refused to participate — is the most celebrated magazine piece in American journalism and demonstrates the method at its peak. Around 368 pages and the craft entry on this list: the reader who wants to understand how serious longform journalism is constructed comes here. Cross-seeds with the Craft, Skill & Mastery list.

books.title: Notes of a Native Son
books.author: James Baldwin
books.blurb: Baldwin wrote these essays between 1948 and 1955 — on Harlem, on his father's death, on the specific experience of being Black in America and in Europe, on the machinery of American racial self-deception — and published them in 1955 at 175 pages. The title essay, which interweaves his father's funeral with the Harlem riots of 1943, is the finest personal essay in American literature. Around 175 pages and the short entry on this list. The AoM reader who approaches Baldwin as a political writer will find he is primarily a literary writer whose subject happens to be the most important unresolved question in American history, which makes the politics more not less powerful. Cross-seeds with the American History list. The reader who wants more Baldwin goes directly to The Fire Next Time, the essential companion.

books.title: Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community
books.author: Robert D. Putnam
books.blurb: “Financial capital — the wherewithal for mass marketing — has steadily replaced social capital — that is, grassroots citizen networks — as the coin of the realm.” Like The Lonely Crowd, Bowling Alone is more dry and academic than fiery and opinionated. But because it highlights a negative trend of declining community involvement in America, this seminal work finds a home in the jeremiad genre. Written by Harvard political scientist Robert D. Putnam, Bowling Alone uses sociological surveys and data to showcase the decline of “social capital” — civic and community engagement — in America. The title from the book stems from the fact that while the number of people bowling is at an all-time high, the number of people bowling in leagues and on teams is at its all-time lowest. A similar decline can be seen amongst traditional civic and community-focused pursuits. Instead of spending time with their neighbors, Americans are increasingly inclined towards activities that are oriented towards the individual — television, internet surfing, and consumer spending. According to Putnam, if this shift continues it will have negative effects on democracy as well as individual well-being, and he therefore argues that all citizens should strive to establish stronger community bonds.

books.title: The Decline of the West
books.author: Oswald Spengler
books.blurb: “One day the last portrait of Rembrandt and the last bar of Mozart will have ceased to be – though possibly a colored canvas and a sheet of notes will remain – because the last eye and the last ear accessible to their message will have gone.” I have admittedly only begun reading this seminal two-volume work. Working my way very slowly through both tomes is a long-term goal of mine. The argument is surely intriguing enough: Oswald Spengler argues that cultures are essentially living organisms that pass through four seasons of development and decline, which parallel the four seasons of the year. In the early seasons, the culture is full of creative energy that leads to inward-focused growth. This spark of creativity dies out once the culture develops into a full-fledged civilization and enters the “winter” season. While we often think of civilization as a positive progression, for Spengler it is the last stage of the cultural organism’s lifespan (every culture lasts about 1,000 years) — a twilight of decay. Instead of growing, civilizations emptily expand outward. Vital life lies in the “things-becoming,” Spengler argues, not in “things-become.”

books.title: Manufacturing Consent: The Political Economy of the Mass Media
books.author: Edward S. Herman and Noam Chomsky
books.blurb: “The question is whether privileged elite should dominate mass communication and should use this power as they tell us they must — namely to impose necessary illusions, to manipulate and deceive the stupid majority and remove them from the public arena. The question in brief, is whether democracy and freedom are values to be preserved or threats to be avoided. In this possibly terminal phase of human existence, democracy and freedom are more than values to be treasured; they may well be essential to survival.” Noam Chomsky is one of the 20th century’s most polemic political and social critics. Whether you agree with his radical anacro-sydicalism or not, his critique of the self-censorship that happens in mass media in Manufacturing Consent should be read and considered by everyone. The main thesis of Manufacturing Consent is that because most large mass media companies are for-profit entities that rely on advertising to support the business, media firms will often self-censor themselves in order to prevent upsetting advertisers and losing money. Thus, when you watch or read the news, you might not be getting the full story. Chomsky and his co-author Edward S. Herman provide examples of when this non-coercive censorship occurred. Ever since I read Manufacturing Consent, I always read the news (from any source) with a bit of a suspicious squint.

books.title: No Logo
books.author: Naomi Klein
books.blurb: “Four years ago, when I started writing this book, my hypothesis was mostly based on a hunch. I had been doing some research on university campuses and had begun to notice that many students I was meeting were preoccupied with the inroads private corporations were making into their public schools. They were angry that ads were creeping into cafeterias, common rooms, even washrooms; that their schools were diving into exclusive distribution deals with soft-drink companies and computer manufacturers, and that academic studies were starting to look more and more like market research.” When No Logo was published in 1999, Naomi Klein lamented the infiltration of advertisements and branding into every nook and cranny of American life. While the culture of branding has changed in the years since (people aren’t as keen to wear clothes emblazoned with large names anymore, for example), in many ways the book is more relevant than ever. Companies have found even more nooks in which to place their branding; when you’re watching a football bowl game, it’s probably the Outback Bowl featuring the yard marker sponsored by GEICO, the red zone by Old Spice, the halftime show by Pepsi, the instant replay by Cadillac, and the field goal net by Allstate. Klein not only criticizes the ubiquity of branding, but the stranglehold corporations put on the number of consumer choices, and their exploitation of workers in the name of the free market.

books.title: The Closing of the American Mind: How Higher Education Has Failed Democracy and Impoverished the Souls of Today’s Students
books.author: Allan Bloom
books.blurb: “Students these days are, in general, nice. I choose this word carefully. They are not particularly moral or noble. Such niceness is a facet of democratic character when times are good. Neither war nor tyranny nor want has hardened them or made demands on them…Students these days are pleasant, friendly and if not great-souled, at least not particularly mean-spirited. Their primary preoccupation is themselves, understood in the narrowest sense.” Allan Bloom’s influential, oft-debated jeremiad takes as its focus the hollowing out of the once hallowed halls of higher education. But the book’s critiques range far wider to examine the shallowness of our culture’s intellect as a whole. Bloom argues that because the modern university has turned from the humanities, the philosophy of the ancients, and the idea of absolute Truth as the touchstone of education, students graduate without the ability to grapple with the serious questions, engage in vital self-examination, and choose the path to a meaningful life. Steeped in relativism, their only virtue is tolerance, and they see all truth claims as merely a set of different, and equally valid, “lifestyles.” Without the tools of philosophy to guide their decisions and thinking, students, and citizens as a whole, are ill-equipped to determine what “the good life” is. The solution, Bloom argues, is a return to an education rooted in the Great Books.

books.title: The Death of Character: Moral Education in an Age Without Good or Evil
books.author: James Davison Hunter
books.blurb: “We say we want a renewal of character in our day but don’t really know what we ask for. To have a renewal of character is to have a renewal of a creedal order that constrains, limits, binds, obligates, and compels. This price is too high for us to pay. We want character but without unyielding conviction; we want strong morality but without the emotional burden of guilt or shame; we want virtue but without particular moral justifications that invariably offend; we want good without having to name evil; we want decency without the authority to insist upon it; we want more community without any limitations to personal freedom. In short we want what we cannot possibly have on the terms that we want it.” James Davison Hunter traces the changing meaning of character, demonstrating how it went from being rooted in community-specific, externally-imposed standards, to being something each individual can define for themselves. Instead of basing the motivation to seek character on an understanding of good and evil, we offer the possibility of self-actualization; instead of speaking of “virtues,” we celebrate “values,” which are subjective and based on personal preference. He focuses on how this shift has affected “moral education” (how character is taught in schools) and covers the three main new alternatives to traditional character education: developmental psychology (you should do the right thing because it will make you feel better about yourself), neoclassicism (you should do the right thing because that’s the way it’s always been done), and communitarian (you should do the right thing so you can get along with others). Hunter argues that these new moral education programs are doomed to fail since they are not rooted in an ultimate truth and authority.

books.title: The Lonely Crowd: A Study of the Changing American Character
books.author: David Riesman
books.blurb: If the other-directed people should discover how much needless work they do, discover that their own thoughts, and their own lives are quite as interesting as other people’s, that, indeed, they no more assuage their loneliness in a crowd of peers than one can assuage one’s thirst by drinking sea water, then we might expect them to become more attentive to their own feelings and aspirations.” The Lonely Crowd is different from the traditional jeremiad — more dry and academic than angry and opinionated. But as it maps and predicts a potentially negative trend in American culture, and creates the kind of thought-provoking reflection that characterizes the jeremiad, I felt it belonged on this list. First published in 1950 as a sociological analysis of American life, the book continues to be called one of the most, if not the most, influential book of the 20th century. In the text, Riesman sets forth three types of “social character” — three mechanisms by which people conform to the society in which they live: tradition-directed, inner-directed, and other-directed. He posited that other-directed types — individuals who are sensitive to the opinions of their peers — were growing in number. But he also optimistically projected that a fourth type — the autonomous individual — could emerge in greater numbers over the decades as well. For a full exposition of the takeaways of The Lonely Crowd, check out this post.

books.title: Empire of Illusion: The End of Literacy and the Triumph of Spectacle
books.author: Chris Hedges
books.blurb: “Washington has become our Versailles. We are ruled, entertained, and informed by courtiers — and the media has evolved into a class of courtiers. The Democrats, like the Republicans, are mostly courtiers. Our pundits and experts, at least those with prominent public platforms, are courtiers. We are captivated by the hollow stagecraft of political theater as we are ruthlessly stripped of power. It is smoke and mirrors, tricks and con games, and the purpose behind it is deception.” Chris Hedges laments the splitting of the country into two camps: those who continue to grapple with rational, literate discourse and exist in reality, and the barely literate masses who increasing retreat from reality and into a world of illusion and spectacle. Hedges decries the dumbing down of political rhetoric, the insipid popularity of celebrity culture, and the way in which the media now caters to the lowest common denominator. Corporatism creates a craven consumerism that has suffocated our morals, and made self-gratification our only shared value. Everything from college to psychology must be feel-good, entertaining, and conveyed through images as to not tax our short attention spans. Yet beneath this flashy facade of superficiality, the culture is decaying. The country, Hedges worries, is headed for destruction unless we embrace serious discourse again and address problems like the rising cost of health care, the marginalization of the working class, and pending environmental catastrophes.

books.title: The Death of the West: How Dying Populations and Immigrant Invasions Imperil Our Country and Civilization
books.author: Patrick J. Buchanan
books.blurb: “In half a lifetime, many Americans have seen their God dethroned, their heroes defiled, their culture polluted, their values assaulted, their country invaded, and themselves demonized as extremists and bigots for holding on to beliefs Americans have held for generations.” This would probably be a good time to remind folks that jeremiads are supposed to make you angry, and that you don’t have to agree with them in order to get something out of them. No list of jeremiads could be complete without the controversial Mr. Buchanan, as he’s essentially made them his life’s work, and he’s one of the few remaining pundits who will actually criticize both his own political party as well as his opponent’s. In this book, Buchanan argues that the Western world will reach its demise not because of military conquest or catastrophe, but because of slowly changing population demographics. Because the affluent but morally decadent upper classes are not having children, and those in developing countries are, the latter will grow and subsume the former. He contends that immigrants are not assimilating and embracing Western values as they used to, so that when the old guard dies out, the traditional culture of the West will die with them.

books.title: The Culture of Narcissism: American Life in an Age of Diminishing Expectations
books.author: Christopher Lasch
books.blurb: While it was written nearly 25 years ago, many would argue that Christopher Lasch’s Culture of Narcism is even more relevant today. Lasch contends that the anomie that many feel in modern society is due to the rise of a “culture of narcissism” that has been brought about not by increasing vanity and puffed up self-esteem among the populace, but rather by a diminishing of the self thanks to the growth and intrusion of anonymous networks (government, corporations, media entities) into our everyday lives. According to Lasch, because people no longer have a solid sense of self and identity, they’re constantly seeking external validation and must make themselves “seen” by others to get it. He argues that this all-consuming craving for attention has had a damaging effect on the emotional, mental, and social health of our society.

books.title: The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains
books.author: Nicholas Carr
books.blurb: “The Net’s interactivity gives us powerful new tools for finding information, expressing ourselves, and conversing with others. It also turns us into lab rats constantly pressing levers to get tiny pellets of social or intellectual nourishment.” A jeremiad for a uniquely modern concern: the internet and its effect on our lives. Carr explores the way our brains not only shape the mediums we apply them to, but how those mediums in turn shape our brains. Which is to say, the different kinds of ways we use our brains creates different kinds of neural pathways in them. Carr worries that while internet surfing may be a boon in numerous ways, it’s weakening our minds, so that we can deftly skim through many things, but struggle to plunge deeply into just one.

books.title: Coming Apart: The State of White America, 1960-2010
books.author: Charles Murray
books.blurb: “A man who is holding down a menial job and thereby supporting a wife and children is doing something authentically important with his life. He should take deep satisfaction from that, and be praised by his community for doing so. If that same man lives under a system that says the children of the woman he sleeps with will be taken care of whether or not he contributes, then that status goes away. I am not describing a theoretical outcome, but American neighborhoods where, once working at a menial job to provide for his family made a man proud and gave him status in his community, and where now it doesn’t. Taking the trouble out of life strips people in major ways which human beings look back on their lives and say, ‘I made a difference.'” Charles Murray centers Coming Apart on the changing culture of white America over the last decades in order to illuminate his central thesis: that there is a new class divide in America that isn’t based on race, but on behavior and values. The lower class eschews work, marriage, and higher education, would rather drink and get high than get a job, doesn’t go to church, and doesn’t care what their neighbors are doing. In contrast, those in the upper class have strong, stable families, work hard, attend religious services, and are involved in their communities. In some ways it represents an inversion of the old order of things, when the working classes were more religious and apt to marry than their upper class counterparts. Murray contends that the classes have never been so far apart in mindset and lifestyle, and can barely understand each other anymore. He argues that the values of the lower class will have deleterious effects on the entire country, and exhorts all citizens to once again embrace what he sees as our four founding values: honesty, marriage, religiosity, and industry.

books.title: Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business
books.author: Neil Postman
books.blurb: “Americans no longer talk to each other, they entertain each other. They do not exchange ideas, they exchange images. They do not argue with propositions; they argue with good looks, celebrities and commercials.” Neil Postman spent his career critiquing our culture’s obsession with technology, mass-media, and entertainment. In his best known book, Amusing Ourselves to Death, Postman explored the impact “of the most significant American cultural fact of the second half of the twentieth century: the decline of the Age of Typography and the ascendancy of the Age of Television.” Postman argues that the medium greatly influences the message and that electronic and digital mediums are more conducive to mindless entertainment than to serious rational thinking. Because we live in an age of digital mediums, weighty topics that affect important parts of human life like politics, religion, and education are forced to be more entertaining to capture people’s attention. Hence, we are amusing ourselves to death.

books.title: Life Without Principle
books.author: Henry David Thoreau
books.blurb: “What is called politics is comparatively something so superficial and inhuman, that practically, I have never fairly recognized that it concerns me at all. The newspapers, I perceive, devote some of their columns specially to politics or government without charge…but as I love literature and to some extent the truth also, I never read those columns at any rate. I do not wish to blunt my sense of right so much. I have not got to answer for having read a single President’s Message. A strange age of the world this, when empires, kingdoms, and republics come a-begging to a private man’s door, and utter their complaints at his elbow!…The newspapers are the ruling power. Any other government is reduced to a few marines at Fort Independence. If a man neglects to read the Daily Times, government will go down on its knees to him, for this is the only treason in these days.” The Transcendentalists were some of America’s original cultural critics, and Henry David Thoreau penned many texts that have a jeremiad-like flavor. His “Life Without Principle” is a particularly worthwhile read. The wide-ranging essay decries the country’s narrow focus on business and making money, as well as the superficial nature of people’s conversations and their mindless devotion to equally superficial news. He argues that the news, particularly of the international variety, makes people feel like they’re engaging in something significant, when it really does not affect their lives at all. It is a distraction from higher things, so that his fellow citizens end up living in a free country, while remaining slaves to the profane and trivial.

books.title: Dumbing Us Down: The Hidden Curriculum of Compulsory Education
books.author: John Taylor Gatto
books.blurb: “Whatever an education is, it should make you a unique individual, not a conformist; it should furnish you with an original spirit with which to tackle the big challenges; it should allow you to find values which will be your road map through life; it should make you spiritually rich, a person who loves whatever you are doing, wherever you are, whomever you are with; it should teach you what is important: how to live and how to die.” John Gatto was a New York City public school teacher for 30 years. He was named NYC Teacher of the Year three times as well as New York State Teacher of the Year. After receiving the latter award in 1991, Gatto resigned, and began issuing jeremiads against compulsory public education – the very field in which he excelled and made his living for most of his life. Dumbing Us Down is a collection of essays and speeches by Gatto about the problems of public education. Gatto argues that public schools have several negative effects on children, including making them emotionally and intellectually dependent on others for motivation and affirmation. Instead of public schooling, Gatto encourages things like homeschooling and open source online education.

books.title: Spectatoritis
books.author: Jay B. Nash
books.blurb: “Granted freedom, many men go to sleep – physically and mentally, organically and cortically. Not having the drive for creative arts they turn to pre-digested pastimes, prepared in little packages at a dollar per. This has literally thrown us into the gladiatorial stage of Rome in which the number of participants becomes fewer and the size of the grandstands, larger. Spectatoritis has become almost synonymous with Americanism and the end is not yet. The stages will get smaller and the rows of seats will mount higher.” Published in 1938, this hard-to-find book is one of my favorites. Nash laments the fact that while machines have opened up greater amounts of leisure time for the country’s citizenry, people are using that time for increasingly passive and mindless entertainment. He dubs this plague “spectatoritis,” and warns that it will bring about the downfall of civilization if not curbed. For, he argues, every human needs real rejuvenation from work or will succumb to a variety of mental and physical ills. Thus what we need, Nash writes, is a “philosophy of leisure” that can guide people in how to use their free time in more fulfilling ways.

books.title: Over the Edge of the World: Magellan's Terrifying Circumnavigation of the Globe
books.author: Laurence Bergreen
books.blurb: In 1519 Ferdinand Magellan left Spain with five ships and 270 men to circumnavigate the globe. Three years later one ship and 18 men returned. Magellan himself was killed in the Philippines in a skirmish he had no business fighting, having already achieved the navigational feat that secured his legacy. Bergreen follows the expedition from its chaotic departure through the Pacific crossing — weeks without wind, men dying of scurvy, a mutiny suppressed at sword-point — to the skeleton crew that finally limped home to Spain. The first circumnavigation of the earth told as the survival story it actually was, without the triumphalism that usually attaches to tales of exploration.
