Deighton's Berlin — divided, paranoid, saturated with history — is one of the great settings in spy fiction, and Samson is one of the great spy protagonists: competent, weary, funny, and slowly realizing that something is very wrong in his own department. The twist at the end of Berlin Game is one of the best in the genre.

books.title: The Manchurian Candidate
books.author: Richard Condon
books.blurb: A Korean War veteran returns home a hero, decorated and celebrated — and also secretly brainwashed by Soviet and Chinese intelligence, programmed as a sleeper assassin to be activated on command. His handler is his own mother. Condon wrote it in 1959 as a savage satirical assault on Cold War paranoia, McCarthyism, and the American political machine, and the result is one of the most purely original novels in the espionage genre: genuinely funny, genuinely disturbing, and structured with a clockwork precision that makes the mounting horror feel inevitable. The 1962 Frank Sinatra film is one of the great political thrillers in cinema. The novel is darker, sharper, and considerably more unhinged.

books.title: Rogue Male
books.author: Geoffrey Household
books.blurb: A British sportsman, hunting in Central Europe in the late 1930s, finds himself with a clear shot at an unnamed European dictator — almost certainly Hitler — and on a whim, takes aim. He doesn't fire, but he is captured, tortured, and thrown off a cliff, left for dead. He survives, makes his way back to England, and is then hunted across the English countryside by foreign agents who want to finish the job. Published in 1939, Rogue Male is one of the purest and most propulsive thrillers ever written — a man, alone, on the run, using nothing but fieldcraft and intelligence to survive. Le Carré and Greene both acknowledged it as an influence. If you haven't read it, you are in for a genuine treat.

books.title: Where Eagles Dare
books.author: Alistair MacLean
books.blurb: The purest fun on this list, and unapologetically so. A small team of British commandos and American Rangers must infiltrate an impregnable Nazi fortress in the Bavarian Alps to rescue a captured American general — or so they are told. MacLean structures the novel around a series of increasingly outrageous reversals, and the plotting is so confident and so propulsive that you barely notice how preposterous the whole enterprise is until you've finished it and are immediately tempted to read it again. Richard Burton and Clint Eastwood starred in the 1968 film adaptation, which is one of the great WWII action films. The novel is better plotted and faster.

books.title: The Ipcress File
books.author: Len Deighton
books.blurb: Deighton's unnamed cockney spy — later named Harry Palmer in the Michael Caine films — is the anti-Bond: working class, sardonic, perpetually underpaid, and far more interested in cooking a decent meal than in seducing exotic women. The Ipcress File is propulsive, funny, and genuinely inventive in its plot, which involves brainwashing, defectors, and the specific grubby bureaucracy of postwar British intelligence. Deighton writes with a wit and an economy that make the book feel completely contemporary despite being published in 1962. If you've only seen the film, the novel is a different and richer experience.

books.title: A Coffin for Dimitrios
books.author: Eric Ambler
books.blurb: Ambler invented the modern spy thriller in the 1930s — le Carré and Greene both said so — and this is his best novel. Charles Latimer, a mild-mannered English mystery writer on holiday in Istanbul, becomes obsessed with the life of Dimitrios Makropoulos, a criminal whose body he has viewed in the city morgue. What follows is a journey backward through the criminal underworld of interwar Europe — across Turkey, Greece, Bulgaria, Switzerland, and France — as Latimer pieces together the career of a man who lived entirely without principle in a world that seemed to reward that choice. Ambler writes with a moral seriousness and a narrative elegance that make his thrillers feel like literature without ever sacrificing the pleasure of the plot.

books.title: Ashenden: Or the British Agent
books.author: W. Somerset Maugham
books.blurb: The first honest spy novel ever written, published in 1928 by a man who actually worked for British intelligence during World War I. Maugham's Ashenden is a writer recruited as an agent, and the stories that follow — linked short fiction rather than a conventional novel — are notable for being almost entirely without glamour. The work is boring, the moral compromises are real, the agents Ashenden handles are often pathetic rather than heroic. Maugham influenced everyone who came after him in the genre, and le Carré has cited Ashenden as the direct precursor to his own work. It is also, because Maugham is one of the great prose stylists in English, a pleasure to read on every page.

books.title: The Thirty-Nine Steps
books.author: John Buchan
books.blurb: The grandfather of the modern thriller, published in 1915, and still one of the most purely enjoyable reads in the genre. Richard Hannay — a bored mining engineer just back from South Africa — stumbles into a conspiracy involving German agents, a murdered American, and a mysterious organization called the Black Stone. What follows is a cross-Scotland chase across moors and mountains that invented the template for every wrong-man thriller that came after it. Hitchcock's 1935 film adaptation is a classic in its own right but takes considerable liberties with the source material. The novel is shorter, faster, and in several ways more fun.

books.title: Say Nothing
books.author: Patrick Radden Keefe
books.blurb: In 1972, Jean McConville — a widowed mother of ten — was dragged from her Belfast apartment by the IRA and never seen again. Keefe reconstructs her disappearance and the full arc of the Troubles through the specific people involved: Dolours Price, who helped kill McConville and later couldn't live with it; Gerry Adams, who spent decades denying IRA membership while leading its political wing; and the Boston College oral history project that tried to archive the conflict and ended up reopening its wounds. Around 368 pages and the best book written about Northern Ireland — narrative rather than academic, specific rather than polemical, and honest about what political violence costs the people who commit it long after it ends. Cross-seeds with the British History and Irish history territory covered on the St. Patrick's Day list.

books.title: Dubliners
books.author: James Joyce
books.blurb: Joyce wrote these fifteen stories about Dublin life in 1914 before he became James Joyce — before Ulysses and Finnegans Wake made his name synonymous with difficulty — and the result is the most accessible thing he ever published and one of the most perfect short story collections in the English language. The stories move from childhood through adolescence through maturity to public life, and the final story, The Dead, in which a man realizes at a party that his wife has loved someone else more than she will ever love him, is the most moving piece of prose in the canon. Around 256 pages. The canonical entry on this list — the book everyone has heard of and few have actually read, which is the condition that makes a canonical entry worth identifying. It is not difficult. It is just very good.

books.title: Trinity
books.author: Leon Uris
books.blurb: Uris spent years in Ireland researching this sweeping saga of three families — Catholic, Protestant, and Anglo-Irish landlord — whose fates intertwine across the brutal decades leading up to the 1916 Easter Rising. At over 750 pages it's a commitment, but like all great epics it flies. Uris has a gift for making history visceral and personal, and by the time you reach the Rising itself you'll feel like you've lived through the whole preceding century alongside these characters. Few novels have done more to make Irish history legible and emotionally alive to an American audience, and none has done it with more narrative momentum. Read Michael Collins first for the history. Then read this for what it felt like.

books.title: The Famine Ships
books.author: Edward Laxton
books.blurb: Between 1845 and 1852, a million Irish people died of starvation and another million fled on ships so overcrowded and so poorly provisioned that passengers arrived — if they arrived at all — skeletal, diseased, and destitute. Laxton reconstructs the crossings through passenger testimony, ship manifests, and the records of the ports that received the survivors. The ships themselves are the subject: the conditions below decks, the mortality rates, the captains who ran tight ships and those who didn't, and the specific experience of leaving a dying country for a continent that wasn't certain it wanted you. The Famine is the event that created the Irish-American. This is the book about the crossing that made it permanent.

books.title: Michael Collins
books.author: Tim Pat Coogan
books.blurb: The Easter Rising of 1916 failed militarily and its leaders were executed, which turned a botched insurrection into the founding mythology of modern Ireland. The man who took that mythology and converted it into actual independence was Michael Collins — a 28-year-old Cork man who built the first modern urban guerrilla network, ran British intelligence inside out, negotiated the Anglo-Irish Treaty in London, and was assassinated at 31 in the Civil War that followed. Coogan's biography is the standard account: thorough, warm, and fully alive to the paradox of a man who won the war and lost the peace. The Liam Neeson film covers the broad strokes. The book goes considerably deeper and doesn't simplify what the film has to.

books.title: How the Irish Saved Civilization
books.author: Thomas Cahill
books.blurb: When Rome fell and the lights went out across Europe, it was Irish monks — inspired directly by the mission of St. Patrick — who copied, preserved, and ultimately returned the great books of Western civilization to a continent that had lost them. Cahill's beloved popular history makes that case with the confidence of a man who has done the research and the wit of a man who knows how to use it. Funny, accessible, and genuinely moving, it will leave you with a completely different understanding of what Ireland contributed to the world and why that contribution was neither accidental nor inevitable. The entry point for this entire list.

books.title: The Táin
books.author: Anonymous
books.blurb: Ireland's great mythological epic, equivalent in Irish culture to what the Iliad is to the Greeks. The Cattle Raid of Cooley tells the story of the teenage hero Cú Chulainn single-handedly defending Ulster against the armies of Queen Medb of Connacht — a warrior queen whose ambition and ferocity make her one of the great characters in world mythology. Thomas Kinsella's translation is the gold standard: muscular, readable, and faithful to the original's wild energy. If you've ever wondered where Ireland's reputation for warriors, poets, and larger-than-life characters came from, the answer is here, in stories that are roughly 2,000 years old and have lost none of their force.

books.title: St. Patrick of Ireland: A Biography
books.author: Philip Freeman
books.blurb: Most people know the legends — snakes, shamrocks, the whole mythology — but almost nobody knows the actual man. Freeman, a classics professor, goes back to Patrick's own surviving writings to reconstruct who he really was: a Roman-British teenager kidnapped into slavery in Ireland, who escaped, found faith, and then voluntarily returned to the land of his captors to spend the rest of his life there. It is a genuinely remarkable story, and Freeman tells it with the accessible pace of a thriller rather than a theology lecture. The man behind the parade is more interesting than the parade, and this is the book that proves it.

books.title: Borstal Boy
books.author: Brendan Behan
books.blurb: Playwright and poet Brendan Behan was arrested in Liverpool at age 16, carrying explosives for the IRA. Borstal Boy is his memoir of the years he spent in British reform institutions as a result. What makes it extraordinary — and very Irish — is that it's not particularly angry or bitter. It's funny, tender, and full of unlikely friendships between a young Irish republican and the English boys he was supposed to hate. Behan could drink a small country under the table and frequently did, but he could also write, and this book proves it on every page. It's the kind of memoir that makes you understand how an entire culture can carry both deep political wounds and an almost supernatural capacity for warmth at the same time.

books.title: McCarthy's Bar
books.author: Pete McCarthy
books.blurb: Pete McCarthy, a British travel writer who was half-Irish, decided to travel the length of Ireland with one rule: he could never pass a pub that had his surname on the sign. What followed was one of the funniest travel books ever written — a warm, hilarious, and quietly profound journey through Irish pub culture, landscape, and craic. McCarthy died young, which makes the book feel even more precious. If How the Irish Saved Civilization is the book that explains why Ireland matters to the world, McCarthy's Bar is the book that explains why Ireland is irresistible to anyone who has spent more than a week there.

books.title: At Swim-Two-Birds
books.author: Flann O'Brien
books.blurb: One of the funniest novels ever written, and one of the strangest. A lazy Dublin student writes a novel about a novelist whose fictional characters get fed up and revolt against him — while Irish mythological figures, cowboys, and fairies wander through the margins causing chaos. It is completely, gloriously unhinged. James Joyce, not a man who handed out compliments lightly, called it his favorite Irish novel after his own. Flann O'Brien — real name Brian O'Nolan — wrote it at age 26 and it never found a proper audience in his lifetime, which is one of literature's great injustices. If you've ever felt that Irish wit at its best is a kind of controlled explosion, this book is the proof.

books.title: Round Ireland with a Fridge
books.author: Tony Hawks
books.blurb: Englishman Tony Hawks, slightly drunk at a party, makes a bet that he can hitchhike around the entire coastline of Ireland — with a full-size mini-fridge in tow — within one month. He wins the bet and in doing so writes one of the funniest travel books ever put to paper and an accidental love letter to the Irish people and their baffling willingness to help a stranger with a large kitchen appliance. Every character he meets is more memorable than the last. Pairs perfectly with McCarthy's Bar as a one-two punch of books that will make you genuinely fond of Ireland regardless of whether you have a drop of Irish blood in you.

books.title: Into Thin Air: A Personal Account of the Mt. Everest Disaster
books.author: Jon Krakauer
books.blurb: In May 1996, eight people died on Everest in a single storm, including two of the most experienced guides on the mountain. Krakauer was there as a journalist and wrote this within months of coming down — the account is raw in ways that a longer retrospect would have smoothed over. Around 300 pages of the best disaster journalism in print: the specific sequence of decisions that killed people, the altitude-induced judgment failures, and the specific horror of watching men die at 28,000 feet where there is nothing to be done. The mountain entry on this list. Beck Weathers — left for dead twice during the same storm, blind and frostbitten, who walked out on his own — tells the same disaster from the survivor's interior in Left for Dead, the essential companion. Cross-seeds with the Mountain & Rock Climbing list, where Krakauer appears twice.

books.title: The Worst Journey in the World
books.author: Apsley Cherry-Garrard
books.blurb: Back before getting to Antarctica became so accessible and easy, gliding over the choppy Drake Passage in your palatial suite with champagne and gourmet meals, getting to and then exploring Antarctica was a real ordeal; some would call it the worst journey in the world. British explorer Apsley Cherry-Garrard did and he made that the title of his account of Robert Falcon Scott’s Terra Nova expedition, a scientific and exploratory expedition that resulted in Scott’s death. As a zoological assistant on the expedition (for which he lacked the proper education and training), Cherry-Garrard was part of a small team that traversed the Ross Ice Shelf to fetch emperor penguin eggs at a rookery. It was this journey, through negative double-digit temperatures and brutal winter storms, that makes up the bulk of the narrative, and which Cherry-Garrard deemed “the worst journey in the world.” But he also talks about how he was part of the team that went in search of Scott and his team after they went missing returning from the South Pole, and how they found the bodies. Unlike many other accounts of Antarctic travel, this one is frank in its questioning of whether all the suffering and loss is worth it, and delves into difficult questions about human nature. Sobering and direct, this is a good one to read to remember the human sacrifice it took to open this continent to the world.

books.title: In the Heart of the Sea
books.author: Nathaniel Philbrick
books.blurb: In November 1820, the Nantucket whaleship Essex was rammed and sunk by a sperm whale in the Pacific Ocean — the event that inspired Moby-Dick. The twenty men who escaped spent three months in open whaleboats crossing three thousand miles of open ocean, and the ones who survived did so partly by eating the ones who didn't. Philbrick reconstructed the full account from the first mate's journal and the captain's later memoir in 2000, and the result is the best maritime disaster account available: the specific decisions that killed men and the specific ones that saved them, the Nantucket whaling culture that produced both the voyage and the response to its end, and the specific moral weight of what was required to survive. Around 238 pages. Cross-seeds with the Sea & Nautical Fiction list.

books.title: The Man Eaters of Kumaon
books.author: Jim Corbett
books.blurb: Corbett was a British hunter in colonial India who spent decades tracking and killing man-eating leopards and tigers in the Kumaon Hills — animals that had killed hundreds of villagers and that no one else could stop. He wrote these accounts in 1944 with the specific authority of a man who had spent nights alone on a machan above a kill site waiting for an animal that knew he was there. Around 240 pages and the deep cut entry — surprisingly unknown given how good it is. The hunting and survival worlds overlap completely here: each chapter is simultaneously a hunting account and a survival story, since Corbett was operating in terrain where the animal held every tactical advantage. Cross-seeds with the Hunting & Fishing list. The reader who finishes The Tiger wanting more man-eater accounts comes directly here.

books.title: Adrift: Seventy Six Days Lost At Sea
books.author: Steven Callahan
books.blurb: On February 5, 1982, Callahan's 21-foot sloop Napoleon Solo sank six days out of the Canaries. He escaped onto a five-and-a-half-foot inflatable life raft with limited supplies and spent the next 76 days alone in the Atlantic — spearing fish, collecting rainwater, repairing the raft with improvised tools, and documenting everything in a journal he kept throughout. Around 211 pages and the purest survival narrative on this list: one man, one raft, one ocean, no rescue coming. Callahan is an engineer and sailor who thinks clearly under pressure and writes about what he did and why with the precision of a man who understood that systematic thinking was keeping him alive. The primary source sea entry. The reader who wants a second Atlantic survival account at considerably greater length goes to Jonathan Franklin's 438 Days.

books.title: Alive
books.author: Piers Paul Read
books.blurb: On October 13, 1972, a chartered flight carrying a Uruguayan rugby team crashed in the Andes at 11,800 feet. Of the 45 people aboard, 16 survived — including 72 days at altitude in temperatures that dropped to minus 40 at night, with no rescue coming and no food except the bodies of those who had died in the crash. Read reconstructed the full story from survivor interviews and the result is the most morally serious survival account in print: the specific decision to eat the dead, the Catholic framework through which the survivors processed it, and the specific physical and psychological deterioration of men who refused to stop. Around 352 pages. The subject matter is confrontational and the book handles it without flinching and without exploiting it. The disaster entry and the moral philosophy entry simultaneously.

books.title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
books.author: Aron Ralston
books.blurb: On April 26, 2003, Ralston was canyoneering alone in Blue John Canyon in Utah when an 800-pound boulder shifted and pinned his right arm against the canyon wall. He spent the next 127 hours trying to free himself before amputating his own forearm with a dull multi-tool, rappelling out of the canyon, and hiking five miles to a trailhead. He wrote this himself and the account is exactly as harrowing as the facts suggest — the systematic attempts to free himself, the specific decision to amputate, and the specific mental discipline of a man who refused to die in a canyon alone. Around 354 pages. The film 127 Hours covers the same events well; the book goes further into what those hours actually required. The wilderness entry and the primary source entry simultaneously.

books.title: Deep Survival
books.author: Laurence Gonzales
books.blurb: Gonzales spent years studying the neuroscience and psychology of survival — why some people live when others in identical situations die — and the answers are counterintuitive throughout. It is not the strongest or the most experienced who survive. It is the people who can accurately perceive reality under extreme stress, stay emotionally engaged rather than going cold, and convert fear into focused action rather than paralysis. Around 295 pages and the overview entry on this list — the one book that explains the others. Read it first and every subsequent account of survival will make more sense: what Callahan did right on his raft, what went wrong on Everest, why Ralston kept his head in a Utah canyon. The science is accessible and the case studies are harrowing. The reader who thinks he knows how he would respond in an emergency will finish this book less certain.

books.title: 438 Days
books.author: Jonathan Franklin
books.blurb: On November 17, 2012, Mexican fisherman Salvador Alvarenga left the coast of Mexico on a shark-fishing trip and was blown into the open Pacific by a storm. He survived for 438 days on the open ocean — 6,700 miles — before washing ashore in the Marshall Islands in January 2014. His fishing partner died within the first weeks. Alvarenga survived alone by eating raw fish, birds, and turtles, drinking rainwater and turtle blood, and talking to the dead man to stay sane. Franklin reconstructed the full account from extensive interviews and the result is the deep cut entry on this list — largely unknown despite being the longest open-ocean survival in recorded history. Around 258 pages. The reader who finishes Adrift wanting more open-ocean survival comes directly here.

books.title: The Tiger
books.author: John Vaillant
books.blurb: In December 1997, an Amur tiger began systematically hunting and killing humans in the Russian Far East — not attacking opportunistically but returning to specific locations, destroying the possessions of a poacher who had wounded it, and ambushing men with a patience that suggested deliberate planning. Vaillant spent years reconstructing the full account: the specific ecology of the Amur tiger, the specific poverty of the post-Soviet Russian Far East that drove men into the taiga as poachers, and the wildlife inspector tasked with tracking an apex predator that was tracking him back. Around 329 pages and the most frightening book on this list — frightening because the tiger is not a monster but an animal behaving rationally within its own logic. The predator entry and the unexpected angle simultaneously. Cross-seeds with the Russian History list.

books.title: In the Kingdom of Ice
books.author: Hampton Sides
books.blurb: Hampton Sides’ In the Kingdom of Ice recounts the doomed 1879 USS Jeannette expedition, which attempted to reach the North Pole via that theorized warm sea channel. Trapped in the ice for nearly two years before the ship was crushed, the crew was forced into an epic, thousand-mile trek across the Arctic via both land and sea. Sides excels at combining cinematic storytelling with meticulous research, bringing to life not only the expedition’s leader, George Washington De Long, but also the men who followed him and those at home who were waiting on his return. The result is a powerful reminder that courage and determination are not always enough, especially when leadership is guided more by theory and pride than by reality. It’s a gripping, tragic tale that underscores how unforgiving the polar world can be.

books.title: Open
books.author: Andre Agassi
books.blurb: Agassi won eight Grand Slams, was ranked number one in the world, and hated tennis for most of his career. His father built a ball machine in the Las Vegas backyard and made him hit thousands of balls a day before he was old enough to choose otherwise. He wore a hairpiece at Wimbledon because his hair was falling out from stress. He used crystal meth in 1997 and lied to the ATP about it. He married Brooke Shields, divorced her, married Steffi Graf, and found something resembling peace in his thirties just as his body began to fail. Ghost-written by J.R. Moehringer with full access and no apparent filter, this is the most honest sports autobiography on this list and one of the best ever written. The overview entry for the non-fan — read this first and the sport will make sense in ways it didn't before.

books.title: Short Circuit
books.author: Michael Mewshaw
books.blurb: Mewshaw is a novelist who spent the 1981 tennis season following the professional circuit — not Wimbledon and the US Open but the satellite tournaments in between, where the mid-ranked players grind for ranking points and prize money that barely covers travel expenses. What he found was not the gentleman's sport of its reputation: the petty corruption, the fixed matches, the players and coaches working the system at every level, and the specific dark comedy of professional athletics conducted far from the cameras. Around 274 pages and the funniest book on this list — funny the way that things are funny when they are also genuinely depressing. Published in 1983 and out of print, which makes it the deep cut simultaneously. The reader who finishes Open wanting to know what the tour looks like three hundred rankings spots below Agassi comes here.

books.title: Broken Code
books.author: Rohan Nadkarni
books.blurb: Professional tennis has a match-fixing problem it has spent two decades pretending is smaller than it is. Nadkarni spent years documenting the specific mechanisms: the lower-ranked players who supplement income by losing sets to order, the betting syndicates that identified and exploited them, and the ATP's systematic failure to investigate corruption it had more than enough evidence to pursue. Published in 2024 and the most recently reported entry on this list. Note the institutional argument embedded throughout — this is a story about a governing body that prioritized the sport's reputation over the sport's integrity for long enough that the problem became structural. The uncomfortable entry. The reader who watches tennis casually will finish this book watching it differently.

books.title: String Theory
books.author: David Foster Wallace
books.blurb: Wallace wrote five pieces about tennis across his career — he was a junior tournament player in Illinois before he became a novelist — and collected them here at 154 pages. The centerpiece is his 2006 New York Times essay on watching Federer play, which is the best piece of sports writing of the decade and possibly longer: an argument that watching Federer is a religious experience available to the secular, that his movement constitutes a form of beauty that has no adequate equivalent in ordinary life. The other four essays cover Wallace's own junior career, Michael Joyce on the satellite circuit, and the specific loneliness of professional tennis. Cross-seeds with the Essays & Longform Journalism list. The reader who thinks sportswriting cannot be literature has not read this book.

books.title: You Cannot Be Serious
books.author: John McEnroe
books.blurb: McEnroe was defaulted from the 1990 Australian Open for telling a line judge he was the pits of the world, which is a relatively mild sample of what he was capable of on a tennis court. He was also the most gifted player of his era and possibly any era — a serve-and-volley game built on feel rather than power, a touch at the net that Borg and Connors could not replicate, and a competitive fury that expressed itself in a running argument with every official he ever encountered. McEnroe tells all of it in his own voice: the rivalry with Borg, the rivalry with Connors, the marriages, the art collection, and the specific psychology of a man who played his best tennis while apparently losing his mind. The humor entry and a primary source simultaneously. Around 304 pages and not a dull one among them.

books.title: Levels of the Game
books.author: John McPhee
books.blurb: McPhee took a single 1968 US Open semifinal between Arthur Ashe and Clark Graebner and used it to write a dual portrait of two men and two Americas. Ashe is Black, intuitive, improvisational, playing tennis as a form of expression; Graebner is white, mechanical, systematic, playing it as a form of control. The civil rights movement runs beneath every point. McPhee alternates between the match as it unfolds and the biographies of the two men, and the construction is so precise that the tennis becomes a form of argument about what kind of country America was in 1968. Under 150 pages and the most formally elegant book on this list. The reader who picks this up for tennis will find himself reading about something considerably larger by page thirty.

books.title: Big Bill Tilden
books.author: Frank Deford
books.blurb: Tilden won six consecutive US championships through the 1920s and was the most famous athlete in America for a decade — more recognizable than Babe Ruth, more celebrated than Jack Dempsey. He died in 1953 in a Los Angeles rooming house with forty dollars to his name, his belongings in a suitcase, waiting for a ride to a tournament he never reached. In between: two convictions for soliciting minors, the complete destruction of a career and a reputation, and the specific trajectory of a genius who could not manage the distance between his public greatness and his private life. Deford is one of the finest sports writers who ever worked and this is among his best books. The biography entry and the darkest life on this list.

books.title: Strokes of Genius
books.author: L. Jon Wertheim
books.blurb: The 2008 Wimbledon final between Federer and Nadal lasted four hours and forty-eight minutes across five sets, was interrupted twice by rain, and ended in near-darkness. Most people who watched it consider it the greatest tennis match ever played. Wertheim, a Sports Illustrated tennis writer, spent the following year reconstructing it point by point — the tactical adjustments, the psychological shifts, and the specific physical and mental demands of sustaining that level of play for that long against that opponent. Around 224 pages and the deep dive entry on this list: one match examined with the same granular attention that Coffey brought to the Miracle on Ice and Feinstein brought to The Punch. The reader who saw the match will find things he missed. The reader who didn't will feel like he was there.

books.title: Pilgrim at Tinker Creek
books.author: Annie Dillard
books.blurb: Dillard spent a year making close observations of Tinker Creek in Virginia's Blue Ridge Mountains — the insects, the light, the specific texture of a creek in each season — and wrote about what she found with an intelligence and strangeness that won the 1975 Pulitzer Prize and has never been adequately explained by its admirers. Around 290 pages and the most formally ambitious book on this list: structured like a theological argument, written like a novelist, and grounded in the natural world with the precision of a field biologist. The unexpected angle entry — not a journey, not a survival story, not a political argument, but a sustained act of attention to one small place that somehow becomes an account of what it means to be alive. The AoM reader who approaches this skeptically will find himself underlining sentences by page thirty.

books.author: Charles C. Mann
books.blurb: As we all know from the schoolroom rhyme, in 1492 Columbus sailed the ocean blue. Then he "discovered" the Americas. This, of course, is an accurate depiction of history only if you're willing to ignore the millions of people who were already living in complex societies when he got there. In this book, Mann not only dispels the myth of Columbus's discovery, but details the various civilizations residing in North, Central, and South America, explaining their customs and cultures, providing a glimpse into a lost way of life, and reminding us that -- for better or worse -- history tends to be told by the victors rather than the vanquished.

books.title: The Art of Eating
books.author: M.F.K. Fisher
books.blurb: Fisher wrote about food during WWII rationing, during her years alone in Provence, during poverty and grief and pleasure, and what she produced was not recipes but the argument that eating well is a moral and intellectual practice available to anyone willing to pay attention. The five books collected here — How to Cook a Wolf, The Gastronomical Me, Consider the Oyster, and two others — established the vocabulary that all American food writing since has used. The artsy entry on this list and the literary anchor: the reader who finds food writing frivolous will find Fisher's refusal to apologize for the subject both bracing and instructive. W.H. Auden said she was one of the best prose writers in America. He was right. Cross-references to the Essays & Longform list.

books.title: Paper Lion
books.author: George Plimpton
books.blurb: Thanksgiving and football are inseparable, and this is the best football book ever written. In the early 1960s, George Plimpton — journalist, amateur athlete, and founding editor of The Paris Review — talked his way into Detroit Lions training camp as a last-string quarterback and actually played in a preseason game. What followed was one of the great feats of participatory journalism in American letters. Plimpton writes about football the way a man who genuinely loves the game but has no illusions about his own abilities would write about it — with humor, with awe, and with a precise eye for the physical and psychological reality of professional sport that no sportswriter observing from the press box could ever achieve.

books.title: The Name of War: King Philip's War and the Origins of American Identity
books.author: Jill Lepore
books.blurb: King Philip's War — the conflict that erupted between the Pilgrims' children and the Wampanoag people in 1675 — was proportionally the deadliest war in American history, and it happened a single generation after the first Thanksgiving. Lepore, one of America's best historians, uses the war to examine something deeper: how the two sides told the story afterward, and how those competing narratives shaped the American identity that emerged from the wreckage. It is a precise, honest, and deeply intelligent book about the gap between the stories a nation tells about itself and what actually happened. It belongs on this list because genuine gratitude for what America became requires an honest accounting of what it cost.

books.title: Mayflower: A Story of Courage, Community, and War
books.author: Nathaniel Philbrick
books.blurb: The essential Thanksgiving book, and one of the best works of American popular history ever written. Philbrick takes the full arc of the Pilgrim story: the crossing, the desperate first winter, the genuine and complicated friendship between the colonists and the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, and then the catastrophic unraveling of that relationship two generations later in King Philip's War, one of the bloodiest conflicts in American history relative to population. The first Thanksgiving was real, and the alliance behind it was real, and Philbrick honors both without sentimentality or cynicism. This is the book that replaces the grade-school version of the story with something far more interesting and far more true.

books.title: Lake Wobegon Days
books.author: Garrison Keillor
books.blurb: The definitive portrait of small-town American life and the particular comedy and tenderness of large family gatherings. Keillor's fictional town of Lake Wobegon, Minnesota — where all the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average — is the most fully realized version of a certain kind of American experience ever put on the page: the church suppers and the passed dishes and the relatives who drive you absolutely crazy and whom you would not trade for anything. Nobody has ever captured the specific feeling of being home for the holidays — the warmth, the dysfunction, the food, the stories told for the hundredth time — with more honesty or more affection.

books.title: Gratitude
books.author: Oliver Sacks
books.blurb: Four short essays written by neurologist and author Oliver Sacks in the final months of his life, after receiving a terminal cancer diagnosis at age 81. They are among the most quietly beautiful things ever written about what it means to have lived — to have worked, loved, thought, and been given the specific and unrepeatable experience of being a particular human being on this particular earth. At under 50 pages it is the shortest book on this list and can be read in a single sitting. For a holiday built around the concept of thankfulness, there is no more direct or more moving statement of what that concept actually means at its deepest level.

books.title: Washington: A Life
books.author: Ron Chernow
books.blurb: There have been thousands of books published about George Washington, the first appearing nearly right away after his passing in 1799. Since then, there’s been a steady stream of award-worthy titles and series, including Douglas Southall Freeman’s 7-volume set from the 1950s and James Flexner’s 4-volume treatment which came about a decade later. (Each also has a single-volume abridgement!) So where do you possibly start with the man who set the most important precedents for the office of President of the United States? For the modern reader, there’s no doubt that Ron Chernow’s Washington: A Life is where to turn. While Chernow’s books are long and admittedly intimidating (and aren’t exactly easy reads), he’s indisputably a master storyteller who has a knack for cracking the inner psyche of his characters better than nearly any biographer I’ve encountered. Washington inevitably retains some of his stone-like stature, but Chernow chips away at it better than most in order to reveal the human being inside. Washington: A Life is an incredibly rewarding read which will leave you certain that George Washington was the perfect man to be America’s first president.

books.title: Master of the Senate
books.author: Robert A. Caro
books.blurb: When it comes to the art of presidential biography, there is Robert Caro and there is everyone else. After writing his first (and now classic) biography on New Yorker Robert Moses 50 years ago, Caro has dedicated the decades since to studying the mechanics of power through the inimitable character of Lyndon B. Johnson. Through four volumes and more than a few thousand pages, Caro profiles not only Johnson, but also the major characters who surrounded his life and political rise, and even the hardscrabble Texas landscape itself. The best of the series (so far) is a title that can be read on its own: Master of the Senate. This third volume details the years between 1948 and 1957, when Johnson displayed a mastery of the United States Senate not seen before or since. It’s not an easy book to get through, but the prose is often jaw-droppingly good and I can guarantee it’ll be among the more memorable reading experiences of your lifetime. Amazingly, Caro has yet to finish his epic series. He’s hard at work on the fifth and final volume, which means that readers only get through Johnson’s first year or so of the presidency. To get the full life in a single volume, Randall Woods’ LBJ is very good.

books.title: Grant
books.author: Ron Chernow
books.blurb: Though ignored and written off for a long time as a bad president, Civil War general-turned-politician Ulysses S. Grant has been re-invigorated in a handful of major biographies in the last decade or so. While there are a number of quality options, Ron Chernow’s epic, 1,000-page Grant is impossible to beat. The best biographies are those that not only reveal their subject, for both good and bad, but also provide a moving and even inspiring reading experience. Grant does that in spades. The psychological penetration that Chernow achieves is eye-opening and often rousing. A number of biographers have captured the war years quite well — it was a dramatic period that just isn’t too hard to make exciting and evocative. The real trick is to capture Grant’s eight years as president with the same verve, which the master historian undoubtedly does. As with the other Chernow title on this list, it will take some dedication, but the effort is well worth it. Grant, in my opinion, is Chernow’s best book.

books.title: Bully Pulpit
books.author: Doris Kearns Goodwin
books.blurb: I came to have quite a soft spot for our 27th president, William Howard Taft, after reading about him in Doris Kearns Goodwin’s The Bully Pulpit. Theodore Roosevelt actually gets top billing in the subtitle of this book, but I imagine that has more to do with the publishing marketing machine than the content of the book, which is more about Taft and his relationship with TR. It certainly functions quite well as a biography of Big Bill. As Doris Kearns Goodwin often does, she weaves in a number of tangential plot threads, but always comes back to the tender-turned-fraught relationship between TR and Taft. It’s a wonderful read with a compelling narrative and a number of inspiring takeaways. I’m glad Goodwin chose to give William Howard Taft the spotlight here; hardly any other biographers or historians have.

books.title: An Unfinished Life
books.author: Robert Dallek
books.blurb: With John Fitzgerald at the center of the Kennedy universe, nearly every member of the family has been studied and written about a number of times — grandparents, parents, children, and all eight of his siblings. The books about them could fill entire shops. Perhaps surprisingly, though, comprehensive biographies of John himself are somewhat of a rarity. A number have been started and abandoned due to uncooperative surviving family members (Jean Kennedy, the final living sibling, died just last year), unclassified top secret documents (much of his presidency, and especially his death, was shrouded in secrecy), and his famously impenetrable inner psyche. Robert Dallek penned what I believe to be by far the best treatment of JFK with An Unfinished Life. While unsparing in detailing the flaws of Kennedy’s personal life, Dallek unveiled for the first time the depth of his debilitating medical problems and also offered a well-balanced and dramatic account of his 1,000 days as president. One more book worth mentioning in regard to JFK: William Manchester, famed biographer of Winston Churchill, wrote an oft-overlooked account of his death in 1967’s The Death of a President. It doesn’t get the same attention as Manchester’s other books, but is just as expertly written.

books.title: American Sphinx
books.author: Joseph Ellis
books.blurb: Thomas Jefferson has become the poster boy of public opinion’s changing tides in regards to the Founding Fathers. For nearly 200 years he was revered without reservation; but as his relationship with his slaves came to light in the last couple decades, Jefferson has swung the other way almost towards villainy. So which is it, hero or scoundrel? To read any biography of our third president is to understand what an enigma he was; even historians who have spent their careers studying the man have ultimately found him to be, as Merrill Peterson puts it, “impenetrable.” Suffice it to say, modern readers have no shortage of options for digging into Thomas Jefferson’s life. I began with Jon Meacham’s The Art of Power, which was a very good place to start. I also found our third president “impenetrable,” though, and so continued on to Joseph Ellis’ fascinating and enlightening American Sphinx. Less a cradle-to-grave biography than a series of essay-like chapters on Jefferson’s life, this book gets at the heart of what has made the man so appealing and, as of late, so pilloried. Inside its pages, you’ll find treasures about character, independence, and America’s contradictory founding legacy.

books.title: The Accidental President
books.author: AJ Baime
books.blurb: Though David McCullough’s Truman is often cited as one of the great presidential biographies (which it is!), AJ Baime’s more efficient volume is actually the POTUS bio I recommend most to average readers. Distilled into 360 jam-packed pages of inspiring leadership and unbreakable character, Baime shows us that Truman was one of the truly decent men to have held the office of President of the United States. Spending the entire first chapter on April 12, 1945 — the day FDR died and Truman became president — Baime sets the scene for how out of his depth the Missouran really was. The reader then gets a bit about Truman’s beginnings, before embarking on the bulk of the book, which focuses on the spring and summer months of 1945 as WWII approached its end on both the European and Pacific fronts. You’ll most certainly come away from The Accidental President with a greater appreciation of who Harry S. Truman really was.

books.title: Lincoln
books.author: David Herbert Donald
books.blurb: How does someone possibly pick a single book to study up on the most written about man in American history? It’s a tall task, to be sure. Estimates put the number of published books about him at around 16,000, with more and more hitting shelves each year. From dual biographies (of, say, Lincoln and John Brown, or Lincoln and Frederick Douglass), to his frontier boyhood, to his parenting, and even to his specific speeches, you can find books on just about any aspect of Lincoln’s life and presidency. The job of picking a biography among this trove is actually made a little easier when you focus on cradle-to-grave biographies and not those that narrow in on a single element. If you’re looking for a one-volume option, there’s a general consensus among both readers and historians that David Herbert Donald’s Lincoln or Ronald White’s A. Lincoln are where to turn. I read Donald’s work and immensely enjoyed it. Given the enormity of the man, the book’s 600 pages seemed to go by in a flash, and every period of Lincoln’s life is given the proper space — some give too much time to his youth; some give too much to the war years; Donald nailed a perfect balance. If a really deep dive is what you’re after, Michael Burlingame’s two-volume Abraham Lincoln: A Life will keep you busy for a while, as will Sidney Blumenthal’s series — of which three of a proposed five volumes are currently done.

books.title: Richard Nixon: The Life
books.author: John Farrell
books.blurb: Humans love to not only study and learn from failure, but gawk at it too. Given Nixon’s place in the pantheon of disgraced presidents, there’s been a lot of books about the man. The true task of any Nixon biographer goes beyond presenting the unflinching truth (and uncovering the question of why he did what he did), but also in providing context from his boyhood, innate personality, and learned behaviors to not necessarily inspire sympathy, but at least understanding. No man is one-dimensional, Richard Nixon included. The biographer who unveils the true man best, in my opinion, is John Farrell in Richard Nixon: The Life. The narrative is remarkably readable and penetrative; there were, no doubt, clues throughout Nixon’s life that he would be a gifted politician but also a nefarious one, willing to do just about anything in order to win. Farrell certainly doesn’t explain away Nixon’s failures, but he does provide the nuance needed to come away from the book with a more complete picture of our 37th president. Plus, the Watergate drama makes for flat-out gripping reading.

books.title: The Rise of Theodore Roosevelt
books.author: Edmund Morris
books.blurb: America’s most charismatic president has been written about extensively and unendingly since the day he died. It takes a talented writer to fully capture Roosevelt’s energy and vitality — something that only a handful of historians have really done. For the complete picture, you simply cannot beat Edmund Morris’ epic and stirring trilogy: The Rise of Theodore Roosevelt, Theodore Rex, and Colonel Roosevelt. In a Top 10 article, however, I didn’t want to officially take up three spots with the trilogy, so I picked the first volume, which details Roosevelt’s path up until the day he became president (a shorter path than any other president; he remains our youngest POTUS). From the very beginning, Morris captures the reader’s attention and brings us breathlessly along from TR’s aristocratic upbringing and meteoric rise in politics, to the heartbreaking loss of his first wife and subsequent time in the literal wilderness, and back again to Washington, DC as a politician with some serious life experience. You could read The Rise of Theodore Roosevelt on its own and get a fuller picture of the man than a lot of one-volume cradle-to-grave bios would offer. And I can pretty much guarantee you’ll be sucked in enough to read the other two volumes. It’s worth noting that Candice Millard also captures the strenuosity of Roosevelt in documenting his post-presidency travels to South America in her thrilling book, River of Doubt.

books.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: While A Study in Scarlet serves as a great introduction to Holmes and Watson, no story itself is as well done as The Hound of Baskervilles. Using the length of a novel rather than just a short story, and without the need for much expository ramp-up, Conan Doyle is able to fully explore the depths of the most head-scratching case in the series. Sir Charles Baskerville is found dead near his manor in the craggy moors of southern England. There’s no outward evidence of murder, but there are suspicious signs, including the frozen look of horror on Baskerville’s face. There aren’t many clues to work from, except for an old legend about a monstrous hound that has attacked Baskerville heirs for generations. Part of the fun of this story are the various writing devices — between firsthand accounts, journal entries, and Watson’s dispatches to Holmes, the reader slowly begins to piece together what’s going on. But, of course, only Holmes himself can place the final piece of the puzzle. Could the solution really lie in the supernatural? You’ll have to read the tale.

books.title: A Study in Scarlet
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: For any new reader of Sherlock, A Study in Scarlet is undoubtedly the place to start. There could be no better introduction than the blind meeting of Mr. Holmes, amateur sleuth, and his new roommate, Dr. John Watson. They quickly learn about each other: Watson is neat, curious, good at his work, but generally unremarkable. (Though he provides Holmes his much-needed flattery.) Sherlock is utterly brilliant when it comes to detective work, but ignorant of most other subjects. He can be cold, aloof, and spectacularly arrogant, though very rarely in a vindictive way. Watson, perhaps surprisingly to the new Sherlockian, is pretty quickly revealed as the more likable fellow. The first case that Watson records involves a murder in an abandoned house with “RACHE” written on the wall. Scotland Yard investigator Lestrade (we never learn his first name) invites Holmes to consult on the case; though the budding detective initially feigns reluctance, his intellect won’t let him turn down the chance to solve a mystery. Contained within the tale are numerous examples of Holmes’ classic methodology, which relies less on the mistakes of the criminals — as had largely been the case in earlier detective fiction — than on the investigator’s supreme wits and inductive reasoning skills. Across the entire canon, it’s not that the criminals are dumb; it’s that Holmes is smarter. From the numerous twists and turns, to a fun trip to America’s Western frontier, to the delightful construction of the characters’ charms and personalities, and finally to the unforgettable conclusion, I can’t think of a better introduction to a detective series than A Study in Scarlet.

books.title: The Final Problem
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: Though he takes a central role in only this one story (he’s reminisced about in others), no Sherlockian villain is as nefarious as Professor James Moriarty; “He is the Napoleon of crime,” Sherlock tells Watson. “He is the organizer of half that is evil and of nearly all that is undetected in this great city. He is a genius, a philosopher, an abstract thinker. He has a brain of the first order.” Holmes has been tracking him and his gang for some time and is on the verge of putting all of them away. But when Moriarty discovers who’s on his tail, the tables are turned and Holmes and Watson end up on the run themselves. Can they escape the grips of this heartless monster? The end of this story nearly caused riots in London when it was published. Bonus: You should definitely read “The Adventure of the Empty House” right after finishing this one.

books.title: The Adventure of Silver Blaze
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: On the eve of an important horse race, a prized thoroughbred, Silver Blaze, has gone missing, his trainer has been murdered, and some sheep in a nearby pasture have been found lame. Will the horse be found in time for the race? Will the trainer’s murderer be found? What about those dang sheep? There are a couple different threads here which feature some of Doyle’s finest and most memorable writing and reasoning. The famous exchange about “the curious incident of the dog in the night-time” in fact inspired an excellent novel which used that line as the title. Some of the better-written Holmes stories are somewhat predictable, and some of the better plot lines aren’t as well written or structured; “The Silver Blaze” is one of those that combines all the best elements of Doyle’s work.

books.title: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: The beauty of the Sherlock Holmes stories is that you’re sure to find one with a tone that appeals to you; there’s quite a range on a scale that runs from fun and playful to dark and twisted. This story falls on that latter end of things and offers a darker glimpse into Doyle’s mind than we get in most of the other stories. That said, it’s not so twisted as to be off-putting, and, spoiler alert, there’s ultimately a happy ending. The charming Miss Violet Hunter visits Holmes and asks his opinion on taking a job as a nanny which, though it pays well, also comes with a number of peculiar conditions, including cutting her hair short and wearing particular clothes. She takes the job, but as things in the house get stranger and stranger, she calls on Holmes to come help her out. The riddle turns out to be more far-reaching and twisted than either Holmes or Watson thought possible.

books.title: The Adventure of the Norwood Builder
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: This story has as memorable a start as you’ll find in the canon: a young lawyer, John McFarlane, comes into Holmes’ office knowing full well he’s going to be arrested and charged with murder. The day before, McFarlane had been made the beneficiary in the will of one of his clients; later that evening, the client was violently bludgeoned to death and his body lit in flames to hide the evidence. Of course, all signs point to the guilt of McFarlane. Inspector Lestrade holds McFarlane in custody for the time being, giving Holmes some time to prove his innocence before the young lawyer is charged. Can he do it? It’s fun seeing Holmes have to work backwards from his usual methodology. We also see a fuller picture of Lestrade in this story; rather than just begrudging competition, the relationship between him and Holmes seems to flourish into real comradeship.

books.title: A Scandal in Bohemia
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: This is another of Doyle’s more playful stories and involves the most memorable female character of the entire series; in Sherlock’s eyes, “she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex.” On the eve of his marriage, the King of Bohemia needs help not with solving a crime, but in simply keeping an old affair on the hush-hush. In his youth, the king had a romp with an American opera singer named Irene Adler. During their relationship, the king sent her a large photograph of them together, which is still in her possession. Should Irene turn sour towards him, it could come out and embarrass the king’s pious fiancee. Holmes takes the case, thinking it’ll be a piece of cake to trick the woman and retrieve the photograph. Turns out, Irene is quite a bit more cunning than Holmes initially suspects. With a number of disguises used on both sides, one of them finally and permanently gains the upper hand. But is it Adler or Holmes who wins the day?

books.title: The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: While Holmes always has justice in the eyes of the law as his primary pursuit, every once in a while a case comes up that challenges his ideas about right and wrong. The most memorable of those is the story of Charles Augustus Milverton. He’s a wealthy loner whose primary income comes from the business of blackmailing. He buys seedy letters and photographs and then sells them to whoever the highest bidder is, regardless of whose lives are destroyed in the process. Holmes is enlisted in the fight against Milverton by Lady Eva Blackwell, who’s keen on retrieving some compromising documents. Milverton is as dastardly a fellow as London has ever seen, and though Holmes is aware of him, he hasn’t had the chance to nail down evidence of his breaking the law; this is his opportunity and he leaps at it. The reader gets the gift of clever disguises, a false engagement, breaking and entering, safe-cracking, and as surprising an ending as you’ll come across in these stories. It’s a delight.

books.title: The Red-Headed League
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.blurb: Now we enter the realm of the short story. Jabez Wilson, a man with flaming red hair, consults with Holmes about a mysterious job he took in reply to a want ad in the newspaper. Placed by “THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE,” it announced that “All red-headed men who are sound in body and mind and above the age of twenty-one years” were eligible for a well-paying but non-descript job. Wilson showed up for the interview, was declared to have just the right hue of red in his locks, and was set to work copying the encyclopedia. After getting through the “A’s,” he returned to the office only to see a sign on the door which read “THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED.” What’s going on? Surely there’s more to these strange circumstances than meets the eye. Only Holmes can solve such a riddle. With this story, Doyle shows the fun, playful side of his mystery-writing chops.

lists.title: The 10 Most Banned Books in Ame

books.title: The Perks of Being a Wallflower
books.author: Stephen Chbosky
books.blurb: Published twenty-five years ago, The Perks of Being a Wallflower is a seminal classic of young-adult literature. In a series of letters to an unknown friend, an introverted teenager confesses the highs of his freshman year—first kiss, first girlfriend, first experience behind the wheel—along with the traumatic lows, like the suicide of his best friend and the death of his aunt. Perks has been widely banned for decades, with challengers citing its “sexually explicit” content, as well as rape, drugs, and profanity. But where it remains on shelves, the book has saved lives. In 2013, Chbosky told the National Coalition Against Censorship that he’s received thousands of appreciative letters from young readers around the globe, some of whom credit his novel with inspiring them to decide against suicide. “Every time this happens, I just think about that one kid in the community who could really use the book,” Chbosky said.

books.title: Tricks
books.author: Ellen Hopkins
books.blurb: Told in verse, Tricks traces five teenagers struggling through turbulent adolescences, facing problems like sexual violence, drug abuse, and conversion therapy. Their stories converge in Las Vegas, where each character is drawn into the underworld of selling sex. Parents have condemned the novel as “sexually explicit”; they’ve also cited drugs, rape, and LGBTQ content in their efforts to ban the book. “It’s unthinkable that a handful of people have been allowed to remove any books from library shelves, to decide for everyone else what is or isn’t appropriate reading material,” Hopkins wrote in a blog post for the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of South Carolina, where she holds the distinction of being the state’s most frequently banned author. “As for protecting our kids, I often say ignorance is no armor. Knowledge is their absolute best weapon, and books are among the safest spaces to gather information.” Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, by Jesse Andrews Awkward teenager Greg Gaines plans to make it through high school by keeping a low profile and making mediocre movies with his best friend, Earl, but everything changes when his mother forces him to befriend Rachel, a classmate with leukemia. As Greg makes a movie about Rachel’s life and traces her deteriorating health, he’s forced to reconsider the wisdom of living on the sidelines. Me and Earl and the Dying Girl is a gutting, unflinching novel: Rachel doesn’t get better, and Greg doesn’t fall for her. Parents slammed the novel as “pornographic” and degrading to women, but teens fell hard for it—so much so that it was adapted into a feature film. “Anyone calling it pornographic has no idea what that word means,” Andrews tweeted. “I guarantee you, no one has ever been, or will ever be, sexually aroused by this book. It’s berserk to me that I even have to say that.”

books.title: Let's Talk About It
books.author: Erika Moen
books.blurb: and Matthew Nolan Let’s Talk About It is an illustrated guide to sex designed for teens, featuring comprehensive information about essential topics like orgasms, masturbation, and birth control. But it’s also so much more. Moen and Nolan expand their purview from the body to the soul, offering wisdom about rejection, jealousy, body image, and other matters of the heart. The book has been challenged for “sexually explicit” material and LGBTQ content, but the authors insist that even if teens are forbidden to read Let’s Talk About It, they’ll find that same material elsewhere. In an interview with Publishers Weekly, Moen said, “Teens are on the Internet and they’re coming into contact with all of this and way more. Our philosophy is you can either give them a book that’s been reviewed and approved by multiple professionals in the sex education and health fields, or you can give them a phone and let them figure it out for themselves on PornHub.”

books.title: Sold
books.author: Patricia McCormick
books.blurb: Sold is the National Book Award–nominated story of Lakshmi, a thirteen-year-old girl who leaves her rural Nepalese village to work as a maid in India, only to discover that she’s been trafficked into sexual slavery. McCormick interviewed real women in India and Nepal to craft this poignant fiction, but it’s nonetheless been widely banned due to rape and “sexually explicit” material. In an op-ed in The New York Times, McCormick wrote, “That’s what is consistently missing in the national conversation about book banning: the voices of those children and teenagers who see their experiences in print and finally realize they aren’t alone. And the ones who, fortunately, are not suffering such trauma, but who now have a window into the lives of their peers who do. We talk at them. And we talk about them. We try to control what they can read, think, and do. What we don’t do is listen to them.”

books.title: Flamer
books.author: Mike Curato
books.blurb: In this autofictional graphic novel, Curato introduces Aiden Navarro, a Filipino teen who’s long been bullied about his weight and his race, as well as targeted for “being gay.” Aiden is certain he isn’t gay, but during the summer between middle school and high school, everything changes. At scouting camp, Aiden is in his element—but there are new bullies there, and meanwhile, he can’t stop thinking about his friend Elias. Flamer is a moving story of self-discovery and self-acceptance, but bans have targeted the book for “LGBTQ content” and “sexually explicit” material. “What was shocking to me is that people care more about banning the book than trying to protect children’s physical lives in this day and age of mass shootings,” Curato told PEN America. The Bluest Eye, by Toni Morrison Morrison’s visionary first novel is the painful and poignant story of Pecola Breedlove, an abused and unloved Black girl, pregnant by her own father, who suffers relentless oppression and cruelty in her rural Ohio town. Pecola wishes desperately for blue eyes, convinced that conventional white beauty is the ticket to a better life, but she soon finds her mind colonized to the brink of madness. In 1970, The Bluest Eye put Morrison on the map as a once-in-a-century writer of preternatural gifts; in the decades since, it has remained a mainstay on banned-books lists, with states citing “offensive language” and “sexually explicit material” as justification for excluding it from academic curricula. But The Bluest Eye is a groundbreaking text with an important place in the American canon. Saturated with sorrow and charged with wonder, it remains an indelible study of trauma, shame, and internalized racism.

books.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance: An Inquiry into Values
books.author: Robert M. Pirsig
books.blurb: The anchor of this list. A father and son ride from Minneapolis to San Francisco on a Honda CB77, and Pirsig uses the trip as scaffolding for a 400-page argument about the nature of quality — what it means to do something well, why modern culture has separated intellectual work from manual work, and what that separation has cost us. The motorcycle maintenance is literal: he explains what he's doing and why it matters. The philosophy is difficult in places but never inaccessible. Published in 1974, it was rejected by 121 publishers before becoming one of the best-selling philosophy books ever written. Cross-references to the Craft, Skill & Mastery list. Read Shop Class as Soulcraft immediately after.

books.title: The Checklist Manifesto
books.author: Atul Gawande
books.blurb: Gawande is a surgeon who noticed that aviation had solved the problem of complex operations under pressure through checklists and that medicine hadn't — and spent years figuring out why, and whether the solution transferred. Around 209 pages and the most surprising entry on this list: the specific argument that checklists are not an insult to expertise but the mechanism through which expertise becomes reliable under pressure turns out to be one of the few genuinely transferable insights from one industry to another. The short entry and the unexpected angle simultaneously. The Goal by Eliyahu Goldratt makes a complementary operational argument through a novel about a failing manufacturing plant — around 384 pages and the deep cut for the reader who wants operations theory in narrative form rather than Gawande's analytical register.

books.title: The Endurance
books.author: Caroline Alexander
books.blurb: The Endurance was a sensational bestseller when it came out more than 20 years ago, and for good reason: it is a superb telling of one of the greatest survival stories of the 20th century, and it will be as moving a read in another hundred years as it remains today. This is the true story of an ordeal suffered by men trapped for nearly two years at the proverbial bottom of the Earth on Antarctica. It is harrowing, inspiring, terrifying, and ultimately extremely uplifting, both with all the many displays of indomitable human spirit and for the fact that, amazingly, no one died.

books.title: Becoming
books.author: Michelle Obama
books.blurb: Yes, Becoming is a memoir, not a call to action, a history book, or a political manifesto. But through her competent writing and casual grace, the former First Lady of the United States manages to inspire the reader to play his or her own part in the American story, to get more involved in community and politics, and to experience much of recent American history vicariously. Easy to read yet elegant and insightful, this book is inspiring without ever coming across as preachy.

books.title: A Testament of Hope: The Essential Writings and Speeches of Martin Luther King, Jr.
books.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
books.blurb: The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. died before he reached the age of 40. Let that sink in a bit: the man gave his entire adult life, brief though it was, so fully to a noble cause that now, more than a half-century after his death, we are still looking to him for an example of how to be. And yes, in one sense, that’s horridly depressing that some 50 years on, we still, as a society, have so much work to do. On the other hand, it’s a testament to what a fine example this man set, one that still inspires today and surely always will.

books.title: My Life On the Road
books.author: Gloria Steinem
books.blurb: A bit of fair warning: Celebrated author, feminist activist, and general rockstar of the 20th century (and into our own times) Gloria Steinem’s memoir is all but sure to inspire wanderlust, and travel isn’t exactly a good idea until the pandemic has ended. But perhaps for now, you can live vicariously through the eyes of this well-traveled and always outspoken icon who both lived through and left her mark on so much of the history of America. The world she inherited and that she bequeaths are different places, the latter one where, by in large, the “otherness” of many is no longer a thing. And that should inspire us all.

books.title: The Power of Positive Thinking
books.author: Norman Vincent Peale
books.blurb: In some ways, this book is a bit outdated, frankly. It leans on prayer a bit more than our increasingly secular world tends to see fit. It wasn’t written with the perspective gained through the Civil Rights Era, the Vietnam protests, Women’s Lib, and so on. But in other ways, it’s refreshing to see that a book written when most of our grandparents were in their heyday still has plenty of offer to lots of readers looking for help keeping their chins up. Agnostics, atheists, and frankly, most non-Christians should be ready with their proverbial grains of salt, but for the Christian believer, it’s kind of a charming book, really.

books.title: Tuesday’s With Morrie
books.author: Mitch Albom
books.blurb: Originally titled Letting Go , this is a book about death, if that’s how you choose to look at it. But that’s the wrong lens. Rather this is a book about life, simply told through the lens of a man who is gracefully winding his own life down. The book, an international bestseller, will make you weep more than once, but it will leave you feeling richer for having seen life through the eyes of the late Morrie Schwartz, as shared with author Mitch Albom, and ideally, it will help you appreciate all the time you have left here, be it years or decades.

books.title: Make Your Bed
books.author: Admiral William McRaven
books.blurb: It might seem almost flippant to say that major success starts with making your bed, and indeed, that would probably be inaccurate, too. Retired Navy Admiral William McCraven’s point in writing the book can indeed be viewed with that simple of an act as a starting point. See, it’s not making a bed that leads you to success in business, politics, the arts, fitness , and so on, it’s the simple willpower of taking care of what needs taking care of, no matter how seemingly small, that gets you there. This former Navy SEAL wrote a bestselling book about the premise — what will you do once you have committed to doing what needs to be done?

lists.title: The 13 Books That Have Taught M

books.title: The Code of Man: Love, Courage, Pride, Family, Country
books.author: Waller R. Newell
books.blurb: The Code of Man is Waller Newell’s follow-up to his first book What is a Man? In The Code of Man Newell argues that modern men have lost touch with values and virtues that have defined manliness for thousands of years. Consequently, many men (particularly young men) are lost, confused, and angry. Newell believes that the road to recovery is taken along the five paths to manliness: love, courage, pride, family, and country. Using Western writers and thinkers like Aristotle and Hemingway, among others, Newell attempts to guide men down the path to achieving a “manly heart.” I really enjoyed The Code of Man, and I thought it was a much better book than What Is a Man?. The great introduction makes checking out the book worthwhile in and of itself. Newell’s idea of honorable and virtuous manliness is much more clear in The Code of Man than in What Is a Man? I think if you enjoy the idea of manliness that we espouse on AoM, then you’ll enjoy this book.

books.title: Roman Honor: The Fire in the Bones
books.author: Carlin A. Barton
books.blurb: Back in 2012, we published a series on the history and decline of traditional manly honor in the West. I thought I had turned over every rock when researching those posts, but a few months after we wrapped up the series, I came across Roman Honor: The Fire in the Bones by Carlin Barton, a professor of ancient history at the University of Massachusetts. I wish I had known about this book when I was researching and writing my series on honor. Roman Honor is the best book I’ve read on honor — bar none. Barton masterfully explores how honor shaped the lives of ancient Rome from the early days of the Republic and all the way through the fall of the empire. She shows how small, intimate groups are vital for honor to survive and how imperialism kills it. This book is a hard read, but it’s well worth the effort. The insights are so brilliant they’re almost startling, and even the footnotes are packed with fascinating asides.

books.title: Manhood in the Making: Cultural Concepts of Masculinity
books.author: David Gilmore
books.blurb: If you enjoyed our 3 P’s of manhood series, then you’ll want to read the book that inspired it. Manhood in the Making is the most enlightening book on manhood I’ve read. In it, anthropologist David Gilmore shares the results of his cross-cultural study of manliness around the globe. Gilmore found that the concern for being manly and the idea of being a “real man,” is hardly a culturally-relative, social norm-based phenomenon, but instead has been shared by nearly every culture in the world, both past and present. While every society’s idea of what constitutes a “real man” has been molded by their unique histories, environments, and dominant religious beliefs, Gilmore found that almost all them share three common imperatives or moral injunctions — what I call the 3 P’s of Manhood: a male who aspires to be a man must protect, procreate, and provide. Despite being an academic book, Manhood in the Making is a fairly easy and enjoyable read. I couldn’t put it down after I started it and several times could sense a veritable light bulb going off above my head.

books.title: Is There Anything Good About Men? How Cultures Flourish by Exploiting Men
books.author: Roy F. Baumeister
books.blurb: In Is There Anything Good About Men?, eminent professor of psychology Roy F. Baumeister flips the feminist argument that it’s only women who have been oppressed and exploited from the beginning of time. Baumeister argues that, in many ways, men are the ones that society “exploits” (even if they accept their responsibilities willingly). He explores the fact that throughout history men have been seen as far more expendable than women; they’re the ones who went to war, took the dirty jobs, and sacrificed their lives to advance civilization. That might seem like a controversial thesis to some, but Baumeister lays it out in a very sensible, straightforward, non-inflammatory, and ultimately hard-to-argue-with way. He uses studies from the growing fields of evolutionary psychology and sociobiology to explain why cultures have exploited men the way they have. And he explains how and why certain aspects of male and female behavior are hardwired and that these differences should be used to complement each other rather than as fodder in the gender wars.

books.title: Plato and the Hero: Courage, Manliness, and the Impersonal Good
books.author: Angela Hobbs
books.blurb: I’m a classics guy, so the ancient Greeks and Romans inform a lot of my ideas about what manliness means, particularly how they equated manliness with living a life of virtue. One of the best books that I’ve come across on how the Greeks saw manliness as intertwined with virtue is by professor of philosophy Angela Hobbs. In Plato and the Hero: Courage, Manliness, and the Impersonal Good, Hobbs goes into detail clarifying Greek concepts related to manliness, including andreia (courage), thumos (spiritedness), and time (honor). She hones in on Plato’s uneasiness with these wild, masculine, Homeric virtues and shows how part of his philosophy was an attempt to harness these virtues for the greater good of society.

books.title: The Way of Men
books.author: Jack Donovan
books.blurb: Arguably the modern classic on masculinity. Jack Donovan works to strip away all the culturally/religiously relative definitions of manhood that exist in order to arrive at the very essentials of what makes men, men. He calls these essentials the “tactical virtues” and they include: strength, courage, mastery, and honor. While the amoral nature of Donovan’s idea of masculinity may make some uncomfortable, that is in many ways its greatest strength.
