Read Losing Earth’s stunning story of human greed and human folly to determine if you share his optimism.

books.title: The Case for the Green New Deal
books.author: Ann Pettifor
books.blurb: You’ve likely heard a lot about the Green New Deal, but you’d be forgiven if you’re not up to snuff on all the ins and outs of the meticulously-crafted policy. Pettifor, a British economist and a co-author of the Green New Deal, inspires and informs in this succinct book debunking claims that we can’t afford the legislation—in fact, she argues, we can’t afford not to pass it. Though the Green New Deal will require a complete overhaul of the international monetary system, Pettifor lays out a clear road map for the way forward, crafting a persuasive case for why we must act now. At just over two hundred pages, you could read this in an afternoon, then emerged a changed thinker.

books.title: A Terrible Thing to Waste: Environmental Racism and Its Assault on the American Mind
books.author: Harriet A. Washington
books.blurb: Environmental racism is a widespread and life-threatening danger; in this enraging exposé, Washington illuminates the staggering extent of it, connecting corporate greed and government irresponsibility to housing discrimination practices, which leave Black Americans experiencing record exposure to pollution. Washington also challenges the dangerous and biased IQ myth, arguing that Black Americans are exposed to lead, mercury, and other toxins at exponentially higher rates than white Americans, leading to lifelong complications like Alzheimer’s, memory loss, and impaired cognitive function. In the final chapter, she lays out a wide variety of solutions to fight environmental racism, from community involvement to nationwide activism. It’s imperative that we reverse this unconscionable discrimination soon, as millions of lives, quite literally, depend on it.

books.title: The Uninhabitable Earth: Life After Warming
books.author: David Wallace-Wells
books.blurb: “This is not a book about the science of warming; it is a book about what warming means to the way we live on this planet,” Wallace-Wells writes in The Uninhabitable Earth. Visceral and alarming, The Uninhabitable Earth transforms scientific predictions into lyrically-rendered realities, with Wallace-Wells painting grim portraits of what life will be like at each degree of warming. He predicts climate displacement, food insecurity, geopolitical war, global plagues, and cascading natural disasters, among other grim realities. The doom Wallace-Wells predicts is terrifying, merciless, and entirely self-inflicted. Consider The Uninhabitable Earth an impossible-to-look-away-from wake-up call, because as Wallace-Wells writes, “It is worse, much worse, than you think.”

books.title: Eating Animals
books.author: Jonathan Safran Foer
books.blurb: Beginning with the question of whether or not he and his family should eat meat, the novelist Jonathan Safran Foer interrogates this complicated personal choice through a journalistic lens, interviewing everyone from family farmers to slaughterhouse workers to anti-meat activists. Foer addresses our willful ignorance about the inhumane realities of the meat supply chain, as well as the escalating effects of factory farming on the fragile environment. At once a personal and philosophical meditation on the familial meanings of food, as well as a rigorous investigation into the dangerous business of animal products, Eating Animals presents readers with a compelling body of research about one of our most important lifestyle choices.

books.title: Our House Is on Fire: Greta Thunberg's Call to Save the Planet
books.author: Jeanette Winter
books.blurb: Struggling to explain climate change to the little ones in your life? This inspiring and informative picture book, targeted at children between the ages of three and eight, chronicles Greta Thunberg’s environmental awakening, from how she learned about the climate crisis in the classroom to how she took action for change. The book lays down a galvanizing challenge, asking its young readers what they will do to be a force for change, while celebrating the ability of children to be leaders. Share it with the little ones you love to start an important conversation.

books.title: How to Avoid a Climate Disaster: The Solutions We Have and the Breakthroughs We Need
books.author: Bill Gates
books.blurb: In 2019, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation committed $310 million to support climate adaptation efforts benefitting farmlands around the world. In this wonklike and persuasive book, Gates takes his environmental activism a bridge further, laying out an ambitious plan to reduce greenhouse emissions to zero by 2050. Drawing on data from researchers, policymakers, and engineers, Gates advocates for solutions both scientific (like developing alternative fuels) and personal (like increasing civic engagement in environmental justice issues). If you feel a radical shred of hope reading these galvanizing pages, dare to let in—without hope, we’ll get nowhere.

books.title: The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable
books.author: Amitav Ghosh
books.blurb: In this surprising synthesis of disciplines, a novelist accustomed to writing climate fiction examines history, literature, and politics to understand why our foremost thinkers so often fail to confront the climate crisis. He argues that there lies “an imaginative and cultural failure” at the heart of the climate crisis, as storytellers and public intellectuals eschew the vital, "unthinkable" task of grappling with this singular moment. In a galvanizing and clear-eyed call to action, he urges that we must find artistic and cultural frameworks to move through and combat this crisis together, as going it alone spells our doom.

books.title: Under a White Sky: The Nature of the Future
books.author: Elizabeth Kolbert
books.blurb: The Pulitzer Prize-winning author of The Sixth Extinction returns with another sobering look at our Anthropocene Epoch, this time centered not on the countless calamities ahead, but on the trailblazing efforts of scientists to turn back the doomsday clock. Kolbert describes the subjects of Under a White Sky as “people trying to solve problems created by people trying to solve problems”; she turns her lens to human interventions in nature, like the storied redirection of the Chicago River, and to the pressing need for further intervention to correct our folly. Traveling everywhere from the Great Lakes to the Great Barrier Reef, she chronicles her encounters with scientists, who are pioneering cutting-edge technologies to turn carbon emissions to stone and shoot diamonds in the stratosphere. Heralded by everyone from Barack Obama to Al Gore, Kolbert’s urgent, deeply researched text asks if our ingenuity can outrun our hubris.

books.title: This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. The Climate
books.author: Naomi Klein
books.blurb: “Our economy is at war with many forms of life on earth, including human life,” the acclaimed author of The Shock Doctrine writes in this radical study of the fateful incompatibility between climate justice and capitalism. Klein lays out the disastrous consequences of deregulated global capitalism, arguing that corporations are profiting massively off their destruction of the planet, permitted to occur at a breakneck pace by lobbyists and politicians. The only way forward, Klein insists, is a radical structural overhaul of the global economic system, one foregrounding social and environmental justice. This Changes Everything is a crucial clarion call demanding that we reorganize our economic priorities before it’s too late.

books.title: Don't Even Think About It: Why Our Brains Are Wired to Ignore Climate Change
books.author: George Marshall
books.blurb: Ever had a maddening argument with a climate change denialist, or wondered why policymakers remain immovable on addressing the growing climate crisis despite the mountain of scientific evidence available? In Don’t Even Think About It, Marshall, the founder of the Climate Outreach and Information Network, investigates how our psychology stymies substantive action, arguing that our innate sense of tribalism prevents us from operating in our best interest as a united collective. He also proposes a new language of outreach for the environmental movement—one optimized to win over even the staunchest denialist. Keep this shrewd and actionable book close in advance of your next family Thanksgiving.

books.title: Circe
books.author: Madeline Miller
books.blurb: tales of witches, harpies, and other female monsters are burned into our cultural imagination, but in the lush, luminous pages of Circe, a minor sorceress from Homer’s Odyssey receives a long-overdue feminist reimagining. Miller charts the lesser goddess Circe’s exile to the enchanted island of Aiaia, where Circe’s prison soon becomes her paradise. For centuries, she lives a free, feral life, honing her divine gifts of witchcraft and transfiguration while bedding down with lions and wolves. When Odysseus is shipwrecked on Aiaia, Miller reimagines the power dynamics of their entanglement, chipping away at Homer’s fabled myth of one man's greatness to expose a selfish man as flawed as any other. In Miller’s masterful hands, a long-overlooked goddess steps into the spotlight, giving rise to a powerful story of independence and self-determination in a man’s world.

books.title: Whipping Girl: A Transsexual Woman on Sexism and the Scapegoating of Femininity
books.author: Julia Serano
books.blurb: With transgender Americans facing new heights of violence and discrimination, it’s more important than ever that men understand what's going on. In this twenty-first century cornerstone of transfeminism, Serano, a transgender woman, exposes the myriad ways in which trans women have been stereotyped and disregarded in popular culture. Serano challenges the hyper-sexualization of trans women and connects transphobia to misogyny, while also debunking dangerous and deeply-rooted cultural mistruths about femininity as weakness and passivity. Her acute analysis builds to a rousing manifesto for a new framework of gender and sexuality: one rooted in inclusivity and empowerment, designed to embrace femininity in all its many varied forms. —Adrienne Westenfeld

books.title: The Bluest Eye
books.author: Toni Morrison
books.blurb: choose a single work from Toni Morrison’s prolific and peerless oeuvre is a daunting task, but when in doubt, begin at the beginning. Morrison’s visionary first novel is the painful and poignant story of Pecola Breedlove, an abused and unloved Black girl, pregnant by her own father, who suffers relentless oppression and cruelty in her rural Ohio town. Pecola wishes desperately for blue eyes, convinced that conventional white beauty is the ticket to a better life, but soon finds her mind colonized to the brink of madness. In 1970, The Bluest Eye put Morrison on the map as a once-in-a-century writer of preternatural gifts; in the decades since, it has remained a mainstay on banned books lists, with states citing “offensive language” and “sexually explicit material” as justification for excluding it from academic curriculum. Oprah Winfrey once said of Morrison, “She is our conscience, she is our seer, she is our truth-teller.” May the lightning rod of Morrison’s truth strike these states, as The Bluest Eye is a groundbreaking text with an important place in the American canon. Saturated with sorrow and charged with wonder, it remains an indelible study of trauma, shame, and internalized racism.

books.title: Girl Decoded: A Scientist's Quest to Reclaim Our Humanity by Bringing Emotional Intelligence to Technology
books.author: Rana el Kaliouby
books.blurb: At once a moving memoir of one woman’s becoming and a fast-paced story set on the bleeding edge of artificial intelligence, Girl Decoded traces el Kaliouby’s personal and professional journey as a Muslim woman in the overwhelmingly white and male world of technology. Raised by conservative parents in Egypt, el Kaliouby broke with obedient daughterhood to earn a PhD at Cambridge, then moved to the United States to pursue her dream of humanizing the tech industry. As she recounts her quest to bring emotional intelligence to emerging technologies, el Kaliouby writes beautifully about the personal challenge of learning to “decode” her own feelings. Her efforts led her to found Affectiva, a software company pioneering artificial intelligence that can understand human emotions. As women in STEM continue to fight misogyny, racism, and countless other challenges, Girl Decoded is a rousing reminder that women can and should be able to succeed without sacrificing any part of their wholeness.

books.title: Good and Mad: The Revolutionary Power of Women's Anger
books.author: Rebecca Traister
books.blurb: Released just five days after Dr. Christine Blasey Ford’s historic congressional testimony and four days before Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court confirmation, Good and Mad is the rare book published exactly when the culture needed it. Through exhaustive and compelling historical research, Traister illuminates female fury as a powerful political tool—one that’s long been ignored and suppressed, to the great detriment of American society. Traister traces women’s rage to the roots of the abolition and labor movements, exploring the forces that have sought to curb and marginalize women’s voices, while also emphasizing the ways in which Black women have long laid the foundation for the activism of American women. Powered by Traister’s own anger and laced through with compelling anecdotes from women about wielding righteous rage for constructive purposes, Good and Mad is galvanizing proof that hell hath no fury like half a nation’s population silenced.

books.title: Men Explain Things to Me
books.author: Rebecca Solnit
books.blurb: From one of our most imaginative and incisive writers comes a contemporary classic: seven sharp essays, each one an exceptionally hewn gem, beginning with the rousing title essay about how conversations between men and women are often driven off-course by mansplaining. In the ensuing essays, Solnit peers through politics, history, art, and media as lenses on cultural misogyny, arguing that seemingly isolated acts of sexism, like mansplaining, exist on a dangerous continuum of gendered exploitation and abuse, leading perilously to sexual violence. Solnit writes, “It’s a slippery slope. That’s why we need to address the slope, rather than compartmentalizing the varieties of misogyny and dealing with them separately.” Candid, courageous, and unflinchingly honest, Men Explain Things to Me is a powerful polemic for a future where women can enjoy equal power and respect.

books.title: The Will to Change: Men, Masculinity, and Love
books.author: bell hooks
books.blurb: In this seminal excavation of patriarchy’s devastating effect on the male psyche, hooks describes an endemic pattern of “psychic self-mutilation,” which drives men to lead lives of spiritual barrenness when they lose touch with love, self-expression, self-knowledge. Hooks addresses common male fears of intimacy and loss of patriarchal status while encouraging men to enrich and share their inner lives. Although hooks wrote The Will to Change with an eye toward reforming the emotional and spiritual lives of male readers, it nonetheless contains troves of wisdom for women. After all, as hooks writes, “Anytime a single male dares to transgress patriarchal boundaries in order to love, the lives of women, men, and children are fundamentally changed for the better.”

books.title: Entitled: How Male Privilege Hurts Women
books.author: Kate Manne
books.blurb: The visionary author of Down Girl returns with a bracing and brilliant study of male entitlement, bound to become a cornerstone of contemporary feminist canon. In a far-ranging analysis, Manne explores the myriad manifestations of male entitlement in American society, from Brett Kavanaugh’s Supreme Court appointment to the unequal division of domestic labor. So too does her scrutiny fall on incels, the medical undertreatment of female pain, and the myth of female politicians as “unelectable,” among other forces that police and punish women. Manne interrogates how entitlement gives rise to misogynist violence, making for a perceptive, precise, and gut-wrenching account of a social framework with devastating consequences.

books.title: The Witches Are Coming
books.author: Lindy West
books.blurb: Only Lindy West, one of our foremost thinkers on gender, could capture the agony and the ecstasy of 21st century life in one slim volume. In this searing collection of seventeen laser-focused essays, she unveils her unifying theory of America: that our steady diet of pop culture created by and for embittered, entitled white men is directly responsible for our sociopolitical moment. Adam Sandler, South Park, and Pepe the Frog all come under her withering scrutiny in this uproarious, hyper-literate analysis of the link between meme culture and male mediocrity. West crafts a blistering indictment of the systems that oppress us—the government that denies our rights, the media that denies our stories, and the society that denies our dignity.

books.title: Bury My Heart at Chuck E. Cheese's
books.author: Tiffany Midge
books.blurb: What’s the Lakota word for intersectional feminism? Is it just an emoji of a knife? asks prolific humorist Tiffany Midge in this uproarious, truth-telling collection of satirical essays skewering everything from white feminism to “Pretendians” to pumpkin spice. Midge, a member of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, muses bitingly on life as a Native woman in America, staring colonialism and racism in the face wherever she finds them, from offensive Halloween costumes to exploitative language. This collection’s deliciously sharp edges draw laughter and blood alike.

books.title: I Must Be Living Twice: New and Selected Poems
books.author: Eileen Myles
books.blurb: In the past decade, a new generation of feminists awakened to the work of Eileen Myles, whose lifetime of intimate and inimitable poetry is collected in I Must Be Living Twice. Spanning almost four decades of visionary work, this collection assembles an eclectic blend of Myles’ finest work, from their reminiscences on life as a young creative in New York City to more universal reflections on falling in love. Resisting heteronormative modes and subverting facile labels, Myles reminds us that poetry is a form of activism—one that can shift how we understand and empathize with the world around us. The Feminist Porn Book: The Politics of Producing Pleasure, edited by Tristan Taormino, Constance Penley, Celine Parrenas Shimizu, and Mireille Miller-Young Can pornography and feminism coexist? At the heart of this informative and far-reaching volume is that thorny question, explored in a series of gripping and provocative essays authored by producers, actors, consumers, and scholars of feminist pornography. From plus-size porn to disability in porn to trans women’s fight to be included as frequently as trans men, these essays demand an inclusive new future for erotic representation—one where fantasies of power and pleasure are egalitarian, in front of and behind the camera. The Feminist Utopia Project, edited by Alexandra Brodsky and Rachel Kauder Nalebuff What would a feminist utopia look like? Just ask any one of the fifty-seven cutting edge feminists whose voices resound in this expansive collection, which invites us to imagine a radically different world of freedom, safety, and equality. With essays by Janet Mock, Sheila Heti, Melissa Harris-Perry, and more, The Feminist Utopia Project proposes vigorous and compelling thought experiments: how might birth control be different if it were designed by an abortion provider? What would our economy look like if it valued caregiving and domestic labor? What would “good sex” mean through a framework of female pleasure? Next time you feel the feminist project is doomed, dive into this galvanizing book for a curative and necessary dose of hope.

lists.title: Treat your mind The 13 best sho

books.title: The Complete Tales and Poems of Edgar Allan Poe
books.author: Edgar Allan Poe
books.blurb: Edgar Allan Poe is the mac daddy of scary story writers. The Tell-Tale Heart is one of his masterpiece Gothic lit shorts that was published back in 1843 (years before we had so much as a prototype phone, let alone Stephen King to scare the crap out of us). The narrator of the story basically freaks the F out while trying to convince readers of his sanity… all while explaining his insane murder of an old man. Quote: “ For his gold I had no desire. I think it was his eye! Yes, it was this! He had the eye of a vulture –a pale blue eye, with a film over it. Whenever it fell upon me, my blood ran cold; and so by degrees – very gradually –I made up my mind to take the life of the old man, and thus rid myself of the eye forever.”

books.title: Giovanni’s Room
books.author: James Baldwin
books.blurb: In this short, seminal novel by the great James Baldwin, David, an American expat living in Paris circa the 1950s, wrestles with his identity and his sexuality as his lover awaits the guillotine. In a heartbreaking study of character, Baldwin lays bare David’s denial and self-deception, illuminating how his inability to live authentically bears fatal consequences for the alluring and vulnerable Giovanni. Before the novel was published in 1956, Baldwin’s publisher encouraged him to burn the draft, fearing that he would alienate his readership with a story of gay love. Today, Giovanni’s Room is widely recognized as one of the best LGBTQ+ novels of all time—a one-sitting must-read for anyone seeking to understand the pain and power of love under threat.

books.title: A Good Man Is Hard to Find
books.author: Flannery O'Connor
books.blurb: O'Connor was a Catholic novelist writing about the Protestant South, which gave her the outsider's eye for exactly how much violence, self-deception, and grotesquerie the region's religiosity was containing. The stories in this 1955 collection end badly — characters meet escaped convicts, traveling salesmen with prosthetic legs, and their own worst impulses, and the collisions are rarely survivable. The title story, in which a family road trip ends with a grandmother facing execution in a ditch, is the finest American short story of the postwar era and one of the most theologically serious pieces of fiction in the language. Around 251 pages. O'Connor died of lupus at thirty-nine with two collections completed — this one and Everything That Rises Must Converge, the right next step for the reader who finishes this wanting more.

books.title: The Metamorphosis
books.author: Franz Kafka
books.blurb: Kafka wrote about bureaucracy, bodily transformation, inexplicable guilt, and systems of authority that cannot be appealed to or understood — and he wrote about them as comedy, which is the thing most readers miss on first encounter. The Metamorphosis, in which a man wakes up as a giant insect and his family's main concern is how to manage the inconvenience, is funny in the way that things are funny when they are also completely true. This complete collection covers the full body of work in a single volume. Around 486 pages. The international entry and the canonical entry simultaneously — Kafka is the most referenced writer in the twentieth century literary tradition and among the least actually read. The AoM reader who works inside any large organization will find the stories less like fantasy and more like documentary.

books.title: The Yellow Wallpaper
books.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
books.blurb: Published in 1892, The Yellow Wallpaper is another classic of early-modern gothic horror, though it emphasizes psychological distress over some of the more fantastic elements embraced by Gilman’s peers. The tale of a woman who is confined to her bedroom as part of a rest cure for her so-called hysteria, as the narrator slips into madness she becomes increasingly enamored by the yellow color of her room. Considered a cornerstone of early American feminist writing, its commentary on the oppressive impact of patriarchy remains relevant to this day.

books.title: Stories of Your Life and Others
books.author: Ted Chiang
books.blurb: Chiang is a technical writer who publishes science fiction stories at the rate of roughly one every few years and has won more awards per word than any writer in the genre — the Hugo, the Nebula, and the Theodore Sturgeon repeatedly, for a body of work that fits in a single volume. The stories use science fiction premises — a linguist learning an alien language that restructures her experience of time, a mathematician proving that the Tower of Babel was physically possible — to examine questions about free will, language, and what it means to know the future. The film Arrival is adapted from the title story. Around 281 pages and the genre entry on this list. The reader who thinks science fiction is plot machinery rather than literature has not read Ted Chiang.

books.title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
books.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
books.blurb: A great short story doesn't need a lot of words to leave a lasting impression. And that's never more true than for sci-fi great Ursula K. Le Guin's creation, The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas . Published in 1973, it describes a society which is apparently perfect and full of happiness, but at a cost: There is a single child who is forced to live in misery and deprivation. How the people of the society react to the knowledge that their happiness depends on the suffering of an innocent provides a disquieting and uncomfortable parallel for many of our lives today. It's the kind of story that stays with you and is returned to as a moral conundrum again and again.

books.title: The Dead
books.author: James Joyce
books.blurb: The most renowned installment in Joyce’s Dubliners, The Dead is about a young Irishman whose family holds him in the highest regard thanks to his practicality and level-headedness. When he attends a party, however, his principles are challenged as he is pushed to confront his own mortality. Arguably the famed writer’s most accessible work, it nonetheless shows his ability to bury deep themes in seemingly straightforward stories.

books.title: The Lottery
books.author: Shirley Jackson
books.blurb: First released in The New Yorker in 1948, The Lottery is a masterwork of grim atmosphere and troubling themes. The story of a small village lottery — the winner of which will be stoned to death — it almost singlehandedly created the modern concept of gothic horror thanks to its gloomy atmosphere and use of thought-provoking, disturbing irony.

books.title: We Can Remember It for You Wholesale
books.author: Philip K. Dick
books.blurb: No list of short story greats would be complete without a nod to Philip K. Dick, the prolific sci-fi author who single-handedly created many of the staples of the genre. Even if you've never read a Dick novel, you know his work from countless adaptations and movies. The short story We Can Remember It For You Wholesale is best know as the inspiration for the classic sci-fi movie Total Recall , and it delves into the same questions of reality, memory, and consciousness. When an average guy with an office job decides to have memories of an exciting trip to Mars implanted into his mind, it kicks off a cascade of confusion and questioning as he struggles to decide which of his memories are real and which have been manipulated.

books.title: Cathedral
books.author: Raymond Carver
books.blurb: By the late 1970s, short stories were waning in their public appeal. Then Raymond Carver rose to prominence and wrote some life back into the format with his unrivaled application of minimalism. The most renowned example of this was Cathedral , which is about a man’s jealousy toward his wife’s blind friend. By the time the two men bond over the image of a cathedral — which only one of them can actually see — the reader is left floored by the elegant simplicity of the story’s deceptively powerful ending.

books.title: On the Honeymoon
books.author: Javier Marias
books.blurb: One of the greatest writers of the past several decades, Javier Marias’ name is essentially on every shortlist for the Nobel Prize in literature. While novels account for the vast majority of his work, he did release a collection of short fiction called When I Was Mortal . Perhaps the best story in the book is On the Honeymoon , which tells the story of a newly married man who watches the street outside a hotel window as his wife is sick in bed. Drama ensues when he catches the eye of a distraught looking woman. Within 20 pages, Marias uses all the literary tools that he is known for wielding in books 20 times longer.

books.title: Hills Like White Elephants
books.author: Ernest Hemingway
books.blurb: Papa Hemingway wrote several short stories that could be ranked among the best of all time, but Hills Like White Elephants is perhaps his most brilliant effort thanks to how he talks directly about a subject without ever bringing it up at all. The story of a young couple waiting for a train as they discuss some never-clarified operation, it is nevertheless obvious that the man is attempting to pressure the woman into having an abortion. It is a masterpiece of subtlety and simplicity from a writer who is perhaps the greatest at packing an abundance of meaning into a minimal word count.

books.title: In Cold Blood
books.author: Truman Capote
books.blurb: In November 1959, two men drove to a farmhouse in Holcomb, Kansas and killed the four members of the Clutter family for $40 and a radio. Capote spent six years reporting the story — the crime, the investigation, the killers' backgrounds, and the execution — and published it in 1966 as the book that invented literary true crime. The prose is as controlled as fiction, the portrait of Perry Smith is one of the most empathetic accounts of a killer ever written, and the moral argument about capital punishment runs underneath every page without ever surfacing as editorializing. Around 343 pages and the anchor entry on this list. Cross-seeds with the Halloween list. The reader who finishes this and wants more Capote goes to Music for Chameleons; the reader who wants more literary true crime starts with everything else on this list.

books.title: The Devil in the White City
books.author: Erik Larson
books.blurb: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago was the greatest engineering achievement of the nineteenth century — built in two years on a swamp, visited by 27 million people, and responsible for introducing Americans to the Ferris wheel, the dishwasher, and Cracker Jack. H.H. Holmes used it to lure victims to his hotel a mile from the fairgrounds, where he had installed a kiln, a gas chamber, and a dissection table. Larson tells both stories simultaneously and the effect is the most purely readable true crime book in print — the architecture and the murder feeding each other's momentum. Around 447 pages and the literary true crime entry on this list. Cross-seeds with the US History list, where it belongs equally. The reader who thinks history is dry will find Larson a reliable cure.

books.title: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil
books.author: John Berendt
books.blurb: In 1981, an antiques dealer named Jim Williams shot his young lover in his Savannah mansion and was tried four times for murder — acquitted the fourth, dead of pneumonia eight months later. Berendt arrived in Savannah as a tourist and stayed four years, and the book he produced is as much about the city as about the case: the drag queen who threatened powerful men with a bottle of poison, the society balls held in cemeteries, the root doctor operating in the squares, the specific social order of a city that never fully entered the 20th century. The humor entry on this list, though the comedy is Southern Gothic throughout. Cross-references to the True Crime list, where it appears in a different context. The best single portrait of a Southern city written by an outsider who had the sense to stay.

books.title: Killers of the Flower Moon
books.author: David Grann
books.blurb: In the 1920s, members of the Osage Nation in Oklahoma were being murdered systematically after oil was discovered beneath their land. The killings went on for years, involved the most prominent men in the county, and became the founding investigation of J. Edgar Hoover's FBI. Grann spent years in the archives and the result is the most important true crime book published in the last twenty years — not a whodunit but a documented account of institutional complicity, racial violence, and the specific American capacity to look away from evidence when the perpetrators are the right kind of people. Around 338 pages. Cross-seeds with the US History list. Note the argument running underneath the narrative: this book is making a case about what American institutions protect and what they ignore, and the evidence is overwhelming.

books.title: I'll Be Gone in the Dark
books.author: Michelle McNamara
books.blurb: McNamara spent years hunting the Golden State Killer from her laptop — a serial rapist and murderer who operated in California in the 1970s and 1980s and was never caught — and died in 2016 before she finished the book. Her husband Patton Oswalt and two researchers completed it from her notes, and the result is the most formally unusual entry on this list: as much a portrait of obsession as an investigation, as much about what cold cases do to the people who pursue them as about the killer himself. Around 360 pages. The unexpected angle entry on this list — McNamara's first-person voice makes the reader complicit in the hunt rather than merely a spectator. Published in 2018; the Golden State Killer was identified and arrested the same year, which gives the book an ending McNamara never wrote.

books.title: Helter Skelter
books.author: Vincent Bugliosi
books.blurb: Bugliosi prosecuted Charles Manson for the Tate-LaBianca murders and wrote the definitive account of the case: the killings, the investigation, the trial, and the specific mechanism by which Manson controlled the people around him without personally committing most of the murders. Around 528 pages and the iconic murder entry on this list — the Manson case is the most written-about crime of the twentieth century and this is the book that established everything subsequent writers have had to reckon with. Bugliosi is a prosecutor rather than a literary writer, which means the account is relentlessly evidentiary rather than atmospheric: he is building a case on every page, and the case is airtight. The reader who wants to understand how Manson actually worked — the psychology, the control mechanisms, the specific vulnerability of the people he recruited — comes here.

books.title: The Stranger Beside Me
books.author: Ann Rule
books.blurb: Rule was working the night shift at a Seattle crisis hotline in 1971 when she was paired with a charming, intelligent volunteer named Ted Bundy. She liked him. They became friends. She was already under contract to write a book about an unknown serial killer operating in the Pacific Northwest when Bundy was arrested, and the book she wrote is the definitive Bundy account precisely because she knew him before she knew what he was. Around 438 pages and the most unsettling entry on this list — not because of the murders, which are documented with appropriate restraint, but because Rule's portrait of Bundy-before-capture is so ordinary. The reader who finishes this will spend time afterward thinking about the specific difficulty of identifying dangerous people who are also genuinely pleasant, which is the question the book is actually asking.

books.title: Mindhunter
books.author: John Douglas
books.blurb: Douglas spent his career at the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit developing the methodology of criminal profiling — the systematic analysis of crime scenes, victimology, and offender behavior that made it possible to build a psychological portrait of an unknown killer before he was caught. This memoir covers the cases that built the methodology: the interviews with Manson, Bundy, and Ed Kemper in prison; the Atlanta child murders; the development of the organized-disorganized framework that became the foundation of modern forensic psychology. Around 370 pages and the serial killer forensics entry on this list. The television series Mindhunter is based on this book and is considerably less accurate than it suggests. The reader who wants to understand how the FBI actually catches serial killers — the specific intellectual work of it — comes here rather than to the screen adaptation.

books.title: The Executioner's Song
books.author: Norman Mailer
books.blurb: Gary Gilmore was executed by firing squad in Utah in January 1977 — the first execution in America after the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty — and Mailer spent years reconstructing his life, his crimes, his relationships, and his insistence on his own execution with the thoroughness of a biographer and the prose of a novelist. Technically a novel but reported with journalistic precision from thousands of interviews and documents. Around 1,056 pages and the most demanding entry on this list — also the most complete account of a specific American criminal life available anywhere in the literature. Won the Pulitzer Prize in 1979. The reader who commits to the length will find Mailer's portrait of Gilmore and the Utah communities around him more honest about American violence and American punishment than anything shorter could manage.

books.title: Just Mercy
books.author: Bryan Stevenson
books.blurb: Stevenson founded the Equal Justice Initiative in Alabama and this book covers his work representing death row inmates — many of them demonstrably innocent — in a state whose criminal justice system had accumulated decades of racial bias into its machinery. The central case involves Walter McMillian, a Black man sentenced to death for a murder he did not commit and whose conviction Stevenson eventually overturned. Note the political argument throughout: this book is making an explicit case about race, the death penalty, and American justice that argues from a progressive framework and supports it with prosecutorial precision. Around 336 pages and the wrongful conviction entry on this list. The reader who disagrees with Stevenson's politics will find the documented evidence harder to dismiss than the argument; the reader who agrees will find the specific cases more disturbing than the general argument prepared him for.

books.title: The Power Broker: Robert Moses and the Fall of New York
books.author: Robert A. Caro
books.blurb: Robert Moses never held elected office. He also shaped the physical landscape of New York — and by extension the template for American urban life in the 20th century — more decisively than any elected official in the country's history. Caro spent seven years reporting this book, and the result is the greatest work of American biography ever written and the most thorough examination of how power is actually accumulated and what it does to the man who holds it. At 1,200 pages it is the longest book on this list by a significant margin. It rewards every page. Caro's multi-volume LBJ biography is arguably the superior achievement; start here first, because this is where he figured out what he was doing.

books.title: The Devil in the White City
books.author: Erik Larson
books.blurb: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago was the greatest engineering achievement of the nineteenth century — built in two years on a swamp, visited by 27 million people, and responsible for introducing Americans to the Ferris wheel, the dishwasher, and Cracker Jack. H.H. Holmes used it to lure victims to his hotel a mile from the fairgrounds, where he had installed a kiln, a gas chamber, and a dissection table. Larson tells both stories simultaneously and the effect is the most purely readable true crime book in print — the architecture and the murder feeding each other's momentum. Around 447 pages and the literary true crime entry on this list. Cross-seeds with the US History list, where it belongs equally. The reader who thinks history is dry will find Larson a reliable cure.

books.title: The Warmth of Other Suns
books.author: Isabel Wilkerson
books.blurb: Between 1915 and 1970, six million Black Americans left the South. Wilkerson followed three of them: Ida Mae Brandon Gladney, who left Mississippi for Chicago in 1937; George Starling, who left Florida for New York in 1945; Robert Foster, who left Louisiana for Los Angeles in 1953. The Great Migration reshaped American cities, American politics, and American music — and Wilkerson reconstructed it through three individual lives rather than statistics. The most complete account of why Black Southerners left, what the leaving cost, and what it produced. Cross-references to the US History list for the political context, and to the Books About Cities list, where the cities these migrants transformed are documented from the receiving end. The reader who wants the companion structural analysis should read The Mind of the South on this list first.

books.title: Killers of the Flower Moon
books.author: David Grann
books.blurb: In the 1920s, members of the Osage Nation in Oklahoma were being murdered systematically after oil was discovered beneath their land. The killings went on for years, involved the most prominent men in the county, and became the founding investigation of J. Edgar Hoover's FBI. Grann spent years in the archives and the result is the most important true crime book published in the last twenty years — not a whodunit but a documented account of institutional complicity, racial violence, and the specific American capacity to look away from evidence when the perpetrators are the right kind of people. Around 338 pages. Cross-seeds with the US History list. Note the argument running underneath the narrative: this book is making a case about what American institutions protect and what they ignore, and the evidence is overwhelming.

books.title: Undaunted Courage
books.author: Stephen Ambrose
books.blurb: Jefferson commissioned Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to find a water route to the Pacific and document everything they found along the way. What they found was a continent — the grizzly bears, the Rockies, the Columbia River system, the specific quality of a landscape no American had ever described. Ambrose covers the full expedition from its planning through the return, with particular attention to Lewis himself — the ideal explorer who turned out to be a man who couldn't survive peace, dead by his own hand three years after the journey ended. Around 500 pages and the most purely enjoyable American exploration biography available. Cross-seeds with the US History list. The Journals of Lewis and Clark in Bernard DeVoto's abridgment give the primary source voice for the reader who wants the continent described in real time.

books.title: Battle Cry of Freedom
books.author: James McPherson
books.blurb: The single best one-volume history of the Civil War ever written, and the only entry this list needs on the subject. McPherson covers the political, economic, social, and military dimensions of the war across 900 pages without losing the narrative thread or settling into the comfortable myths that most Civil War history either perpetuates or spends all its energy dismantling. The causes are treated honestly, the campaigns are traced clearly, and the human cost is never abstracted into statistics. The Shelby Foote trilogy is longer and more literary. This is more complete and more honest. Pulitzer Prize, 1989. If you read one Civil War book, it's this one.

books.title: Empire of the Summer Moon
books.author: S.C. Gwynne
books.blurb: The Comanche economy was built on raiding, hunting, and the specific labor of women who processed buffalo — skinning, curing, cooking, managing camp — while men controlled the violence and the horses. Gwynne's account of the rise and fall of the Comanche empire is not primarily a labor history, but the economic organization it documents — who does what work, who owns the product of that work, and what happens when a more efficient economic system arrives and destroys the existing one — makes it the most illuminating case study on this list of how economic disruption operates at civilizational scale. Already on AoM's US History list. Cross-references to the American West History list. The unexpected-angle entry: approaches labor and economic transformation through the history of a people who had no concept of wage labor and were destroyed partly because of it.

books.author: David McCullough
books.blurb: Not a survey of the founding era and not a biography — a single year of military history, told at ground level, when Washington's Continental Army was weeks from collapse and the revolution was genuinely close to dying in its first winter. McCullough follows the campaign from the disaster at Brooklyn through the retreats across New Jersey to the crossing of the Delaware, and the result is as suspenseful as any novel despite the fact that you know how it ends. The founders get their monuments elsewhere. This book is about the ordinary and extraordinary men who held the line long enough for those monuments to become necessary.

books.title: One Summer: America, 1927
books.author: Bill Bryson
books.blurb: In the summer of 1927, Charles Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic alone, Babe Ruth hit 60 home runs, Al Capone ran Chicago without meaningful interference, the Mississippi flooded on a biblical scale, and a sitting President quietly decided not to seek re-election without telling his own cabinet. Bryson runs all of these stories in parallel, finds the absurdity and the grandeur in equal measure, and produces the most purely enjoyable American history book on this list. It is funny in the way that only a writer who genuinely loves the material can be funny — not mocking, but delighted. The 1920s look different after this book, and so does the America that was about to drive itself off a cliff two years later.

books.title: Seabiscuit
books.author: Laura Hillenbrand
books.blurb: The Depression-era racehorse and the three broken men who built him into a national obsession: a half-blind jockey, a near-deaf trainer, and a self-made millionaire owner who had lost most of what he'd built. Hillenbrand wrote this from her bed while suffering from a chronic illness severe enough that she couldn't attend the races she was writing about, which gives the story of improbable physical endurance a biographical shadow the text never mentions. The sports history is meticulous. The real subject is what America needed to believe about itself in 1938 and why a small, crooked-legged racehorse could briefly provide it. The most underrated book on this list.

books.title: All Quiet on the Western Front
books.author: Erich Maria Remarque
books.blurb: The deliberate counterpoint to Storm of Steel and one of the best-selling novels of the 20th century. Paul Bäumer enlists at eighteen with his classmates, full of the rhetoric of glory and duty their teacher has fed them, and the Western Front systematically strips every illusion away. Remarque served on the front himself and the physical details — the mud, the rats, the gas, the specific sounds of an artillery barrage — carry the authority of a man who was there. The Nazis burned this book in 1933. Jünger declined to condemn the burning. Both facts are more instructive than any literary analysis. These two books should be read back to back, in either order, with the understanding that both men survived the same war and came back with irreconcilable accounts of what it meant.

books.title: The Great War and Modern Memory
books.author: Paul Fussell
books.blurb: The most important book ever written about what WWI did to the way human beings understand war, heroism, and the gap between official language and lived experience. Fussell — a WWII combat veteran and Princeton literature professor — spent years reading the memoirs, letters, and poetry of British soldiers on the Western Front and produced a work that is simultaneously literary criticism, cultural history, and the most devastating indictment of the language of glory ever assembled. His central argument is that WWI invented modern irony — the permanent unbridgeable gap between what leaders say and what soldiers experience — and that we have lived inside that irony ever since. The AoM reader who finishes this will read every subsequent war memoir on this list differently.

books.title: Gallipoli
books.author: Alan Moorehead
books.blurb: In 1915, Winston Churchill devised the plan to knock Turkey out of the war by forcing the Dardanelles, capturing Constantinople, and opening a supply route to Russia. The result was eight months of catastrophic failure, 250,000 Allied casualties, and the founding myth of Australian and New Zealand national identity. Moorehead's account — published in 1956 and still the most readable single-volume history of the campaign — follows the planning, the naval attack, the landings at ANZAC Cove, the stalemate in the hills, and the evacuation with the same narrative economy he brought to his African histories. The portrait of the ANZAC soldiers — men from the other end of the earth, fighting in a place none of them had heard of six months earlier — is one of the great passages in the literature of military courage and military waste.

books.title: Goodbye to All That
books.author: Robert Graves
books.blurb: Graves served as an officer in the Royal Welch Fusiliers, was reported dead at the Somme, survived, and wrote this memoir at 34 in a white heat of anger designed to close the door on England, the war, and everything they had cost him. It is the funniest book on this list and the most English — Graves writes about the absurdities of military bureaucracy, the class system in the trenches, and the social codes of the British officer corps with a mordant precision that makes you laugh and then stops you cold when the casualties arrive. Siegfried Sassoon appears throughout, fully recognizable to anyone who knows his poetry. His companion memoir Memoirs of an Infantry Officer covers the same war from the same circles with more measured fury. Read both.

books.title: Lawrence in Arabia
books.author: Scott Anderson
books.blurb: T.E. Lawrence's own account of the Arab Revolt — Seven Pillars of Wisdom — is 700 pages of brilliant, uneven, self-mythologizing prose that rewards patient readers and defeats impatient ones. Anderson's 2013 biography is the better entry point: it follows four men simultaneously through the Middle Eastern theater — Lawrence, a German intelligence officer, an American Standard Oil agent, and a Zionist diplomat — and uses their intersecting stories to cover the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, the Arab Revolt, and the Sykes-Picot Agreement that betrayed everyone Lawrence had promised independence. The AoM reader who finishes this book will understand the creation of modern Iraq, Syria, Jordan, and Israel — and every subsequent Middle Eastern conflict on the history lists — with a clarity that no amount of news coverage provides.

books.title: Minds at War
books.author: David Roberts (ed.)
books.blurb: No prose account of the Western Front has ever communicated the actual sensory experience of it as precisely as its poetry, and this anthology — collecting the work of the major British and Commonwealth poets who served in the war, with substantial biographical and contextual notes for each — is the most accessible entry point for readers coming to WWI poetry without a literary background. Rupert Brooke's early idealism, Wilfred Owen's gas attacks and Strange Meeting, Siegfried Sassoon's furious protests, Isaac Rosenberg writing from the trenches — Roberts organizes them chronologically so the reader experiences the war's effect on the poets' language in real time. The rhetoric of 1914 gives way to the irony of 1916 gives way to the controlled fury of 1918. For Sassoon in depth, his collected War Poems is the natural follow-on.

books.title: Storm of Steel
books.author: Ernst Jünger
books.blurb: Jünger was wounded fourteen times on the Western Front, received Germany's highest military honor, and wrote this memoir as a young officer who found combat not traumatic but clarifying — a place where the essential things became visible through the removal of everything inessential. It is the most controversial memoir on this list and the most important to read alongside All Quiet on the Western Front: not because Jünger is right and Remarque is wrong, but because both responses were genuine, both were German, and understanding both is the only way to understand how the same war produced both the Weimar Republic and the Nazi Party. Note that Jünger revised the text multiple times across his long life, progressively softening its nationalist passages — the edition matters.

books.title: Verdun
books.author: Alistair Horne
books.blurb: The Battle of Verdun lasted 303 days in 1916, cost France and Germany approximately 700,000 casualties combined, and accomplished nothing strategic for either side. It was designed by the German chief of staff Falkenhayn specifically to bleed France white — to destroy not territory but French soldiers, at a place France could not afford to abandon. Horne's account — still the best popular history of the battle fifty years after its publication — is the essential French entry on this list and the book that explains why France emerged from WWI so broken that it would not fight Germany again twenty years later. The scale of Verdun — the rotating divisions, the sacred road, the men who simply disappeared into the mud and were never recovered — reads like fiction. Every word is documented.

books.title: Over There
books.author: Byron Farwell
books.blurb: America entered WWI in April 1917, nearly three years after it started, and sent two million men to France in eighteen months — the largest overseas military deployment in American history to that point. Farwell's account follows the American Expeditionary Forces at ground level: the infantry soldiers from places like Kansas and Georgia who had been reading about this war for three years without any framework for what it actually was, encountering the industrialized slaughter of the Western Front for the first time in the battles of Belleau Wood, Château-Thierry, and the Meuse-Argonne. The portrait of American soldiers — their specific confidence, their specific shock, and the specific way they fought — is the essential American entry on this list and the book that explains why the doughboys came home so different from the men who had left.

books.title: The First Day on the Somme
books.author: Martin Middlebrook
books.blurb: On July 1, 1916, the British Army suffered 57,470 casualties — 19,240 dead — in a single day. It remains the bloodiest day in the history of the British military. Middlebrook interviewed 500 surviving veterans in the 1960s before they died and combined their testimony with unit diaries and tactical records to produce the most complete reconstruction of a single day of WWI combat ever assembled. The buildup, the seven-day artillery bombardment that failed to cut the wire, the whistles at 7:30 AM, the walk across no man's land, and the collapse of the assault wave by wave — all of it documented with the precision of a man who understood that this single day required its own book. One of the great works of oral history in any conflict.

books.title: Castles of Steel
books.author: Robert Massie
books.blurb: The Battle of Jutland in May 1916 was the only major fleet engagement of WWI — 250 ships, 100,000 men, and the largest naval battle in history to that point. The British lost more ships and more men but the German High Seas Fleet never again left port in force. Massie covers the entire naval war: the construction of the rival fleets in the decades before 1914, the North Sea blockade that slowly strangled Germany, the U-boat campaign that came closest to winning the war, the surface raider campaigns across every ocean, and Jutland itself. At 800 pages it is the longest book on this list and the commitment is worth it — Massie writes naval history the way the best military historians write land campaigns, with command decisions given the same weight as the human experience of the men executing them.

books.title: Sagittarius Rising
books.author: Cecil Lewis
books.blurb: Lewis flew with the Royal Flying Corps from 1915 to 1918 in wood-and-canvas biplanes with no parachutes, no heating, and machine guns synchronized to fire through the propeller — mechanisms that occasionally failed. He survived when most of his contemporaries did not, and wrote this memoir with the literary instinct of a man who had genuinely processed what he experienced rather than simply documented it. The portrait of aerial combat over the Western Front — the loneliness, the beauty, the specific terror of being shot at two miles above the earth in an aircraft that caught fire readily — is unlike anything else in the literature of WWI. Manfred von Richthofen, the Red Baron, is present throughout as both opponent and inadvertent subject — his own memoir The Red Baron covers the same skies from the other cockpit.

books.title: In Flanders Fields
books.author: Leon Wolff
books.blurb: The third battle of Ypres — Passchendaele, 1917 — cost 600,000 casualties on both sides to advance the Allied line five miles through mud so deep that wounded men drowned in shell holes. Wolff's account, published in 1958, remains the most literary and emotionally immediate history of the battle: he is less interested in the tactical diagrams than in what it felt like to be ordered across that ground, wave after wave, by commanders who continued the offensive long after the strategic logic had collapsed. The portrait of Field Marshal Haig persisting through conditions that every officer below him understood to be catastrophic is one of the most damning passages in military history. The companion piece to Middlebrook's Somme: the British Army's two worst sustained nightmares, twelve months apart.

books.title: The Eastern Front 1914-1917
books.author: Norman Stone
books.blurb: While the Western Front ground itself to a standstill in the mud of France and Belgium, the Eastern Front moved — enormous armies sweeping back and forth across Poland, Galicia, and the Baltic states in campaigns that dwarfed anything in France in scale and cost. Stone's history remains the essential English-language account of the Eastern Front: the German campaigns that nearly knocked Russia out of the war in 1914, the catastrophic failures of the Austro-Hungarian military, and the conditions that produced the Russian Revolution of 1917 and ended three empires simultaneously. The Eastern Front killed more people than the Western Front, destroyed the Romanov, Habsburg, and Ottoman dynasties, and created the political vacuum that both Bolshevism and Nazism filled. The most consequential theater of the war and the least read by English-speaking audiences.

books.title: The Guns of August
books.author: Barbara Tuchman
books.blurb: The essential entry point for WWI and one of the great works of popular history ever written. Tuchman covers the five weeks between the assassination of Franz Ferdinand and the opening of full-scale war — the diplomatic failures, the mobilization schedules that locked Europe into a conflict nobody fully wanted, the Schlieffen Plan and its fatal modifications, and the opening campaigns that set the pattern for the next four years. JFK kept a copy in the White House during the Cuban Missile Crisis and cited it as the book that most shaped his thinking about how wars start without anyone intending them to. Won the Pulitzer Prize in 1963. Tuchman's companion volume The Proud Tower covers the decades of European society before 1914 that made the catastrophe inevitable — read it after this one.

books.title: With the Old Breed: At Peleliu and Okinawa
books.author: Eugene B. Sledge
books.blurb: Sledge enlisted in the Marines at eighteen and fought at Peleliu and Okinawa — two of the most brutal battles of the Pacific War, against an enemy that had decided to die rather than surrender. He kept notes hidden in his Bible and wrote this memoir thirty years later with a clarity and moral seriousness that the passage of time only sharpened. The portrait of what sustained combat does to a man — the specific moral erosion, the specific dehumanization, and the specific acts of both savagery and genuine compassion that combat produces — is unlike anything else written about the Pacific War. Paul Fussell called it the finest memoir to emerge from WWII. Robert Leckie's Helmet for My Pillow covers the same Corps at Guadalcanal and New Britain and belongs on your reading list immediately after this one.

books.title: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
books.author: Richard Rhodes
books.blurb: Rhodes won the Pulitzer Prize, the National Book Award, and the National Book Critics Circle Award simultaneously for this history — a feat never replicated — and the achievement justifies all three. The book covers the physics from Einstein's 1905 papers through the Trinity test in July 1945, the scientists who built the bomb, the industrial and military organization that made it possible, and the specific moral reasoning of the men who decided to use it. At 900 pages it is one of the longer books on this list and rewards every page: Rhodes writes about nuclear physics with a clarity that makes it genuinely comprehensible to the non-scientist, and the portraits of Oppenheimer, Fermi, Bohr, and Teller are among the finest scientific biography in American letters. Kai Bird and Martin Sherwin's American Prometheus covers Oppenheimer's moral aftermath in full — read it next.

books.title: The Cruel Sea
books.author: Nicholas Monsarrat
books.blurb: The Battle of the Atlantic lasted from the first day of the war to the last — six years of convoy escorts, U-boat hunts, and men dying in freezing water. Monsarrat served on convoy escorts for the entire war and wrote this novel immediately after it ended, drawing on everything he had experienced. It is the finest novel about naval warfare in the English language — the relationship between a destroyer commander and his first lieutenant across six years of sustained, unglamorous, necessary work; the specific texture of North Atlantic weather at its worst; the moral weight of command decisions that get men killed while saving more. Hemingway called it the best sea story since Conrad. Das Boot covers the same Atlantic from inside the German submarine — read both and the Battle of the Atlantic becomes three-dimensional.

books.title: Unbroken
books.author: Laura Hillenbrand
books.blurb: Louis Zamperini was an Olympic runner who became a bombardier, survived a plane crash over the Pacific, spent 47 days on a life raft with sharks circling, was captured by the Japanese, and spent two years in POW camps under a guard who had made it his personal mission to break him. Hillenbrand spent seven years on this biography from her bed while suffering from chronic illness — the specific irony of which is not lost — and the result is the most propulsive WWII narrative on this list. The raft sequence belongs on the Man vs. Nature list. The POW camp sequence belongs on the Redemption list. The whole book belongs here as the entry point for the Pacific prisoner experience that military histories don't cover. Eric Lomax's The Railway Man covers the Burma-Thailand Railway POW experience with equal power and a completely different emotional arc — read both.

books.title: An Army at Dawn
books.author: Rick Atkinson
books.blurb: Three volumes, three Pulitzer Prizes, and the most complete account of the American experience of the European war available in any language. An Army at Dawn covers North Africa — the American Army arriving undertrained and getting comprehensively beaten at Kasserine Pass before learning everything it needed to know about fighting Germans. The Day of Battle covers Sicily and the grinding, costly Italian campaign that strategic logic never fully justified. The Guns at Last Light covers Normandy through the Bulge through the Rhine crossing through the Eagle's Nest. Atkinson spent a decade on each volume and the accumulated achievement is extraordinary — military history written with a novelist's ear for character and a journalist's instinct for the telling detail. The Rommel Papers, Rommel's own diaries edited by Basil Liddell Hart, is the essential German companion.

books.title: The Day of Battle
books.author: Rick Atkinson
books.blurb: Three volumes, three Pulitzer Prizes, and the most complete account of the American experience of the European war available in any language.
