Don’t rely on the movie (although it’s a great adaptation) to give you all the juicy, jolting details. Plus, we love the novel’s weird ending way better. Quote: “I am your number one fan.”

books.title: The Silent Patient
books.author: Alex Michaelides
books.blurb: This one hooked me on the premise alone. Alicia Berenson had what seemed like a great life. She had a great career as a painter and was married to Gabriel, a fashion photographer who was popular in his field. They lived in a big house in a good area of London and got along well. Then one night, Gabriel came home late from work, and Alicia shot him in the face five times. After that, she refused to speak again. Theo Faber, a criminal psychotherapist, has been eager to work with Alicia, but once he gets the chance, cracking the case becomes an obsession that threatens everything else.

books.title: Behind Closed Doors
books.author: B.A. Paris
books.blurb: Jack and Grace Angel appear to have a perfect marriage — the house, the clothes, the dinner parties, the way Jack looks at Grace in public. Every chapter alternates between present and past to reveal why the perfection is a performance. Paris writes domestic thriller at its most propulsive — short chapters, relentless pacing, and a male antagonist who is chilling precisely because he presents so well. The AoM reader will finish this in two sittings without quite meaning to. The dinner conversation is about the gap between how relationships look from outside and what they actually are, which is a more interesting conversation than it sounds when you've just watched someone construct the perfect surface for three hundred pages.

books.title: The Big Sleep
books.author: Raymond Chandler
books.blurb: The world of mysteries is just like the real world in that there are many different opinions, so asking readers where they rank Philip Marlowe on the list of best private investigators will get you different answers. That said, one thing is certain: no one will say Marlowe is not on their list. In The Big Sleep, a dying rich man hires Marlowe to take care of a blackmailer who’s messing with one of his two problematic daughters. The case seems simple, but Marlowe soon finds himself involved in kidnapping, seduction, and murder as he tries to get the job done.

books.title: The Only One Left
books.author: Riley Sager
books.blurb: Riley Sager is the pen name for American author Todd Ritter. Sager’s books are carefully crafted suspense novels that you’ll want to leave the light on after you finish. has caregiver Kit looking after a notorious woman nearing the end of her life. The twist is the woman is thought to have killed her family as a teen. Did she, or is she innocent as she cryptically types on an aging typewriter?

books.title: The Perfect Nanny
books.author: Leïla Slimani
books.blurb: If you’re on the hunt for a can’t-put-down suspense novel, fits the bill. It’s a book that will stick with you, which is why it was a New York Times bestseller. The story is not a new one. A couple on the hunt for a reliable nanny to take care of their children so mom can return to work goes horribly wrong. It’s the opening line that grabs you and doesn’t let go; “The baby is dead.”

books.title: The Girl on the Train
books.author: Robert Klanten, Sven Ehmann & Maximilian Funk (Eds.)
books.blurb: Paula Hawkins’ debut thriller is another best seller brought to the big screen. If you’ve seen the movie, but never read the book, check it out. The book is so much better than the movie. is a first-person novel told from the point of view of three of the book’s main characters. There are enough twists and turns in this thriller to keep you reading and on the edge of your seat even if you’ve seen the film.

books.title: The Guest List
books.author: Lucy Foley
books.blurb: A wedding on an isolated island off the coast of Ireland with a storm rolling in coupled with a guest list of people packing secrets is a perfect recipe for a thriller. British author delivers a wedding weekend to die for. The Guest List is also a Reese’s Book Club pick and made the list of The New York Times’ top thrillers.

books.title: Everyone Here is Lying
books.author: Shari Lapena
books.blurb: are notoriously addictive, but the twists and turns in this suspense novel reach new levels. All the characters are hiding something from husband William to nine-year-old Avery and good luck trying to guess what.

books.title: What Makes Sammy Run?
books.author: Budd Schulberg
books.blurb: Schulberg grew up inside Hollywood — his father ran Paramount — then wrote the novel the industry has never forgiven him for. Sammy Glick rises from Manhattan copy boy to studio head through plagiarism, betrayal, and relentless forward momentum, pausing only long enough to make sure everyone who helped him knows he no longer needs them. The fiction entry on this list, and it also belongs on the Self-Made Men and American Fiction Classics lists, where Sammy takes his place alongside Gatsby as the defining portrait of American ambition as pathology. Schulberg was writing from observation. The character is a composite, and the people he was composited from knew it, and were furious. Published 1941. Still accurate.

books.title: Conversations with Wilder
books.author: Cameron Crowe
books.blurb: Crowe had already made Say Anything and Jerry Maguire when he spent several years interviewing Billy Wilder — then in his late eighties, still sharp, increasingly impatient with the world he found himself in. Wilder made Double Indemnity, Sunset Boulevard, Stalag 17, Some Like It Hot, and The Apartment, spanning every genre and four decades, always with a collaborator writing the dialogue he couldn't write himself in English. The book is structured as a conversation about every film, but what it becomes is an apprenticeship — a young director absorbing everything a master is willing to give before the window closes. More useful than any film school course and more personal than a biography. Read this back to back with the Kurosawa autobiography.

books.title: Adventures in the Screen Trade
books.author: William Goldman
books.blurb: Goldman won two Academy Awards for Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid and All the President's Men, then spent a book explaining exactly why nobody in Hollywood actually knows what they're doing, including him. "Nobody knows anything" is the famous line, and he means it as both confession and accusation: no executive, director, or star can reliably predict what will work, which makes every greenlighting decision a structured gamble and every success partly accidental. Goldman writes about the business the way a good soldier writes about war — from inside it, without illusions, with dark humor and no patience for the mythology. The canonical entry on this list. If you read only one book about Hollywood, this is it.

books.title: Hitchcock/Truffaut
books.author: François Truffaut
books.blurb: In 1962, Truffaut — who had already directed The 400 Blows and Jules and Jim — spent a week at Universal Studios interviewing Hitchcock about every film he had ever made. The resulting book is the most important document in the history of film criticism. It established that Hitchcock was not a commercial entertainer but a serious artist in total control of his medium, and it created the vocabulary critics still use to talk about cinema. The conversation ranges from the silent films to the mechanics behind Psycho and Vertigo, always with Truffaut pushing beneath the surface. If film is your subject, this is the primary source. If you haven't read it, that's the gap in your education this list is here to fix.

books.title: Final Cut
books.author: Stephen Bach
books.blurb: Bach was a senior vice president at United Artists when the studio agreed to finance Michael Cimino's follow-up to The Deer Hunter. The follow-up was Heaven's Gate. Bach watched — from inside the decision-making process, having been one of the decision-makers — as Cimino went 500% over budget and produced a film so catastrophically received it effectively ended United Artists as an independent studio. What makes this the most uncomfortable book on the list is that Bach never lets himself off the hook. He is not writing about a disaster he tried to prevent; he is writing about a disaster he helped enable, explaining exactly why every wrong decision seemed reasonable at the time. The primary source entry. Crosses to the Business and Entrepreneurs lists.

books.title: Making Movies
books.author: Sidney Lumet
books.blurb: Lumet directed 12 Angry Men, Dog Day Afternoon, Serpico, and Network — four of the best American films of the 20th century — then wrote a short book explaining exactly how he did it. Not the business of Hollywood but the craft of directing: how to talk to actors, how to choose a lens, what a rehearsal is actually for, how to cut a scene so the audience doesn't notice the cut. At 220 pages it reads in a sitting, which makes it the accessible entry on this list. What separates it from most craft books is that Lumet has nothing to prove and nothing to sell; the films already exist. He's just explaining them after the fact, and the explanation is as good as the films.

books.title: Pictures at a Revolution
books.author: Mark Harris
books.blurb: The idea seems thin at first—pick five movies and write a book about how they represent Hollywood at the moment—but Mark Harris turns the conceit into something you can’t put down. This examination of The Graduate, Bonnie and Clyde, In the Heat of the Night, Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner?, and Dr. Doolittle is fantastic fun. The sections on Bonnie and Clyde have special resonance around these parts, as the film was written by Esquire alum Robert Benton and David Newman. Meanwhile, the section on Mike Nichols and The Graduate is a high point. And while you're at it, do yourself a favor and pick up Harris’s excellent biography of Nichols. Required reading for anyone who wants to act, direct, or get up on stage and try to be funny.

books.title: Easy Riders, Raging Bulls
books.author: Peter Biskind
books.blurb: The definitive oral history of New Hollywood, covering roughly 1967 to 1980, when a generation of film school kids took over the studios and made the greatest run of American movies since the 1940s — then destroyed it all with cocaine, ego, and a budget overrun in Montana. Biskind got everyone to talk: Coppola, Spielberg, Scorsese, Bogdanovich, Ashby, Altman. The picture that emerges is not flattering to anyone, including the women who tolerated decades of behavior that would end careers today. It reads like a thriller about an empire that burned itself down. If you want to understand why modern Hollywood makes what it makes, this is where that story begins. Cross-references to the Self-Made Men list.

books.title: The Big Picture
books.author: Ben Fritz
books.blurb: After a Sony Pictures hack exposed thousands of internal emails, Wall Street Journal reporter Ben Fritz had access no entertainment journalist had ever had before. What he found was a company — and by extension an entire industry — that had stopped betting on original ideas and started betting on intellectual property: sequels, franchises, adaptations, superheroes. The book is not a polemic but a business analysis, and it's more disturbing for that. Fritz doesn't argue that Hollywood sold out; he shows the specific spreadsheets and boardroom decisions that made the transformation feel rational at every step. Nothing explains the current state of cinema — why theaters look the way they do — more precisely than this. The "why it matters now" entry on this list.

books.title: Something Like an Autobiography
books.author: Akira Kurosawa
books.blurb: Kurosawa covers only the first half of his life — up to Rashomon in 1950, the film that introduced him to the world — and the restraint is the point. Where most director memoirs work backward from fame, this one tracks the formation of an artist before anyone was watching: the painting, the failed writing, the long apprenticeship, the three years spent as an assistant director before he shot a single foot of film himself. What emerges is a portrait of how mastery actually develops, not as inspiration but as accumulation. The prose is spare and precise in exactly the way his films are. Crosses naturally to the Craft, Skill & Mastery list for readers interested less in film specifically than in how excellence is built.

books.title: Story
books.author: Robert McKee
books.blurb: McKee's book has been dismissed by serious writers for thirty years, which is a reliable sign that it threatens something. Story is not a manual for formula screenwriting — it is a structural theory of why narrative works at all, why certain stories produce catharsis and others produce nothing, and what the actual difference between a premise and a theme is. The screenwriting examples are the least interesting parts; the underlying argument about how human beings process meaning through conflict and resolution applies to every form of storytelling. Novelists quote it. Journalists quote it. McKee himself is notoriously difficult in person, which the reader should interpret as additional evidence that he knows he's onto something. The craft entry that earns its place by transcending its genre.

books.title: Sculpting in Time
books.author: Andrei Tarkovsky
books.blurb: Tarkovsky made Andrei Rublev, Solaris, Stalker, and The Sacrifice — films that operate at a different frequency than almost anything else in cinema — then wrote a book explaining his theory of what film is for. His argument is that cinema is the only art form that captures time itself, not space or narrative but duration as experienced by a consciousness, and that this makes it either the most spiritual or the most dangerous medium ever invented. The writing is dense and the book requires patience, but the reader who has found the other entries on this list too thin on ideas will find this one almost too thick. The artsy-fartsy entry, mandatory and unashamed. Read Hitchcock/Truffaut first for contrast — the two men's ideas about cinema are almost perfectly opposed.

books.title: My Lunches with Orson
books.author: Henry Jaglom
books.blurb: In the early 1980s, filmmaker Henry Jaglom started secretly recording his weekly lunches with Orson Welles at Ma Maison in Los Angeles. Welles was old, broke, and unable to get a film made; Jaglom was young and connected and trying to help, unsuccessfully. What survives is seventy-odd conversations in which Welles holds forth on Chaplin, Brando, Dietrich, Kubrick, Hollywood, wine, food, and the specific humiliation of being a genius in a business run by accountants. He is alternately hilarious and devastating. The humor entry on this list — Welles at a table with a good bottle is funnier than most comedians — but underneath the performance is a genuine portrait of what it costs to make uncompromising work. The deep cut. Almost nobody has read it.

books.title: Cadillac Desert
books.author: Marc Reisner
books.blurb: The American West does not have enough water for the civilization built on top of it, and the Bureau of Reclamation spent the better part of the twentieth century pretending otherwise — damming rivers, subsidizing agriculture in deserts, and flooding canyons that John Muir and David Brower spent their careers trying to protect. Reisner spent years documenting the full machinery: the political economy of water in the West, the specific dams that should never have been built, and the specific reckoning that arrives when a civilization runs out of the resource it was built around. Note the political argument throughout — this book is making a case about water, public land, and federal subsidy that has gotten more urgent with every passing decade. Around 582 pages. Cross-seeds with the American West History list, where it belongs equally. The most important book on this list for understanding what the parks are actually protecting.

books.title: The Last Season
books.author: Roy MacGregor
books.blurb: In the summer of 1996, Randy Morgenson — a backcountry ranger with twenty-eight seasons in Kings Canyon and Sequoia National Parks — walked into the Sierra Nevada and never came out. Blehm spent years reconstructing both the search for Morgenson and the life that preceded his disappearance: the specific culture of the NPS backcountry rangers who patrol the remote high country alone for months at a time, the specific wilderness that Morgenson had come to know better than anyone alive, and the marriage that had frayed under the weight of a man who was more at home above ten thousand feet than anywhere else. Around 352 pages and the deep cut entry on this list — largely unknown despite being one of the finest pieces of outdoor journalism published in the last twenty years. The reader who finishes this book will look at the backcountry rangers differently for the rest of his life.

books.title: Empire of Shadows
books.author: George Black
books.blurb: Yellowstone was established as America's first national park in 1872 — before anyone had figured out what a national park was or how to protect it. Black spent years reconstructing the first four decades of the park's existence: the explorers who mapped it, the Army that administered it for thirty years in the absence of any civilian authority, the poachers and market hunters who stripped it of wildlife, and the specific political battles that determined what kind of place it would eventually become. Around 464 pages and the deep cut entry on this list — the most thorough account of Yellowstone's founding era available and largely unknown outside park history circles. The reader who has visited Yellowstone and taken its preservation for granted will finish this book with a more accurate understanding of how close it came to becoming something else entirely.

books.title: The National Parks: America's Best Idea
books.author: Dayton Duncan
books.blurb: Duncan wrote this as the companion to Ken Burns's landmark PBS documentary series and the result stands on its own as the most comprehensive account of the national parks system available: the full arc from the Yosemite Grant in 1864 through the establishment of Yellowstone in 1872, the political battles that saved the Grand Canyon from a dam, the specific men and women who fought to keep the parks public when private development interests had the money and the political connections to win. Around 528 pages and the overview entry on this list — the book that explains what the parks are, how they got there, and why the fight to preserve them never fully ends. The AoM reader who has driven through the parks without knowing their history will read this and understand what he has been standing in.

books.title: The Wilderness Warrior
books.author: Douglas Brinkley
books.blurb: When Roosevelt became president in 1901 he was already the most enthusiastic naturalist in American public life — a man who had spent years in the Dakota Badlands, climbed in the Rockies, and published serious ornithological research. Over the next seven years he used the presidency to protect 230 million acres of American wilderness: national parks, national monuments, national forests, and wildlife refuges created by executive order faster than Congress could object. Brinkley spent years reconstructing the full conservation presidency and the result is the definitive account of how the American parks system was built — the specific battles with mining and timber interests, the alliance with Muir, and the specific executive machinery Roosevelt used to move faster than his opponents. Around 780 pages and worth every one of them. Cross-seeds with the American History and Biography lists.

books.title: The Man Who Walked Through Time
books.author: Colin Fletcher
books.blurb: In 1963, Colin Fletcher became the first person to walk the length of the Grand Canyon — below the rim, on foot, alone, resupplied by air drops — over two months. This is his account of what that journey required and what it produced: the specific physical conditions of the inner canyon, the specific solitude of weeks without human contact, and the specific quality of thought that emerges when a man removes everything except the immediate demands of the terrain. Around 247 pages and the primary source entry on this list — a man describing a specific physical achievement in a specific place with the precision of someone who understood that the Canyon was the subject and he was just the instrument of observation. Fletcher later walked the length of California and wrote The Thousand-Mile Summer, the companion entry for the reader who wants more. The solitude entry and the specific park entry simultaneously.

books.title: Encounters with the Archdruid
books.author: John McPhee
books.blurb: David Brower was the executive director of the Sierra Club, the most effective wilderness advocate of the twentieth century, and the man most responsible for saving the Grand Canyon from a Bureau of Reclamation dam. McPhee took him on three separate wilderness trips — each time in the company of a man whose professional interests conflicted directly with Brower's — and wrote about the conversations. A mining engineer in the Cascades. A resort developer on a Georgia barrier island. Floyd Dominy, the Bureau of Reclamation chief who built Glen Canyon Dam, on a Colorado River raft trip below the canyon he flooded. Around 245 pages and the most formally ingenious book on this list: the political fight over American wilderness rendered as walking debate, with McPhee's surgical prose giving both sides exactly as much room as they need. Cross-seeds with the Essays & Longform Journalism list.

books.title: Edward Abbey's Road
books.author: Edward Abbey
books.blurb: Abbey drove the roads of the American Southwest — through Utah canyon country, across the Sonoran Desert, into the parks and monuments of the Colorado Plateau — and wrote about what he found with the specific combination of fury and joy that made him the most cantankerous voice in American outdoor writing. This 1979 collection is the road trip entry and the humor entry simultaneously: Abbey raging at the motor tourists clogging the parks he loved, at the Park Service accommodating them, at the mining companies waiting outside the boundaries, and at himself for being unable to stay away from any of it. Around 209 pages and the lightest book on this list — light being a relative term for a man who called industrial civilization a suicide pact. Desert Solitaire on the Wilderness & Nature Writing list is Abbey at his most philosophical. This is Abbey at his most entertaining.

books.title: The Motorcycle Diaries
books.author: Ernesto Guevara
books.blurb: In 1952, a 23-year-old Argentine medical student named Ernesto Guevara and his friend Alberto Granado rode a decrepit Norton motorcycle named La Poderosa — The Mighty One — through Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia, and Venezuela, watching it fall apart beneath them and eventually abandoning it entirely. Guevara kept a journal. What he saw — the copper miners, the dispossessed indigenous communities, the specific texture of Latin American poverty — radicalized him completely and produced the man who became Che. This journal, published posthumously, is the primary source document of the Cold War's third world revolutionary politics: the moment a young man from a middle-class Buenos Aires family looked at the continent beneath him and decided something had to change. Jon Lee Anderson's Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life is the definitive biography of everything that followed from this journey.

books.title: Arabian Sands
books.author: Wilfred Thesiger
books.blurb: Cultural explorer Wilfred Thesiger went to the wild deserts of the Middle East to seek out respite from the oppression of society. While there he became the first man to cross the Rub' al Khali, aka 'The Empty Quarter.' Thesiger set out to cross this great expanse and planned to create a map of the region during his journey. He succeeded, crossing the vast unknown of the Empty Quarter not once, but twice, between 1946 and 1949. “For years the Empty Quarter had represented to me the final, unattainable challenge which the desert offered…To others my journey would have little importance. It would produce nothing except a rather inaccurate map which no one was ever likely to use. It was a personal experience, and the reward had been a drink of clean, nearly tasteless water. I was content with that.”

books.title: Blue Highways
books.author: William Least Heat-Moon
books.blurb: Heat-Moon lost his job and his marriage on the same day, got in his van, and spent three months driving the back roads of America — the blue highways, the small lines on old road maps that go through actual towns with actual diners and actual people rather than interstate exchanges. The result is one of the great American road books: a portrait of the country's working people and overlooked places written with the curiosity of a scholar and the eye of a novelist. It captures the specific texture of small-town late-summer America — the county fairgrounds, the grain elevators, the coffee shops where the same men have sat in the same chairs for thirty years — better than almost anything else ever written.

books.title: In a Sunburned Country
books.author: Bill Bryson
books.blurb: Bryson traveled Australia and produced the funniest book on this list — and the most instructive, because Australia turns out to be the most dangerous country on earth, with more species capable of killing you than anywhere else, and Bryson documents this with the cheerful terror of a man who cannot quite believe the place exists. Around 307 pages and the palate cleanser this list needs between Kaplan's geopolitics and Thesiger's austerity. The AoM reader who thinks travel writing is a serious business will find out it doesn't have to be, and the AoM reader who thinks Australia is boring will not think so after page twenty. Notes from a Small Island, Bryson's farewell tour of Britain, is the natural companion for the reader who wants the same voice applied to a colder and rainier landscape.

books.title: In Patagonia
books.author: Bruce Chatwin
books.blurb: Chatwin traveled to the southernmost tip of South America in the 1970s following a fragment of what his grandmother claimed was brontosaurus skin — a piece of hide she kept in a cabinet that had fascinated him since childhood. The journey through one of the emptiest landscapes on earth produces a book that is simultaneously travel writing, biography, natural history, and something genuinely unclassifiable. The Welsh colony in Chubut, the outlaws who fled south at the end of their careers — Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid spent their last years in Patagonia — and the specific quality of light at the end of the world. W.H. Hudson's Far Away and Long Ago, written in 1918 about an Argentine pampas childhood in the 1840s, is the older and quieter companion piece for the reader who wants the continent before the twentieth century touched it.

books.title: Full Tilt
books.author: Dervla Murphy
books.blurb: In 1963, Murphy cycled alone from Dublin to India through Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan — carrying a revolver she used twice, sleeping rough, and writing one of the most matter-of-fact adventure travel books available. Around 251 pages, written without complaint or self-congratulation, which is the specific register that makes it work. The deep cut entry on this list: Murphy is the most underread travel writer of the twentieth century and this is her best book. Where the Indus is Young covers Murphy cycling the Karakoram in winter with her nine-year-old daughter at around 207 pages. Eight Feet in the Andes tracks a similar journey through Peru with a mule. Both belong alongside this one for the reader the voice captures.

books.title: The Great Railway Bazaar
books.author: Paul Theroux
books.blurb: Theroux boarded trains in London in 1973 and rode them through Europe, Turkey, Iran, India, Southeast Asia, Japan, and Siberia — four months, around 25,000 miles, and the book that made literary train travel its own genre. Around 342 pages and the most imitated travel memoir of the twentieth century. Honest about the boredom, the discomfort, the people who are awful, and the places that don't live up to their reputations — which is what separates it from every travel piece written to sell airline tickets. The Old Patagonian Express covers trains from Boston to the tip of South America and belongs alongside it. Dark Star Safari, Theroux overland from Cairo to Cape Town, cross-seeds with the African History reading on this project.

books.title: A Time of Gifts
books.author: Patrick Leigh Fermor
books.blurb: A Time of Gifts recalls an unforgettable journey taken in 1933. Smart yet something of a failure at school (and averse to a beckoning army career), eighteen-year-old Patrick Leigh Fermor resolved to embrace the world, setting out on foot from London to Istanbul. Leigh Fermor plodded up the Rhine and down the Danube with a polymath’s fascination for history, geography, art, and architecture, but most of all for the lives of the people he met along the way, a vast jigsaw of European identities that could not conform to the convenient borders drawn up by peace treaties. During World War II, Leigh Fermor became a national hero in Greece after parachuting into Crete and capturing the commander of the occupying German forces. But his biggest achievement remains the trilogy he began with A Time of Gifts, which traces only the first third of his journey. If it’s a vision of a soon-to-vanish world, first in World War II and then the Cold War, the humanity with which he embraces and documents it all—in some of the most perfect prose in the English language—makes it a fascinating education even now. —Nick Sullivan

books.title: Balkan Ghosts
books.author: Robert Kaplan
books.blurb: Kaplan traveled through Yugoslavia, Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, and Turkey in the late 1980s and produced the most urgently prophetic travel book of the post-Cold War era — reportedly the book that convinced President Clinton ancient ethnic hatreds made Bosnia too complicated to intervene in, a claim Kaplan has spent years partially disputing. Around 307 pages. Note the political perspective explicitly: Kaplan is a foreign policy realist arguing that history and geography determine outcomes more than ideology, and the reader can accept or reject the thesis but cannot ignore it. Written before the Balkan wars and read differently after them. Eastward to Tartary applies the same analytical framework to the Caucasus and Central Asia at around 352 pages and belongs alongside it.

books.title: The Road to Oxiana
books.author: Robert Byron
books.blurb: Byron traveled through Persia and Afghanistan in 1933-34, ostensibly to study Islamic architecture, and produced the book that Bruce Chatwin called his bible and that most serious travel writers rank as the founding document of the form. Around 290 pages of diary entries, letters, and set pieces — the specific frustrations of visa delays and bad hotels alongside precise, ecstatic descriptions of mosque domes and minarets that make the architecture comprehensible as the point of everything. Byron was killed in 1941 when a German submarine torpedoed his ship. He was thirty-five. The Road to Oxiana is the only book he wrote that anyone still reads, and it earns that distinction on every page.

books.title: A Short Walk in the Hindu Kush
books.author: Eric Newby
books.blurb: Newby was a London fashion buyer who had never climbed a mountain when he called his friend Hugh Carless and proposed they climb Mir Samir in the Afghan Hindu Kush. Carless agreed. They got two weeks of climbing instruction in Wales and left. Around 249 pages and the most purely funny mountaineering book ever written — a genuine account of physical incompetence operating at altitude that somehow produces both consistent failure and consistent survival. Wilfred Thesiger, whose Arabian Sands appears elsewhere on this list, makes a cameo appearance near the end and is visibly baffled by them. The humor entry, though humor undersells it: Newby is also recording a Afghanistan that no longer exists, and the comedy and the elegy run together throughout.

books.title: West with the Night
books.author: Beryl Markham
books.blurb: Markham grew up in colonial Kenya, trained racehorses, learned to fly, and in 1936 became the first person to fly solo nonstop east to west across the Atlantic — against prevailing winds, in a single-engine plane, from England to a peat bog in Nova Scotia after the fuel ran out. She wrote this memoir at thirty-nine. Around 293 pages and one of the great pieces of English prose — Hemingway wrote to Maxwell Perkins that Markham wrote better than any of them and that it made him feel ashamed. The unexpected angle entry: neither the Africa books nor the aviation books prepare the reader for the specific quality of her attention to landscape, animals, and solitude. Cross-seeds with the African History and Explorers & Adventurers reading on this project.

books.title: The Places in Between
books.author: Rory Stewart
books.blurb: In January 2002 — two months after the fall of the Taliban — Stewart walked across Afghanistan alone, following roughly the route Babur took in 1504, carrying a stick and staying in village guesthouses along the way. Around 299 pages and the most politically urgent travel memoir on this list: the country the United States was about to spend twenty years and two trillion dollars failing to understand, seen on foot and at ground level by a man who spoke Dari and had already walked across Iran, Pakistan, India, and Nepal. Stewart later became a British MP and governor of a remote Afghan province. The why-it-matters-now entry — written before the occupation and read differently after it ended the way it did.

books.title: Video Night in Kathmandu
books.author: Pico Iyer
books.blurb: Iyer traveled through Bali, China, Tibet, the Philippines, India, Burma, Nepal, Japan, and Hong Kong in the mid-1980s and wrote the most prescient account of globalization-meets-tradition available — the specific cultural collision of American pop culture arriving in places that hadn't asked for it, and the ways those places absorbed, resisted, or transformed what arrived. Around 374 pages and the unexpected angle entry: not the Asia of temples and contemplation but the Asia of Rambo posters in Kathmandu and Michael Jackson in a Manila disco. The collision Iyer documented in 1988 is the dominant fact of the twenty-first century, which makes this one of the few travel books that has gotten more relevant rather than less with age. The Lady and the Monk, Iyer spending a year in Kyoto at around 338 pages, is the right companion for the reader who wants Japan specifically.

books.title: Beloved
books.author: Toni Morrison
books.blurb: A single chapter of Beloved contains more pain than most novels can manage from first page to last. That scene, in which Sethe murders her baby to spare her from a life of enslavement, is horribly, appallingly based in fact. Everything that follows is an attempt to bear the weight of personal and national trauma in fiction. The ghost story, it turns out, is the perfect vehicle. When a young woman appears bearing the name of Sethe’s dead infant, she seems to be a blessing. Soon, however, she begins to consume Sethe’s life, and tears open psychological wounds that the freed characters are desperately trying to hold closed. Morrison’s novel is lyrical and fragmentary (terms that tend to suggest an emphasis on style rather than satisfactory story), but Beloved offers both. It is a truly Great American Novel, both a literary testament to the suffering of millions and one of the most emotionally profound ghost stories ever composed.

books.title: The Handmaid's Tale
books.author: Margaret Atwood
books.blurb: There are few images in literary history more ubiquitous, more recognizable—and dreadfully, more relevant today than ever—than the red-hooded handmaids of Margaret Atwood’s 1985 novel. Set in New England after a totalitarian, patriarchal, theological state has overthrown the United States government, this dystopian story follows Offred, a woman who belongs to the class of handmaids: the only remaining fertile women in society, assigned to the most powerful men in order to bear their children. As the militant, fanatical regime of The Handmaid’s Tale increasingly resembles our present-day America, where reproductive rights are actively being stripped away by the highest court in the land, Atwood’s novel is a thunderous, stark plea for the world to wake up—and also a reminder that the resistance will always persevere. —Lauren Kranc

books.title: Gone Girl
books.author: Gillian Flynn
books.blurb: On the morning of their fifth wedding anniversary Amy Dunne disappears and her husband Nick becomes the prime suspect. The novel alternates between Nick's present-tense account of the investigation and Amy's diary leading up to the disappearance, and the two accounts increasingly refuse to reconcile. Flynn is doing something specific underneath the thriller mechanics — a forensic examination of the performance of marriage, the gap between who people present themselves as and who they actually are, and the specific dangerous intelligence of a woman who has spent her life being underestimated. The most purely entertaining entry on this list and the one with the sharpest lesson: pay attention to who people actually are, not who they perform being. Liane Moriarty's Big Little Lies covers the same domestic territory from the Australian suburbs with more warmth and equal precision.

books.title: Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail
books.author: Cheryl Strayed
books.blurb: Strayed's marriage collapsed, her mother died of cancer, and she developed a heroin habit — at which point she decided to hike 1,100 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail alone, with no hiking experience, carrying a pack she could barely lift off the ground. The memoir covers the hike and the history of the decisions that made it necessary. Cross-seeds with the Man vs. Nature list — this is the same territory as the great outdoor survival narratives, told by a woman who had no business being out there and refused to stop. The lesson for men is not inspirational in the airline-magazine sense. It is specific: grief makes people do extreme things, and sometimes the extreme thing is exactly right. Helen Macdonald's H Is for Hawk covers the same grief-through-obsession territory through the training of a goshawk, for the reader who wants the British literary equivalent.

books.title: Know My Name
books.author: Chanel Miller
books.blurb: Miller was sexually assaulted behind a dumpster at Stanford in 2015 by Brock Turner, who was sentenced to six months in jail and served three. She was known publicly only as Emily Doe until this memoir — her account of the assault, the trial, the victim impact statement that went viral, and the years of recovery afterward. The lesson for men is not abstract. Miller describes in granular detail what the criminal justice process does to survivors, what the defense attorney's questions felt like, and what it means to rebuild an identity after it has been publicly dismantled. Around 350 pages and genuinely harrowing in the precise way that changes how you see the world after reading it. This is the book to read before forming any opinion about how assault cases are handled.

books.title: A Room of One's Own
books.author: Virginia Woolf
books.blurb: Woolf delivered this as two lectures at Cambridge in 1929 and it became the foundational text of women's intellectual life — the argument that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction. Around 100 pages and the shortest entry on this list. The lesson for men is not the feminist argument specifically but the precision of Woolf's thinking about what conditions any human being requires to do creative work — the specific way that material security and psychological space are prerequisites for genuine intellectual achievement. Every man who has ever wondered why a talented woman in his life didn't do more with her ability should read this before forming an opinion. Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique makes the same argument for postwar American suburbia specifically and belongs immediately after.

books.title: Educated
books.author: Tara Westover
books.blurb: Westover grew up in rural Idaho in a survivalist family that kept her out of school, denied her medical care, and subjected her to sustained physical and psychological abuse by an older brother her parents refused to confront. She taught herself enough to get into Brigham Young University, then Cambridge, then Harvard, and wrote this memoir of the distance between where she started and where she arrived. The lesson for men is specific and uncomfortable: the people who were supposed to protect her didn't, and the institutions her family had taught her to distrust were the ones that eventually did. Around 350 pages and one of the most gripping memoirs of the last decade. Jeannette Walls' The Glass Castle covers similar territory — brilliant, irresponsible parents, children who survived them — with more complicated love and less linear resolution.

books.title: The Street
books.author: Ann Petry
books.blurb: Published in 1946, The Street was the first novel by a Black woman to sell over a million copies and has been systematically underread ever since. Lutie Johnson is a single mother in Harlem trying to build a decent life for her son against the specific compound pressure of race, gender, and poverty in postwar New York — the landlord, the superintendent, the bandleader, the street itself, all bearing down simultaneously. Petry writes naturalist fiction in the tradition of Richard Wright but with a clarity about the specific experience of Black women that Wright never achieved. Around 340 pages and the entry most likely to make the reader feel he has discovered something the canon failed to preserve properly. Grace Paley's Collected Stories covers working-class New York women across fifty years of short fiction for the reader who wants to stay in that world.

books.title: Invisible Women
books.author: Caroline Criado Perez
books.blurb: Data journalist Criado Perez covers the specific ways the world has been designed around male bodies and male experience as the default — crash test dummies sized for male bodies, medical research conducted on male subjects, urban planning that assumes car travel over walking, smartphone sizes that don't fit female hands. Around 400 pages and the most empirically grounded entry on this list — Perez is not making a political argument but a data argument, which means the reader who resists political framing will find it considerably harder to dismiss. The lesson is specific: the gender data gap is not a conspiracy but a default, and defaults have costs that fall entirely on the people who don't fit the template. Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist covers the same territory through personal essay for the reader who wants the human face alongside the data.

books.title: A History of the Wife
books.author: Marilyn Yalom
books.blurb: Stanford historian covers the institution of marriage from ancient Mesopotamia through the present — what wives were legally, what they were socially, what they actually were in practice, and how the distance between those three things has driven women's history for five thousand years. Around 400 pages and the best single-volume account of how the institution the AoM demographic is most likely to participate in actually developed, what it was designed to do, and how it became what it currently is. The reader who finishes this book will understand his marriage — or his parents' marriage, or his grandmother's marriage — differently than he did before starting it. Not a polemic. A history. The distinction matters and Yalom maintains it throughout.

books.title: I Feel Bad About My Neck
books.author: Nora Ephron
books.blurb: Ephron spent fifty years as the wittiest woman in American letters — screenwriter, novelist, essayist — and this 2006 collection on aging, maintenance, real estate, and the specific indignities of getting older is among the funniest things she ever wrote. The title essay alone, in which she documents the specific grief of a neck that is no longer something she wants anyone to look at, is a comic masterpiece. Ephron writes about being a woman in a culture obsessed with appearance with the humor of someone who has been paying close attention for fifty years and decided that the only reasonable response is to laugh at it. Around 130 pages and finishable in an evening. The AoM reader who finishes this and wants more should go directly to her novel Heartburn, which covers her husband's affair with the same lethal wit.

books.title: The Quilts of Gee's Bend
books.author: Various, ed. Alvia Wardlaw
books.blurb: The women of Gee's Bend, Alabama — a remote Black community descended from slaves on a single antebellum plantation — have been making quilts since the nineteenth century that the art world only discovered in 2002 and immediately declared among the most significant abstract art in American history. The quilts predate and parallel the Abstract Expressionism happening simultaneously in New York galleries, made by women who had never heard of Rothko and working from the same formal instincts through entirely different means. The book documents the quilts alongside the women who made them and the community that produced both. Around 200 pages and the deepest cut on this list — the entry most likely to make the reader feel he has genuinely discovered something that the art world spent a century failing to look for.
